title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-320-178-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-320-178-001
Stipulation
The parties agreed that Claimant earned an average weekly wage (AWW) of
$752.40.
Issues
1. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
sustained a compensable back injury during the course and scope of his employment
with Employer on June 12, 2025.
2. Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that he is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical benefits that are causally
related to his June 12, 2025 industrial injury.
3. Whether the right to select the authorized treating physician (ATP) has
passed to Claimant.
4. Whether Claimant has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence
that he is entitled to temporary partial disability (TPD) benefits for the period July 15,
2025 until August 25, 2025.
5. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
is entitled to temporary total disability (TTD) benefits for the period August 26, 2025 until
terminated by statute.
Findings of Fact
1. Employer is a family-owned Vietnamese restaurant. Claimant worked for
Employer as a cook and performed general cleaning functions. While working at the
restaurant on June 12, 2025 Claimant attempted to pick up a box of chicken from the
floor. He sought to place the box on a shelf in the walk-in cooler. Claimant was
attempting to perform the task quickly because he was also cooking chicken on the grill.
When picking up the box of chicken he felt a sharp pain in the right side of his lower
back. Claimant immediately reported the injury to his supervisor, Cipriano, but
completed his workday.

2. Claimant purchased naproxen after completing his work shift on June 12,
2025. He did not immediately seek professional medical treatment because he believed
the pain would resolve.
3. Claimant testified that a few days after June 12, 2025 he reported to
Employer’s owner Lien that he suffered a work injury. Lien did not provide Claimant with
a list of any medical providers. Notably, Claimant never received a list of medical
providers from Respondents.
4. Claimant remarked that he began working fewer hours for Employer due
to his back pain. He could not perform his job functions and stand on his feet for long
periods. Lien told Claimant she found someone else to replace him because he
frequently needed to leave work early or could not report to work because of his back
pain. Claimant did not return to work for Employer after August 21, 2025.
5. Employer records reveal Claimant continued to work after June 12, 2025
and earned $752.40 per week until July 14, 2025. Between July 14, 2025 and August
25, 2025 Claimant earned less than $752.40 each week. There are no documented
earnings after August 25, 2025.
6. The record reflects Claimant sought chiropractic treatment from Aim High
Health, LLC on August 18-19, 2025. He reported acute complaints in the lumbar, right
sacroiliac, right posterior pelvis/hip, right buttock, right posterior knee and right calf
“since 3 months ago.” Diagnoses included lumbar facet syndrome, lower back pain,
muscle spasm in the back, and pain in the right leg.
7. On August 22, 2025 Claimant sought emergency treatment from Denver
Health for “back pain” and “sciatica of the right side.” Providers prescribed medications
including cyclobenzaprine and naproxen. Claimant returned to Denver Health on
September 24, 2025 for “leg pain” and “right-sided sciatica.” Although providers ordered
an MRI of the lumbar spine, there is no evidence the diagnostic testing was performed.
8. On September 26, 2025 Claimant reported to the HCA HealthONE clinic
for right-sided lower back pain with right-sided sciatica. Travis Barlock, MD remarked he

was concerned Claimant had a herniated disc in the lower back. He recommended an
MRI and prescribed prednisone, naproxen, and gabapentin. Dr. Barlock also suggested
Claimant follow-up with Susan Nack, MD for his back pain.
9. On October 1, 2025 Claimant completed a Workers’ Claim for
Compensation. He recounted that on June 12, 2025 he was lifting a heavy box of
chicken at work and felt a pop in his back. Claimant noted pain in his lower back, right
leg and foot.
10. On October 1, 2025 Claimant visited physician’s assistant (PA) Jason
Bruno at CareNow Urgent Care for treatment. Claimant reported he had been suffering
from right hip and lower back pain since June 12, 2025 after lifting a box of chicken at
work. Diagnoses included unspecified pain in the right hip and lower back. Providers
ordered physical therapy and an MRI of the right hip. Notably, October 1, 2025 was the
first time a WC164 form was completed by a treating provider. PA Bruno assigned work
restrictions of no lifting, repetitive lifting, carrying, or pushing/pulling in excess of 20
pounds. He determined objective findings were consistent with a work-related
mechanism of injury.
11. In a follow-up visit to CareNow Urgent Care on October 22, 2025 Rachel
Ain, MD noted that the original onset date of Claimant’s lower back pain was June 12,
2025. Claimant reported that the injury occurred when he was picking up a box of
chicken. He felt a crack in his lower back/right hip and subsequently experienced pain.
On physical examination, Dr. Ain noted Claimant had an abnormal gait and posture,
right-sided paraspinal tenderness of the lumbar muscles, tenderness over the right hip,
and abnormality of the lower extremity sensation with some decreased sensation along
the right lateral leg. She determined objective findings were consistent with a work-
related mechanism of injury. Dr. Ain assigned work restrictions of no lifting, repetitive
lifting, carrying, or pushing/pulling in excess of 20 pounds. She also recommended an
MRI and six sessions of physical therapy.
12. On December 2, 2025 Claimant returned to Dr. Ain for an examination. Dr.
Ain continued to note that Claimant suffered unspecified pain of the lower back and right

hip. She again remarked that objective findings were consistent with a work-related
mechanism of injury. Dr. Ain continued work restrictions of no lifting, repetitive lifting,
carrying, or pushing/pulling in excess of 20 pounds.
13. On December 15, 2025 Claimant underwent a right hip MRI. The imaging
revealed a localized area of osteonecrosis of the anterosuperior aspect of the right
femoral head with a small tear of the superior aspect of the right acetabular labrum.
14. On December 23, 2025 Dr. Ain explained she was closing Claimant’s case
with CareNow Urgent Care. She noted that “insurance has not approved any treatment
and this led to a significant delay of care.” Dr. Ain remarked that Claimant paid for the
MRI out of pocket, which demonstrated osteonecrosis of the hip. The imaging
corresponded “to where most of his pain is on exam.” Dr. Ain remarked that Claimant
continued to have pain in the lateral spine “and into the hip in that area, and the hip is
his most likely pain generator.” She closed the case because the symptoms were not
work-related. Dr. Ain determined Claimant had reached maximum medical improvement
(MMI) and released him to full duty employment with no permanent impairment.
15. On January 22, 2026 Claimant underwent an independent medical
examination (IME) with John Raschbacher, M.D. Claimant stated to Dr. Raschbacher he
had not been working since August 2025 and denied having a second job. He described
suffering from back or buttock pain on the right side after lifting a box of chicken
weighing 40-50 pounds from the floor to a shelf in a cooler. The reported symptoms
extended to the right foot and toes. After reviewing medical records and diagnostic
imaging, Dr. Raschbacher concluded Claimant suffered from right hip avascular
necrosis (AVN) or osteonecrosis in the right hip. The condition was not caused by lifting,
bending or twisting because AVN is not typically caused by work-related trauma. He
emphasized that “there is simply no work-relatedness with respect to this diagnosis and
his work activities.” Dr. Raschbacher concluded that, because Claimant’s condition was
not related to his work activities, he should be released to regular employment status
with no restrictions or impairment.

16. On March 4, 2026 Qing-Min Chen, MD completed a medical records
review. Dr. Chen agreed with Dr. Raschbacher that Claimant’s hip AVN was not related
to the June 12, 2025 work injury. However, Dr. Chen believed that “this is likely a red
herring.” He remarked that AVN of the hips does not cause numbness or tingling down
the feet. Claimant’s symptoms were more likely related to a nerve injury or some sort of
nerve irritation. Dr. Chen detailed that the hip joint is a deep structure surrounded by a
capsule. Conditions like AVN of the hip and osteoarthritis are not known to cause nerve
irritation going down the leg. He recommended further evaluation, including an MRI of
the lumbar spine. Dr. Chen expected “some sort of disc herniation on the right at L4-L5
or L5-S1 given the distribution of [Claimant’s] symptoms.” He concluded that the original
injury has always been to the lower back and additional treatment might be warranted.
17. Dr. Raschbacher testified at the hearing in this matter. He maintained
Claimant did not suffer a work injury on June 12, 2025. Dr. Raschbacher further
explained that Claimant was diagnosed with AVN or the loss of blood supply to the
femoral head in the hip. AVN is usually an idiopathic condition not caused by any
specific trauma. While any activity, including work, can aggravate the disease, it does
not cause the condition. Moreover, objective findings did not support a compensable
lower back injury. The straight leg raise and tripod sign tests (that indicate a pinched
nerve) were inconsistent. Furthermore, reflex testing was normal and symmetrical.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured
workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-
40-102(1), C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of
proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S.
A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering
all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197
Colo. 306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004).
The facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either

the rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A
Workers' Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of
the issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might
lead to a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings
as unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’ testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
Compensability
4. For a claim to be compensable under the Act, a claimant has the burden of
proving that he suffered a disability that was proximately caused by an injury arising out
of and within the course and scope of employment. §8-41-301(1)(c) C.R.S.; In re
Swanson, W.C. No. 4-589-645 (ICAO, Sept. 13, 2006). Proof of causation is a threshold
requirement that an injured employee must establish by a preponderance of the evidence
before any compensation is awarded. Faulkner v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 12 P.3d 844,
846 (Colo. App. 2000); Singleton v. Kenya Corp., 961 P.2d 571, 574 (Colo. App. 1998).
The question of causation is generally one of fact for determination by the Judge.
Faulkner, 12 P.3d at 846.
5. A pre-existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim
if the employment aggravates, accelerates or combines with the pre-existing condition to
produce a need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d
999, 1001 (Colo. App. 2004). A compensable injury is one that causes disability or the
need for medical treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 162 Colo. 345, 426 P.2d 194 (1967);
Mailand v. PSC Indus. Outsourcing LP, W.C. No. 4-898-391-01, (ICAO, Aug. 25, 2014).

6. The mere fact a claimant experiences symptoms while performing work
does not require the inference that there has been an aggravation or acceleration of a
pre-existing condition. See Cotts v. Exempla, Inc., W.C. No. 4-606-563 (ICAO, Aug. 18,
2005). Rather, the symptoms could represent the “logical and recurrent consequence” of
the pre-existing condition. See F.R. Orr Construction v. Rinta, 717 P.2d 965 (Colo. App.
1985); Chasteen v. King Soopers, Inc., W.C. No. 4-445-608 (ICAO, Apr. 10, 2008). As
explained in Scully v. Hooters of Colorado Springs, W.C. No. 4-745-712 (ICAO, Oct. 27,
2008), simply because a claimant’s symptoms arise after the performance of a job
function does not necessarily create a causal relationship based on temporal proximity.
The panel in Scully noted that “correlation is not causation,” and merely because a
coincidental correlation exists between the claimant’s work and symptoms does not mean
there is a causal connection between the claimant’s injury and work activities.
7. Claimant has established it is more probably true than not that he suffered
a compensable lower back injury during the course and scope of employment with
Employer on June 12, 2025. Claimant credibly testified that he experienced immediate
lower back pain on June 12, 2025 while lifting a box of chicken to place it on a shelf in
Employer’s cooler. He believed the pain would resolve and waited to seek professional
medical care in the form of chiropractic treatment on August 18, 2025. He continued to
experience pain that necessitated multiple emergency room visits at Denver Health.
Claimant’s testimony is consistent with the medical records and reflects that he regularly
reported back pain and sciatica on the right side to his providers.
8. After a right hip MRI discovered an AVN condition, Dr. Ain concluded
Claimant’s continuing pain was not related to his reported June 12, 2025 work injury.
She commented that Claimant continued to have pain in the lateral spine “and into the
hip in that area, and the hip is his most likely pain generator.” Similarly, Dr.
Raschbacher reasoned that Claimant’s AVN was not caused by lifting, bending or
twisting because AVN is not typically caused by work-related trauma. He emphasized
that “there is simply no work-relatedness with respect to this diagnosis and his work
activities.” Nevertheless, medical records from treating providers and Dr. Raschbacher’s
IME report consistently document Claimant’s complaints of back pain with right-sided
radiation down the leg.

9. Although Dr. Chen agreed that Claimant’s AVN was unrelated to his work
activities, he reasoned Claimant had sustained a lower back injury on June 12, 2025.
Claimant’s consistent report of pain in the lower back and distribution of symptoms is
consistent with Claimant’s alleged injury. While Claimant may also suffer from a non-
work-related AVN or osteonecrosis condition as documented in the right hip MRI, that
finding is not pertinent to the determination of whether Claimant suffered an injury to his
lower back on June 12, 2025. Notably, Dr. Chen believed that “this is likely a red
herring.” Dr. Chen explained that AVN of the hips does not cause numbness or tingling
down into the feet. Claimant’s symptoms are thus more likely related to a nerve injury or
some sort of nerve irritation. Dr. Chen detailed that the hip joint is a deep structure
surrounded by a capsule. He expected “some sort of disc herniation on the right at L4-
L5 or L5-S1 given the distribution of [Claimant’s] symptoms.” Dr. Chen concluded that
the original injury has always been to the lower back and additional treatment might be
warranted.
10. Dr. Raschbacher’s opinion that Claimant did not sustain a compensable
work injury on June 12, 2025 because the AVN was idiopathic is not persuasive.
Although he acknowledged that Claimant reported back pain with radiation into the leg,
both in the medical records and during the IME, he failed to provide any causation
analysis regarding the lowerback condition in his written report. His conclusions, like
those of Dr. Ain, rested largely on the assumption that Claimant’s righthip condition was
not work related. However, the evidence demonstrates that it is more likely than not that
Claimant’s injury on June 12, 2025 involved the lower back rather than the hip. Dr.
‑
Chen’s opinion aligns with the medical records and Claimant’s testimony. Accordingly,
Claimant’s June 12, 2025 work activities caused, aggravated, accelerated or combined
with his pre-existing lower back condition to produce a need for medical treatment.
Medical Benefits/Right of Selection
11. Respondents are liable for authorized medical treatment that is reasonable
and necessary to cure or relieve the effects of an industrial injury. §8-42101(1)(a),
C.R.S.; Colorado Comp. Ins. Auth. v. Nofio, 886 P.2d 714, 716 (Colo. 1994). A pre-

existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the employment
aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing condition to produce a need
for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d 999, 1001 (Colo.
App. 2004). The question of whether a particular disability is the result of the natural
progression of a pre-existing condition, or the subsequent aggravation or acceleration of
that condition, is itself a question of fact. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App. 2001). Finally, the determination of whether a
particular treatment modality is reasonable and necessary to treat an industrial injury is
a factual determination for the ALJ. In re Parker, W.C. No. 4-517-537 (ICAO, May 31,
2006); In re Frazier, W.C. No. 3-920-202 (ICAO, Nov. 13, 2000).
12. Section 8-41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. requires that an injury be “proximately
caused by an injury or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of the
employee’s employment.” Thus, the claimant is required to prove a direct causal
relationship between the injury and the disability and need for treatment. However, the
industrial injury need not be the sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant,
direct, and consequential factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
13. Section 8-43-404(5)(a), C.R.S. permits an employer or insurer to select the
treating physician in the first instance. Yeck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 996 P.2d, 228,
229 (Colo. App. 1999). However, the Colorado Workers’ Compensation Act requires
respondents to provide injured workers with a list of at least four designated treatment
providers. §8-43-404(5)(a)(I)(A), C.R.S. Specifically, if the employer or insurer fails to
provide an injured worker with a list of at least four physicians or corporate medical
providers, “the employee shall have the right to select a physician.” §8-43-404(5)(a)(I)(A),
C.R.S. W.C.R.P. Rule 8-2 further clarifies that once an employer is on notice that an on-
the-job injury has occurred, “the employer shall provide the injured worker with a written
list of designated providers.” W.C.R.P. Rule 8-2(E) additionally provides that the remedy
for failure to comply with the preceding requirement is that “the injured worker may select
an authorized treating physician of the worker’s choosing.”

14. The term “select,” is unambiguous and should be construed to mean “the
act of making a choice or picking out a preference from among several alternatives.”
Squitieri v. Tayco Screen Printing, Inc., WC 4-421-960 (ICAO Sept. 18, 2000); see In re
Loy, W.C. No. 4-972-625-01 (ICAO, Feb. 19, 2016). Thus, a claimant “selects” a
physician when she “demonstrates by words or conduct that [she] has chosen a
physician to treat the industrial injury.” Williams v. Halliburton Energy Services, WC 4-
995-888-01 (ICAO, Oct. 28, 2016); Loy v. Dillon Companies, W.C. No. 4-972-625 (Feb.
19, 2016). The question of whether the claimant selected a particular physician as the
ATP is one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Squitieri v. Tayco Screen Printing, Inc.,
WC 4-421-960 (ICAO, Sept. 18, 2000).
15. Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that the right to
select an ATP passed to him through Respondents’ failure to provide a written list of at
least four designated medical providers in violation of §8-43-404(5), C.R.S. and WCRP
Rule 8-2. The record reflects that Claimant did not receive a list of at least four
designated medical providers. Respondents have thus not met the requirements of
WCRP 8-2 by tendering a written letter within seven days of the injury. Because
Respondents failed to provide Claimant with a written list of designated providers, the
right to select an ATP passed to him.
16. Claimant has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that he is
entitled to reasonable, necessary and causally related medical benefits for his June 12,
2025 industrial injury. Claimant sought medical treatment and diagnostic imaging on his
own from Aim High Health, LLC, Denver Health, HCA HealthONE, CareNow Urgent
Care, and SimonMed. These providers offered treatment for Claimant’s lower back and
imaging in effort to diagnose his condition. The preceding providers delivered
reasonable, necessary, and related medical care to Claimant. He has thus proven by a
preponderance of the evidence that all of his medical care was authorized, reasonable,
necessary and causally related to his work-related June 12, 2025 lower back injury.
Temporary Partial Disability Benefits

17. Section 8-42-106(1), C.R.S., provides for an award of TPD benefits to be
based on the difference between the claimant’s AWW at the time of injury and the
earnings during the continuance of the temporary partial disability. In order to receive
TPD benefits the claimant must establish the injury caused the disability and
consequent partial wage loss. §8-42-103(1), C.R.S.; see Safeway Stores, Inc. v.
Husson, 732 P.2d 1244 (Colo. App. 1986) (temporary partial compensation benefits are
designed as a partial substitute for lost wages or impaired earning capacity arising from
a compensable injury). When an employee is only partially disabled, TPD benefits are
calculated by determining 66 2/3 of the difference between the employee’s AWW at the
time of the injury and the employee’s AWW during the continuance of the temporary
partial disability. See §8-42-106(1), C.R.S.
18. Claimant has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that he is
entitled to receive TPD benefits for the period July 15, 2025 through August 25, 2025.
Claimant began earning reduced wages as a result of the June 12, 2025 compensable
injury from July 15, 2025 through August 25, 2025, which constitutes a total of six
weeks. Based on the stipulated AWW of $752.40, Claimant would have received
$4,514.40 in gross earnings ($752.40 x 6). However, based on the earnings records in
evidence, Claimant earned a total of $738.30 in wages. Two-thirds of the difference
between $4,514.40 and $738.30 is $2,517.40. Thus, Claimant is entitled to $2,517.40 in
TPD benefits.
Temporary Total Disability Benefits
19. To prove entitlement to TTD benefits a claimant must demonstrate that the
industrial injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he left work as a
result of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss. See §8-42-105,
C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102 P.3d 323 (Colo. 2004); City of Colorado
Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d 637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-
103(1)(a), C.R.S. requires the claimant to establish a causal connection between a
work-related injury and a subsequent wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. The
term “disability” connotes two elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or
restriction of bodily function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning capacity as
demonstrated by claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace

Electric, 971 P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work, or by restrictions that impair
the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her regular employment.
Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo. App. 1998) (citing Ricks v.
Indus. Claim Appeals Off., P.2d 1118 (Colo. App. 1991)). Because there is no
requirement that a claimant must produce evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s
testimony alone is sufficient to demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952
P.2d 831, 833 (Colo. App. 1997). TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence
of any of the following: (1) the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to
regular or modified employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a
written release to return to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the
employee a written release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered
in writing and the employee fails to begin the employment. §8-42-105(3)(a)-(d), C.R.S.
20. Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he is
entitled to receive TTD benefits from August 26, 2025 until terminated by statute.
Claimant’s credible testimony demonstrates that he was terminated from his
employment as of August 25, 2025 due to his inability to complete a full workday or
perform his prior work with Employer because of his back injury. Claimant’s testimony
was further supported by the imposition of work restrictions beginning on October 1,
2025 when the WC164 form was first completed. Based on an AWW of $752.40,
Claimant’s TTD rate is $501.60. Respondents thus owe TTD benefits beginning August
26, 2025 and continuing until terminated by statute at the rate of $501.60.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant suffered a compensable lower back injury while working for
Employer on June 12, 2025.
2. The right to select an ATP has passed to Claimant. Claimant shall notify
Respondents of his ATP choice within 20 days of the date this order is served.
3. Claimant is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical benefits related
to his June 12, 2025 work injury. Claimant’s treatment at Aim High Health, LLC, Denver

Health, HCA HealthONE, CareNow Urgent Care, and SimonMed was reasonable,
necessary, and related to his June 12, 2025 work injury. Respondents shall pay for the
associated costs of the treatment, as well as other reasonable, necessary and related
medical care.
4. Claimant earned an AWW of $752.40.
5. Claimant is entitled to receive TPD benefits from July 15, 2025 through
August 25, 2025. Respondents shall pay Claimant total TPD benefits of $2,517.40.
6. Respondents shall pay Claimant TTD benefits at a rate of $501.60
beginning August 26, 2025 and continuing until terminated by statute.
7. Respondents shall pay statutory interest at a rate of 8% per annum on
compensation benefits not paid when due.
8. Any issues not resolved in this Order are reserved for future
determination.
If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review
the order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That
you mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For
statutory reference, see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding
procedures to follow when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may
access a petition to review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-285-632-002
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-285-632-002
Issue
Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that the
right foot reconstruction surgery recommended by authorized treating physician (ATP)
Stuart Myers, MD is reasonable, necessary, and causally related to her August 25, 2024
industrial injury.
Findings of Fact
1. On August 25, 2024 Claimant was working as a respiratory therapist on the
Medical/Surgical Acute Care Unit at Employer’s hospital when the code blue alarm was
activated. While running to respond to the code as part of her job duties, Claimant
experienced a sudden pop or pull sensation in her right foot and ankle. She immediately
experienced acute pain.
2. On September 25, 2024 Claimant underwent a right foot MRI with Shayan
Vadie, MD at Spectrum Medical Imaging. The MRI revealed moderate posterior tibialis
tendinosis and tenosynovitis with low-grade partial-thickness interstitial tearing, along
with mild subcutaneous soft tissue edema along the medial ankle.
3. On October 7, 2024 Claimant underwent an initial occupational medical
evaluation with Christian Updike, MD at UCHealth Occupational Medicine. He diagnosed
a severe ankle strain with small tears and determined the mechanism of injury was
consistent with Claimant’s work activities.
4. On October 30, 2024 Claimant visited Stuart Myers, MD for an initial
orthopedic evaluation of her right ankle. Dr. Myers noted that Claimant had been wearing
a boot provided by occupational medicine. However, she continued to experience pain
after 5-6 hours of walking. Dr. Myers diagnosed Claimant with tibial tendon dysfunction.
He recommended orthotics and bracing.
5. On December 4, 2024 Claimant began undergoing physical therapy at
CACC Physical Therapy.

6. Claimant returned to Dr. Myers on December 11, 2024. She reported
continuing pain in her right ankle after 3-4 hours of walking with a lace up brace. Dr. Myers
recommended PRP injections to the right ankle.
7. On January 27, 2025 Dr. Myers administered Claimant’s first PRP injection
under ultrasound guidance into the posterior tibial tendon sheath. On May 5, 2025
Claimant underwent a second PRP injection because of partial but incomplete relief from
the first injection. Later in May 2025 Claimant received a third PRP injection. However, it
also did not provide significant relief.
8. Despite the preceding extensive conservative treatment spanning more
than one year, Claimant continued to experience persistent pain, swelling, the inability to
perform a single-leg heel rise, and an antalgic gait. As of her follow-up appointment with
Dr. Myers on January 6, 2026, she continued to have ankle pain and swelling, was unable
to perform a single-leg heel rise and remained unable to return to work.
9. On October 13, 2025 Respondents retained Nathan C. Hammel, MD to
conduct a records review of Claimant’s claim. Dr. Hammel agreed that the partial
thickness tear from Claimant’s September MRI and her more recent medical records
revealed consistency between the mechanism of injury and her symptoms. He was not
certain if Claimant had reached maximum medical improvement (MMI), although he
thought she had been improving and could be eased back into her regular job duties. Dr.
Hammel recommended additional PRP injections because they provided objective benefit
as measured by reduction in immobilization and decreasing pain scores.
10. In response to Dr. Hammel’s records review report, Respondents filed a
general admission of liability (GAL) on November 7, 2025 recognizing that she was
injured on August 25, 2024.
11. On December 29, 2025 Claimant underwent a repeat MRI of the right ankle.
Douglas Watt, MD remarked that the imaging revealed a full-thickness tear of the
posterior tibial tendon. The imaging reflects progression from the partial-thickness
interstitial tear identified in September 2024.
12. On January 6, 2026 Dr. Myers reviewed the December 29, 2025 MRI and
recommended surgical reconstruction of the right foot. The complete tear of the posterior
tibial tendon could not be repaired by simple suturing. Expected recovery included six
2

weeks of non-weight bearing, followed by one month in a walking boot and transitioning
to a lace-up brace.
13. On January 10, 2026 Respondents obtained a second records review from
Dr. Hammel. He determined that, while the right foot reconstruction surgery is reasonable
and necessary, it is not causally related to Claimant’s work injury. Dr. Hammel reasoned
that, because Claimant has remained off work since the date of injury and the tendon
progressed to a full-thickness tear, the change was attributable to a pre-existing
degenerative condition. He further remarked that the initial MRI showing tendinosis
reflected a "chronic pre-existing degenerative condition," and the work injury only caused
the acute tenosynovitis component.
14. On April 6, 2026 Respondents conducted the post-hearing evidentiary
deposition of Dr. Hammel. Dr. Hammel explained that Claimant initially suffered from
posterior tibial tendonitis. This was based on his review of Claimant’s MRI that showed
fluid around the posterior tibial tendon and its tendon sheath. Claimant’s flat-footedness
was a pre-existing, degenerative, condition that would lead to an eventual full-thickness,
acute-type injury. PRP injections benefited Claimant because they appeared to have the
effect of muting an acute inflammatory response.
15. Dr. Hammel testified that Claimant’s December 29, 2025 MRI showed a full-
thickness tear across the posterior tibial tendon with retraction. He explained that the
initial September 25, 2024 MRI had revealed interstitial partial tearing of the same tendon,
similar to a rope bundle that is beginning to fray. On the original MRI, the rope bundle
was still intact, though there were parts of the outside of the rope that were beginning to
fray. However, by the time of the second MRI in December 2025, the rope had entirely
snapped and was thus no longer functioning.
16. Based on Claimant’s December 2025 MRI findings, Dr. Hammel determined
her condition was not causally related to the work injury. The interstitial partial thickness
tearing was a pre-existing, degenerative condition that progressed to a full-thickness
rupture.
17. Dr. Hammel further explained that the progression of an underlying pre-
existing condition, in the absence of continued trauma or a second injury, reflects that
Claimant’s rupture was from the progression of the underlying condition. The type of
3

progression could be caused by simply walking or stair climbing. Dr. Hammel concluded
that Claimant’s original work injury did not worsen or accelerate Claimant’s degenerative
process.
18. On March 16, 2026 Claimant underwent an independent medical
examination (IME) with Mark Winslow, DO. He concluded that Claimant’s progression
from a partial-thickness tear to a full-thickness tear was the direct result of her August 25,
2024 work-related injury. Dr. Winslow detailed the following:
• Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is a progressive condition, involving
degenerative tendinosis with disruption in collagen bundle structure and
orientation. It compromises the tendon and predisposes it to rupture under
physiologic loads.
• The hypovascularity of the posterior tibial tendon in the region behind the medial
malleolus predisposes this region specifically to degenerative disorders and
rupture.
• The progression of a partial tear to a complete tear does not require additional
trauma. The pathologic changes in posterior tibial tendon dysfunction can lead to
tendon degeneration with an insufficient repair response, culminating in rupture
under normal activities of daily living and not just occupational activities.
Claimant’s physical examination findings including significant acquired pronation
of the right foot since the date of injury, antalgic gait, medial arch tenderness, pain
with resisted dorsiflexion, and asymmetric shoe wear on the right are consistent
with progressive posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
19. Dr. Winslow explained that the present matter “presents a clinically
straightforward progression of a work-related posterior tibial tendon injury.” He recounted
that Claimant sustained an acute injury at work on August 25, 2024 to a previously
asymptomatic foot. An MRI revealed a partial-thickness tear of the posterior tibial tendon.
Despite conservative treatment, including rest, immobilization, physical therapy, and
three PRP injections, her symptoms persisted and the tear progressed to a complete, full
thickness rupture as documented on the December 2025 MRI.
20. Dr. Winslow noted that the denial of surgery is based on the opinion that the
progression of the tear was unrelated to the original injury because Claimant was not
4

working during the time when the tear progressed. However, Dr. Winslow commented
that the reasoning is not supported by the medical literature regarding the natural history
of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
21. Dr. Winslow maintained that Claimant’s absence from work was irrelevant
to a causation analysis. Notably, the posterior tibial tendon functions as the main dynamic
stabilizing tendon of the medial longitudinal arch. It absorbs shock during heel strike,
stabilizes the foot during midstance, and generates force during heel and toe lift. The
preceding functions are required for basic ambulation, not just occupational activities. The
tendon was thus under a physiologic load throughout Claimant’s activities of daily living
regardless of her work status.
22. Dr. Winslow also noted that Claimant’s treating physicians, Dr. Updike and
Dr. Myers, have consistently maintained that Claimant’s condition constitutes a
progression of the initial work injury and have recommended surgery. Their opinions are
consistent with the established medical literature on the natural history of posterior tibial
tendon dysfunction. Notably, Dr. Winslow remarked that the medical literature supports
surgical intervention for complete posterior tibial tendon tears when conservative
treatment has failed after three to six months. Notably, Claimant underwent more than a
year of conservative treatment including immobilization, physical therapy, and three PRP
injections without achieving adequate relief or functional improvement.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured workers
at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-40-102(1),
C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of
the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197 Colo.
306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004). The
5

facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either the
rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A Workers'
Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of the
issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might lead to
a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as
unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
4. Respondents are liable for authorized medical treatment that is reasonable
and necessary to cure or relieve the effects of an industrial injury. §8-42101(1)(a), C.R.S.;
Colorado Comp. Ins. Auth. v. Nofio, 886 P.2d 714, 716 (Colo. 1994). A pre-existing
condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the employment
aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing condition to produce a need
for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d 999, 1001 (Colo.
App. 2004). The question of whether a particular disability is the result of the natural
progression of a pre-existing condition, or the subsequent aggravation or acceleration of
that condition, is itself a question of fact. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App. 2001). Finally, the determination of whether a
particular treatment modality is reasonable and necessary to treat an industrial injury is a
factual determination for the ALJ. In re Parker, W.C. No. 4-517-537 (ICAO, May 31, 2006);
In re Frazier, W.C. No. 3-920-202 (ICAO, Nov. 13, 2000).
5. Section 8-41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. requires that an injury be “proximately
caused by an injury or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of the
employee’s employment.” Thus, the claimant is required to prove a direct causal
6

relationship between the injury and the disability and need for treatment. However, the
industrial injury need not be the sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant,
direct, and consequential factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
6. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that the right
foot reconstruction surgery recommended by ATP Dr. Myers is reasonable, necessary,
and causally related to her August 25, 2024 industrial injury. Initially, on August 25, 2024,
while running to respond to an emergency at work, Claimant experienced a sudden pop
or pull sensation in her right foot and ankle. A September 25, 2024 MRI of Claimant’s
right foot revealed moderate posterior tibialis tendinosis and tenosynovitis with low-grade
partial-thickness interstitial tearing. Claimant subsequently underwent extensive
conservative treatment including physical therapy and three PRP injections.
Nevertheless, Claimant continued to experience persistent pain and swelling. On
December 29, 2025 Claimant underwent a repeat MRI of the right ankle that revealed a
full-thickness tear of the posterior tibial tendon. The imaging documented progression
from the partial-thickness interstitial tear identified in September 2024. The resolution of
the present matter is contingent on whether the progression from a partial to a full-
thickness tear is causally connected to Claimant’s initial work injury on August 25, 2024
or constituted the natural progression of a pre-existing condition. Based on the
determinations of Claimant’s treating physicians and the persuasive opinion of Dr.
Winslow, Claimant’s full-thickness tear and need for surgery are causally related to her
August 25, 2024 industrial injury.
7. Both of Claimant’s treating physicians have repeatedly attributed her
condition to the August 25, 2024 work injury. They have examined Claimant and reviewed
her diagnostic imaging. Dr. Updike documented at each visit from October 2024 through
December 2025 that the mechanism of injury was consistent with a work-related incident.
Dr. Myers diagnosed a right ankle work injury at every encounter from October 2024
through January 2026 and has recognized the relationship between the injury and
Claimant’s continuing condition. He recommended surgical reconstruction of the right
7

foot. The complete tear of the posterior tibial tendon could not be repaired by simple
suturing.
8. In contrast, Dr. Hammel determined that, while the recommended right foot
reconstruction surgery is reasonable and necessary, it is not causally related to
Claimant’s work injury. He reasoned that, because Claimant has remained off work since
the date of injury and the tendon progressed to a full-thickness tear, the progression was
attributable to a pre-existing degenerative condition. Dr. Hammel remarked that the
progression of an underlying, pre-existing condition, in the absence of continued trauma
or a second injury, reflects that Claimant’s rupture was from the advancement of the
underlying condition. The type of worsening could be caused by simply walking or stair
climbing. Dr. Hammel concluded that Claimant’s original work injury did not worsen or
accelerate the degenerative process.
9. Despite Dr. Hammel’s conclusion, Dr. Winslow agreed with Claimant’s
treating physicians and determined that the progression from a partial-thickness tear to a
full-thickness tear was the direct result of Claimant’s August 25, 2024 work-related injury.
Dr. Winslow noted that the denial of surgery was based on the view that the progression
of the tear was unrelated to the original injury because Claimant was not working during
the time when the tear worsened. However, the preceding reasoning is not supported by
the medical literature regarding the natural history of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
10. Dr. Winslow remarked that posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is a
progressive condition, involving degenerative tendinosis with disruption in collagen
bundle structure and orientation. Despite conservative treatment, including rest,
immobilization, physical therapy, and three PRP injections, Claimant’s symptoms
persisted and the tear progressed to a complete, full thickness rupture as documented on
the December 2025 MRI. Dr. Winslow noted that Claimant’s treating physicians, Dr.
Updike and Dr. Myers, have consistently maintained that Claimant’s condition constitutes
a progression of the initial work injury and recommended surgery. Their opinions follow
the established medical literature on the natural history of posterior tibial tendon
dysfunction. Notably, Dr. Winslow remarked that the medical literature supports surgical
intervention for complete posterior tibial tendon tears when conservative treatment has
failed after three to six months.
8

11. The progression of Claimant’s posterior tibial tendon injury from a partial to
a complete tear is the natural and expected consequence of her August 25, 2024 work
injury. Claimant’s treating physicians and Dr. Winslow support the preceding conclusion.
Respondent’s denial of Claimant’s surgical request is based on a paper review by a
physician who has never examined her and whose causation reasoning is contrary to
established medical literature. Accordingly, Claimant’s full-thickness tear and need for
surgery is reasonable, necessary and causally related to her August 25, 2024 industrial
injury. Claimant’s request for the right foot reconstruction surgery recommended by Dr.
Myers is thus authorized.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant has demonstrated that the right foot reconstruction surgery
recommended by Dr. Myers is authorized, reasonable, necessary, and causally related
to her August 25, 2024 industrial injury.
2. All matters not resolved in this Order are resolved for future determination.
9

If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review the

Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after

Based on the evidence presented at hearing, it is hereby ordered:
1. The respondents are liable for medical treatment reasonably needed to

occurrence of a compensable injury does not compel the ALJ to approve all requested
treatment. Where the claimant’s entitlement to medical benefits is disputed, the claimant
must prove the treatment is reasonably needed and causally related to the industrial

preponderance of the evidence. Snyder v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 942 P.2d
1337 (Colo. App. 1997).
2. Claimant proved the TFCC surgery recommended by Dr. Larsen is
reasonably needed and causally related to the work accident. Claimant suffered an

within a month of the accident showed a TFCC tear and an effusion consistent with a
relatively recent, traumatic injury. Dr. Larsen’s opinions are credible and more
persuasive than the contrary opinions of Dr. Worrell. Dr. Larsen credibly opined that the

determination of causation. There is no persuasive evidence of any pre-existing right
wrist or forearm problems, nor of any alternate causal factor besides the work accident.
Dr. Larsen credibly opined that Claimant has exhausted conservative treatment and
surgery is the reasonable next step.

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-285-479-003
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-285-479-003
Issues
Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that she
⮚
is entitled to Temporary Total Disability (TTD) benefits from November 15, 20241 until
November 3, 2025.
If Claimant established entitlement to TTD benefits, whether Respondents
⮚
established by a preponderance of the evidence that Claimant was responsible for her
termination of employment on November 13, 2024, and, therefore, pursuant to section
8-43-103(1)(g), C.R.S., is not entitled to TTD.
Stipulation
1. The parties stipulated that Claimant’s average weekly wage is $1070.19.
Findings of Fact
1. Employer sells roof gutter systems meant to protect gutters from becoming
blocked by leaves and other debris.
1 At hearing Claimant’s counsel originally requested the TTD period began on
November 15, 2024. When Respondents stated that Claimant was terminated on
November 13, 2024, Claimant requested to modify her TTD request to November 13,
2024. The evidence admitted at hearing shows that while Claimant was terminated on
November 13, 2024, she was paid through November 14, 2024. Ex. I. Therefore, the
ALJ concludes that if Claimant is entitled to TTD benefits, the TTD period should begin
November 15, 2024, the first day she was no longer paid by Employer.
1

2. Claimant was hired by Employer on September 21, 2022. Claimant was originally
hired as a promoter working home shows; Claimant was later promoted to field event
marketing manager. Claimant’s job duties included scheduling field events, working field
events, and hiring promoters for field events. While working at field events, Claimant
was required to set up and take down displays including items weighing up to 30
pounds.
3. Claimant suffered an admitted work injury to her lower back on March 27, 2024.
Claimant was ultimately given work restrictions of lifting no more than 10 pounds.
4. Claimant was given job performance goals based in part on the number of leads
she produced at field events. Particularly, Claimant was to meet certain goals
concerning the cost per lead, which cost included the cost of the field event generating
the leads.
5. Claimant’s work restrictions increased Claimant’s cost per lead, as she had to
hire a promoter to help set up and take down displays at field events and the cost of that
promoter was factored into the cost per lead. Prior to her work injury, Claimant was able
to work field events on her own, lowering the cost per lead.
6. Claimant was unable to meet her cost-per-lead job performance goals both
before and after her work injury. Claimant received two disciplinary actions for not
meeting her performance goals.
7. Claimant was terminated by Employer on November 13, 2024.
8. Claimant credibly testified that at the time she was terminated she was told
Employer had eliminated all field event marketing manager positions across the country.
9. Clayton Stackpole, Employer’s Director of Event Marketing during the time period
in question, testified for Respondents. Mr. Stackpole indirectly supervised Claimant and
was in weekly contact with Claimant’s direct supervisor Joey Egbert. Mr. Stackpole
testified that Claimant received written warnings in October 2023 and May 2024 for not
meeting her performance goals.
2

10. Mr. Stackpole testified that field event marketing managers were expected to
generate leads at a cost of less than $400.00 per lead. Claimant was generating leads
at a cost of more than $600.00 per lead. This was the reason for Claimant’s written
warnings. In his opinion, Claimant was terminated for failure to meet her performance
metrics, not because the position of field event marketing manager was eliminated by
Employer.
11. Mr. Stackpole testified that some of the job duties previously performed by field
event marketing managers are now completed remotely by regional managers for
Employer.
12. Employer’s records show the “main reason for the separation of this employee” is
“Position Elimination.” Ex. I.
13. Under “provide more information on the separation reason” Mr. Stackpole wrote
“[p]erformance and documentation throughout the year as well as position elimination in
this branch for restructure plans into 2025 due to performance[.]” Ex. I.
14. Under “Transaction Change History” the “select main reason for the separation of
this employee” was changed from “Unsatisfactory performance” to “Position
Elimination.” Ex. I. That change was made by and was approved by
. Id.
15. In an email to , Mr. Stackpole wrote that he spoke to Claimant telling
her that “due to performance the department in this location has been struggling to be
profitable as a business” and “Colorado along with some others are removing the local
FEM role from the location and will be operated by a senior level manager as it was in
the past prior to the introduction of the FEM role and a reduction in event operations
and activity.” Ex. I (emphasis added). Attached to the email from Mr. Stackpole is an
email from Mr. Egbert sent at 12:22 AM of the day of Claimant’s termination stating
“Here is what I dug up for . I feel like there is more, but this is what i could easily
locate.” Id.
3

16. Based on the documentary evidence provided by Respondents, the ALJ finds it
more likely than not that Employer was eliminating Claimant’s position and sought a
pretextual performance reason for her termination by “digging up” Claimant’s previous
disciplinary actions before telling her she was being let go on November 13, 2024.
17. Claimant was placed at maximum medical improvement on November 3, 2025.
18. Claimant credibly testified that she did not work between November 13, 2024 and
November 3, 2025.
19. The ALJ gives little weight to Mr. Stackpole’s testimony that the reason Claimant
was terminated was because of her performance rather than elimination of the position
by Employer.
20. The ALJ finds the documentary evidence listing Claimant’s reason for separation
as “Position Elimination” persuasive.
21. A preponderance of the evidence supports a finding that Claimant was
terminated from her position because the position was eliminated by Employer.
22. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled
to temporary total disability benefits from November 15, 2024 to November 3, 2025.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Act is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability
and medical benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S.
B. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving entitlement to benefits by a
preponderance of the evidence. § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is
that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact
is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197 Colo. 306, 318 (1979).
4

C. The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted neutrally –
neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of the respondents
– and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
D. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
Univ. Park Care Ctr. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 43 P.3d 637, 641 (Colo. App. 2001).
Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it is for
the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and draw
plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. When determining credibility, the fact finder
should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's
testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or
improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the
testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Bodensieck v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 183 P.3d 684, 687 (Colo. App. 2008).
E. The ALJ’s factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of evidence or
every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected evidence
contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App. 2000).
TTD
F. “Temporary disability benefits are intended to compensate a claimant for actual
wages lost during the time the claimant is unable to work because of injury.” PDM
Molding v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542, 548 (Colo. 1995). To prove entitlement to TTD
benefits, a claimant must prove that the industrial injury caused a disability lasting more
than three work shifts, that he or she left work as a result of the disability, and that the
disability resulted in an actual wage loss. § 8-42-103(1), C.R.S.; § 8-42-105(1), C.R.S.;
see City of Colo. Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d 637, 639 (Colo. App.
1997).
5

G. Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S., requires the claimant to establish a causal
connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent wage loss in order to obtain
TTD benefits. Lindner Chevrolet v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 914 P.2d 496, 498 (Colo.
App. 1995). The term “disability” connotes two elements: (1) medical incapacity
evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning
capacity as demonstrated by claimant’s inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver
v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity
element of disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant’s ability effectively and properly to perform his or her regular
employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo. App. 1998).
Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce evidence of medical
restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to demonstrate a disability.
Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo. App. 1997).
H. TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence of any of the following: (1)
the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to regular or modified
employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a written release to return
to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the employee a written
release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered in writing, and the
employee fails to begin the employment. § 8-42-105(3)(a)-(d), C.R.S.
I. Employers or insurers must pay statutory interest of 8% per annum on all
benefits not paid when due. § 8-43-410(2), C.R.S.; see Subsequent Inj. Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 859 P.2d 276, 278 (Colo. App. 1993).
J. Here, Claimant established by a preponderance of the evidence that she had a
disability lasting more than three work shifts, Claimant was separated from her
employment by elimination of her position by Employer, and Claimant was out of work
from the time she was terminated until she reached MMI on November 3, 2025.
Accordingly, the ALJ concludes that Claimant has established her entitlement to TTD
benefits from November 15, 2024 to November 3, 2025.
6

Responsible for Termination
K. “In cases where it is determined that a temporarily disabled employee is
responsible for termination of employment, the resulting wage loss shall not be
attributable to the on-the-job injury.” § 8-42-103(1)(g), C.R.S.; § 8-42-105(4)(a), C.R.S.
Accordingly, a claimant who is responsible for the termination of employment is not
entitled to temporary disability benefits absent a worsening of condition which
reestablishes the causal connection between the injury and the wage loss. Anderson v.
Longmont Toyota, Inc., 102 P.3d 323, 330 (Colo. 2004); see Grisbaum v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 109 P.3d 1054, 1056 (Colo. App. 2005).
L. The dispositive question in these cases is whether the employee performed a
volitional act or otherwise exercised a degree of control over the circumstances
resulting in her discharge. Poos v. Murfin Drilling Co., W.C. No. 5-185-172-002 (ICAO,
Jan. 17, 2025) (citing Colo. Springs Disposal v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 58 P.3d 1061
(Colo. App. 2002); Padilla v. Digital Equip. Corp., 902 P.2d 414 (Colo. App. 1994)
opinion after remand 908 P.2d 1185 (Colo. App. 1995); Colo. Comp. Ins. Auth. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 18 P.3d 790 (Colo. App. 2000)).
M. Because sections 8-42-103(1)(g), C.R.S., and 8-42-105(4)(a), C.R.S., provide a
defense to an otherwise valid claim for temporary disability benefits, respondents
shoulder the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the claimant
was responsible for her termination and subsequent wage loss. Poos v. Murfin Drilling
Co., W.C. No. 5-185-172-002 (ICAO, Jan. 17, 2025).
N. A preponderance of the evidence supports the conclusion that Claimant was not
responsible for her termination because Employer eliminated Claimant’s position at the
time Employer terminated Claimant. Indeed, Employer’s own paperwork states that
Claimant was terminated because her position was eliminated. Because the elimination
of Claimant’s position was not a volitional act resulting in her discharge, Respondents
have failed to establish Claimant was responsible for her termination. Accordingly,
Respondents are responsible for paying Claimant TTD benefits from November 15,
2024 to November 3, 2025.
7

Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant is entitled to temporary total disability benefits from November 15, 2024
to November 3, 2025.
All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
