title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 4-809-190-003
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 4-809-190-003
Issues
Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that
⮚
the continued opioid prescription medication is reasonable and necessary maintenance
medical treatment?1
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant sustained a compensable workers’ compensation injury on
November 6, 2009. Claimant was injured when his left arm was crushed between two
forklifts. As a result of Claimant’s injury, Claimant underwent surgery that involved
placement of a plate in the area of the left upper extremity fractures. Claimant
eventually underwent partial amputation of the left upper extremity below the left elbow.
Claimant was subsequently diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome
(“CRPS”), phantom limb pain, chronic pain and depression.
2. After Claimant was placed at maximum medical improvement (“MMI”) on
June 27, 2013, Respondents filed a final admission of liability (“FAL”) that admitted for a
1 The original Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Order held that because Respondents
admitted liability for the maintenance medical treatment, including the opioid medications
Claimant was currently being prescribed by Dr. Anderson-Oeser at the time of their final
admission of liability, Respondents bore the burden of proof of pursuant to Section 8-43-201(1)
as the application for hearing was filed seeking to modify an issue determined by a general or
final admission. The Industrial Claim Appeals Office determined that the ALJ erred in placing
the burden of proof on Respondents, and remanded the matter back to the ALJ to apply the
burden of proof on Claimant.
1

scheduled impairment rating of 95% of the left upper extremity and a 5% whole person
impairment rating along with a 9% psychiatric impairment rating. The FAL also admitted
for ongoing maintenance medical benefits. The parties then entered into a stipulation
that settled Claimant’s rights to indemnity benefits while keeping his medical benefits
open in exchange for a certain lump sum payment to Claimant. The Stipulation was
approved by the Division of Workers’ Compensation on October 25, 2013.
3. Claimant has been under the care of Dr. Anderson-Oeser since before
being placed at MMI. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified at hearing that at the time Claimant
was placed at MMI, Claimant’s morphine milligram equivalent (“MME”) was over 200.
Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that an MME over 100 increases the risk of death of the
patient by three times. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that she has attempted to wean
Claimant’s opioid prescription usage and has decreased the MME to 105, but has only
been successful in reducing Claimant’s opioid use to 15 mg of oxymorphone 2 times per
day and 5 mg. of oxycodone 3 times per day. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that the
oxymorphone is a long acting opioid that has some known treatment of neuropathic
pain.
4. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified she last decreased Claimant’s opioid
medication in August 2024 when she lowered Claimant’s oxycodone from 5 mg four
times per day to 3 times per day and Claimant’s oxymorphone from 20 mg 2 times per
day to 15 mg 2 times per day. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that opioids are a
recognized treatment for CRPS and improve Claimant’s function by helping reduce his
pain. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that if Claimant is weaned off the opioid medication,
there is not a good medication to substitute for Claimant that would help relieve his pain.
Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that Claimant is capable of working and performing his
activities of daily living on his current level of opioid medications and was concerned
that if she decreased Claimant’s opioid medications, it would negatively affect
Claimant’s ability to perform his job and activities of daily living.
2

5. Dr. Anderson-Oeser testified that in addition to the opioid medication,
Claimant is also prescribed gabapentin and medication for constipation, which is a side
effect of Claimant’s opioid use.
6. Respondents arranged for an independent medical examination (“IME”) of
Claimant with Dr. Kathy Fine McCranie on May 10, 2023. Dr. McCranie reviewed
Claimant’s medical records, obtained a medical history and performed a physical
examination as part of her IME. Dr. McCranie noted various modalities that had been
attempted through the course of Claimant’s care to address his pain complaints
including ganglion blocks, acupuncture and medications. Claimant reported pain of 10
out of 10 to Dr. McCranie.
7. Dr. McCranie noted in her IME report that as a result of the November 6,
2009 accident, Claimant had (1) left wrist distal radius fracture; (2) left index finger
avulsion fracture; (3) status post open reduction and internal fixation (“ORIF”), left
metacarpal fracture, closed treatment of distal radius fraction; (4) CRPS; (5) status post
left forearm amputation; (6) peripheral nerve stimulator, left upper extremity (which
ultimately resulted in removal); (7) left shoulder impingement; (8) right elbow pain; (9)
adjustment disorder with physical complaints; (10) opioid dependence. Dr. McCranie
recommended that Claimant be tapered off his opioid medication.
8. Dr. McCranie provided an amendment to her IME report on February 9,
2024 after reviewing additional medical records. Dr. McCranie noted in this report that
while Dr. Anderson-Oeser had initiated a taper of opioid medication, since the May 10,
2023 IME, there had only been an attempt to reduce Claimant’s opioid medications by 5
MME’s. Dr. McCranie noted in her supplemental IME report that she continued to
recommend that the opioid medications be tapered as there appeared to be more of a
dependence on opioid medication than any true functional benefit.
9. Dr. McCranie testified at hearing in this matter consistent with her IME
reports. Dr. McCranie noted that at her May 10, 2023 IME, Claimant’s MME was 150,
which is a dangerous amount of opioids to be taking and placed Claimant in a “high risk”
3

category. Dr. McCranie noted that Claimant’s current MME was 105, which is in the
“high risk” category. Dr. McCranie opined at hearing that some patient will resist having
the opioids reduced as the may have a physical dependence of psychological
dependence on the opioid medications. Dr. McCranie noted that the process of
tapering the opioid medications requires a lot of reassurance because during the
tapering program there will be a temporary increase in pain for the patient.
10. Dr. McCranie opined at the hearing that in Claimant’s case, the opioid
medications were not reasonable or necessary medical care because Claimant has not
indicated that they help his pain or functionality. Dr. McCranie recommended a tapering
schedule of 5 mg of oxymorphone per month until Claimant reached 0 mg. Dr.
McCranie recommended that after Claimant’s oxymorphone was reduced to 0 mg.,
Claimant’s oxycodone be reduced 5 mg per month until Claimant reached 0 mg. This
would reduce Claimant’s opioid usage to 0 mg over the course of 21 months.
11. Dr. McCranie disagreed with the opinion of Dr. Anderson-Oeser that
Claimant’s ability to work would be affected by the tapering of the opioid medication.
Dr. McCranie opined that if Claimant had an increase in his pain, she would recommend
Tylenol or Lidoderm patches or topical gels for Claimant’s pain.
12. Claimant underwent a psychiatric IME with Dr. Kleinman on February 26,
2024. Dr. Kleinman noted in his IME report that Claimant had sought psychotherapy
with Dr. Bruns every week, which Claimant reported as helpful, but that treatment had
stopped about five years ago after a disagreement with Dr. Bruns. Dr. Kleinman noted
that Claimant was taking Cymbalta for depression. Dr. Kleinman opined in his IME
report that Claimant was using an excessive amount of opioid medications and agreed
with Dr. McCranie’s opinion that the opioids should be tapered to a safe and reasonable
level. Dr. Kleinman noted that it would not be unexpected for Claimant to have an
increase in his pain complaints during the tapering, but tapering should continue,
regardless. Dr. Kleinman noted that if during the tapering Claimant experienced an
4

increase in irritability or impulsivity, the tapering should be continued and they would
consider four sessions with Dr. Bruns to assist with monitoring Claimant’s mood.
13. Dr. Kleinman testified at hearing in this matter consistent with his IME
report. Dr. Kleinman noted that depression may increase a person’s likelihood of
abusing opioids and can also cause an increase in sensitivity to pain. Dr. Kleinman
noted that opioids are a central nervous system depressive and can cause depression.
Dr. Kleinman opined that if Claimant reported a deterioration of his psychologic
condition during the tapering process, this was not a good reason to stop the tapering
process. Instead, Dr. Kleinman recommended that Claimant’s psychiatric treatments
increase.
14. Dr. Kleinman testified that he would expect Claimant to be able to
continue to work while tapering his opioid medications. Dr. Kleinman testified that if
Claimant experienced an increase in symptoms, the symptoms could be dealt with by
other modalities. Dr. Kleinman testified he would expect Claimant to be able to continue
to function at his current level during the tapering process.
15. Claimant testified at hearing in this matter. Claimant testified he has been
on opioid medication since the date of his workers’ compensation injury. Claimant
testified he is currently in a lot of pain that he described as burning, electrical and
stabling, and at a level of 6 out of 10. Claimant testified that the opioid medications
lessen his pain and make the pain more tolerable. Claimant testified that there are
times when his pain medication will run out if there is a holiday, and when he runs out of
opioid medication his pain worsens. Claimant testified that when this happens, he is
unable to work. Claimant testified that he is currently working cleaning bathrooms and
resident rooms at an assisted living facility. Claimant testified that he has been at this
job since 2022.
16. The medical records in this case are rife with recommendations that
Claimant be weaned off the narcotic medications. For example, physicians’ assistant
(“PA”) Lori Nacius recommended Claimant be weaned off the narcotic medications on
5

October 4, 2012. Dr. Bruns contemplated the need to reduce Claimant’s narcotic
medications on October 8, 2012. Dr. Goldman recommended Claimant be weaned off
the narcotic medications on July 13, 2013. Dr. Henry Roth recommended Claimant be
weaned off the narcotic medications on May 21, 2014.
17. The ALJ notes that Claimant’s current MME of 105 is in excess of the
recommended amount set forth by the Colorado Division of Workers’ Compensation
Medical Treatment Guidelines.
18. The ALJ notes that the testimony of Dr. McCranie and Dr. Kleinman that
Claimant’s opioid medications are not reasonable are based on Claimant’s reports to
the physicians that he is in constant 10 out of 10 pain. Dr. McCranie and Dr. Kleinman
opine that if Claimant is in 10 out of 10 pain, then the opioid medication must not be
helping his level of pain.
19. While the ALJ finds Claimant’s testimony at hearing that he is in a level of
pain of 6 out of 10 to be credible, the medical records document Claimant’s reports of
pain to be at 10 out of 10 when being examined by various medical providers.
Moreover, while the ALJ credits the testimony of Dr. Anderson-Oeser that Claimant’s
use of opioid medications at the current level allow Claimant to maintain functionality to
be credible and persuasive, the medication exceeds the recommendations of the
Colorado Medical Treatment Guidelines. The ALJ finds that the evidence in this case
does not establish that it is more probable than not that Claimant needs medication
prescribed at a level that exceeds the recommendations of the Medical Treatment
Guidelines, and therefore, Claimant has failed to meet his burden of proof for
establishing that the medications are reasonable and necessary maintenance medical
treatment.
20. The ALJ notes that this is a close case, and effectively comes down to
which party bears the burden of proof for establishing which level of medication should
be prescribed. The ALJ notes that Dr. Anderson-Oeser made significant gains in
6

lowering Claimant’s prescribed opioid medication to a level of 105 MME over the course
of Claimant’s recent care.
21. The ALJ credits the testimony of Dr. McCranie and Dr. Kleinman and finds
that Claimant has failed to establish that it is more probable than not that his opioid
prescriptions should not be tapered. The ALJ therefore orders that the Claimant’s
opioid medication regime be tapered pursuant to the recommendations of Dr. McCranie
and Dr. Kleinman.
Conclusions of Law
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101,
et seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of
litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all
of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592
P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted
neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of
respondents; and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-
201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App.
2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it
is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and
draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When determining credibility,
the fact finder should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of
the witness's testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness
(probability or improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness;
7

whether the testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential
Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57 P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Office, 183 P.3d 684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to
conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none of
the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo.
1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to
be dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected
evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
D. Respondents are liable for authorized medical treatment reasonably
necessary to cure and relieve an employee from the effects of a work related injury.
Section 8-42-101, C.R.S.; see Sims v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 797 P.2d 777
(Colo. App. 1990). The need for medical treatment may extend beyond the point of
maximum medical improvement where claimant requires periodic maintenance care to
prevent further deterioration of her physical condition. Grover v. Industrial Commission,
759 P.2d 705 (Colo. 1988). An award for Grover medical benefits is neither contingent
upon a finding that a specific course of treatment has been recommended nor a finding
that claimant is actually receiving medical treatment. Holly Nursing Care Center v.
Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 992 P.2d 701 (Colo. App. 1999); Stollmeyer v. Industrial
Claim Appeals Office, 916 P.2d 609 (Colo. App. 1995). Section 8-42-101, C.R.S., thus
authorizes the ALJ to enter an order for future maintenance treatment if supported by
substantial evidence of the need for such treatment. Grover v. Industrial Commission,
supra.
E. As found, Claimant has failed to establish by a preponderance of the
evidence that his opioid medication should be prescribed at a level that exceeds the
8

Colorado Medical Treatment Guidelines. It is hereby ordered that Claimant’s opioid
medications be tapered pursuant to the recommendations of Dr. McCranie and Dr.
Kleinman.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant’s opioid medication shall be tapered pursuant to the
recommendations of Dr. McCranie and Dr. Kleinman.
2. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-313-385-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-313-385-001
Issues
Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
⮚
sustained injuries, including a L4 endplate fracture arising out of and in the
course of his employment on July 22, 2025.
If Claimant established that he suffered compensable injuries, whether he also
⮚
established, by a preponderance of the evidence, his entitlement to all
reasonable, necessary, and related medical treatment stemming from his July
22, 2025, work injury.
If Claimant established that he suffered compensable work-related injuries on
⮚
July 22, 2025, whether he also established, by a preponderance of the evidence,
that he is entitled to Temporary Total Disability (“TTD”) benefits beginning July
22, 2025, and ongoing.
If Claimant established that he suffered compensable injuries, what was his
⮚
Average Weekly Wage (AWW) on July 22, 2025.
Based on the evidence presented at hearing, the ALJ orders as follows:
Compensability
A. A “compensable injury” is one that requires medical treatment or causes
disability. Romero v. Industrial Commission, 632 P.2d 1052 (Colo. App. 1981);
Aragon v. CHIMR, et al., W.C. No. 4-543-782 (ICAO, Sept. 24, 2004); H & H
Warehouse v. Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167, 1169 (Colo. App. 1990). No benefits flow to
the victim of an industrial accident unless the accident results in a compensable
1

“injury.” Romero, supra; § 8-41-301, C.R.S. To sustain his burden of proof
concerning compensability, Claimant must establish that the condition for which
he seeks benefits was proximately caused by an “injury” arising out of and in the
course of employment. Loofbourrow v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 321 P.3d
548 (Colo. App. 2011), aff’d Harman-Bergstedt, Inc. v. Loofbourrow, 320 P.3d
327 (Colo. 2014); Section 8-41-301(I)(b), C.R.S.
B. The phrases "arising out of” and "in the course of" are not synonymous
and a claimant must meet both requirements for the injury to be compensable.
Younger v. City and County of Denver, 810 P.2d 647, 649 (Colo. 1991); In re
Question Submitted by U.S. Court of Appeals, 759 P.2d 17, 20 (Colo. 1988). The
latter requirement refers to the time, place, and circumstances under which a
work-related injury occurs. Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 381 (Colo. 1991).
C. An injury occurs in the course and scope of employment when it takes
place within the time and place limits of the employment relationship and during
an activity connected with the employee's job-related functions. In re Question
Submitted by U.S. Court of Appeals, supra; Deterts v. Times Publ'g Co., 38 Colo.
App. 48, 51, 552 P.2d 1033, 1036 (1976). Conversely, the "arising out of" test is
one of causation. It requires that the injury have its origins in an employee's
work-related functions and be sufficiently related thereto so as to be considered
part of the employee's service to the employer. Horodyskyj v. Karanian, 32 P.3d
470, 475 (Colo. 2001). Here, there is little question that Claimant’s alleged injury
occurred within the time and place limits of his employment, i.e. during a routine
workday and during an activity related to Claimant’s job duties as a skilled
construction laborer, namely adding an electrical circuit and switch to an existing
residential electrical service panel. Nonetheless, the question of whether
Claimant’s medical condition/symptoms and need for treatment arose out of his
employment must be answered before the injuries can be determined to be
compensable.
2

D. The determination of whether there is a sufficient "nexus" or causal
relationship between the Claimant's employment-related duties and the alleged
injury is one of fact, which the ALJ must determine based on the totality of the
circumstances. In Re Question Submitted by the United States Court of Appeals,
759 P.2d 17 (Colo. 1988); Moorhead Machinery & Boiler Co. v. Del Valle, 934
P.2d 861 (Colo. App. 1996). In this case, the totality of the evidence, including
Claimant’s testimony, supports the conclusion that he presented to the
Emergency Department (ED) at Parkview Pueblo West Hospital on July 22,
2025, after being electrocuted by three 110V wires as he was performing
electrical work at the direction of his boss, Shawn Moyers, who owns and
operates Timberline Custom Builders. Claimant was locked on to electrical
current and shocked for greater than 1 minute, suffered a loss of consciousness
and fell to the floor fracturing the endplate of his L4 vertebral body. (CHE 2).
Treatment for this injury included a kyphoplasty surgery performed by Dr. Craig
Lance on August 22, 2025. (CHE 6, p. 68). Claimant also developed
neuropathic pain, arrythmia and shortness of breath following his electrical
shock, which conditions required additional workup. (CHE 3-5). Based upon the
evidence presented, the ALJ is convinced that not only did Claimant’s injuries
occur within the time and place limits of his employment but also have their
origins in his work-related functions as a skilled laborer for Employer and are
sufficiently related to those functions (making electrical upgrades) so as to be
considered part of his service to Employer. Accordingly, the ALJ is persuaded
that Claimant’s injuries and need for treatment “arose out of” his work duties for
Employer. Because the ALJ is convinced that Claimant has established the
requisite nexus between his work activities and his July 22, 2025, injuries, the
claimed injuries are compensable.
Claimant’s Entitlement to Medical Benefits, Authorization and Right of Selection
3

E. Once a claimant has established the compensable nature of his/her work
injury, he/she is entitled to a general award of medical benefits and respondents
are liable to provide all reasonable, necessary, and related medical care to cure
and relieve the effects of the work injury. Section 8-42-101, C.R.S.; Grover v.
Industrial Commission, 759 P.2d 705 (Colo. 1988); Sims v. Industrial Claim
Appeals Office, 797 P.2d 777 (Colo. App. 1990). However, a claimant is only
entitled to such benefits as long as the industrial injury is the proximate cause of
his need for medical treatment. Merriman v. Indus. Comm’n, 210 P.2d 448 (Colo.
1949); Standard Metals Corp. v. Ball, 172 Colo. 510, 474 P.2d 622 (1970); § 8-
41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. Ongoing benefits may be denied if the current and ongoing
need for medical treatment or disability is not proximately caused by an injury
arising out of and in the course of the employment. Snyder v. City of Aurora, 942
P.2d 1337 (Colo. App. 1997). In other words, the mere occurrence of a
compensable injury does not require an ALJ to find that all subsequent medical
treatment and physical disability was caused by the industrial injury. To the
contrary, the range of compensable consequences of an industrial injury is
limited to those which flow proximately and naturally from the injury. Standard
Metals Corp. v. Ball, supra. As noted above, Claimant has proven that he
suffered compensable injuries to his low back and was treated for other injuries
associated with his electrocution through the ED at Parkview Pueblo West
Hospital and Drs. Sheldon Ravin, Stephen Farkas, and Craig Lance and their
referrals. The content of the medical records from the above-mentioned
providers combined with the testimony received at hearing persuades the ALJ
that the treatment Claimant received after his electrocution has been reasonable,
necessary and otherwise related to that mechanism of injury. Nonetheless, the
question of whether this treatment and the aforementioned providers was/were
authorized to treat Claimant must be addressed.
F. Authorization to provide medical care as part of a work-related claim refers
to a medical provider’s legal authority to provide treatment to the claimant with
4

the expectation that the provider will be compensated by the insurer for said
services. Bunch v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 148 P.3d 381 (Colo. App.
2006); One Hour Cleaners v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 914 P.2d 501
(Colo. App. 1995); In re Bell, W.C. No. 5-044-948-01 (ICAO, Oct. 16, 2018).
Medical services provided during a bona fide emergency are an exception to the
normal requirement that a claimant obtain authorization for all treatment
connected to the industrial injury. Larson's Workers' Compensation Law, §
94.02[6] (1999); Sims v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 797 P.2d 777 (Colo.
App. 1990). Otherwise, authorized providers include those medical personnel to
whom the claimant is directly referred by the employer, as well as providers to
whom an authorized provider refers the claimant in the normal progression of
care. Town of Ignacio v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 70 P.3d 513 (Colo.
App. 2002); City of Durango v. Dunagan, 939 P.2d 496 (Colo. App. 1997).
G. There is no precise legal test for determining what constitutes a medical
emergency.1 Rather, the question of whether a claimant established the
existence of a bona fide emergency is dependent on the particular facts and
circumstances of the claim. Timko v. Cub Foods, W. C. No. 3969-031 (June 29,
2005). In this case, the ALJ is persuaded that the intensity and duration of the
electrical shock Claimant sustained resulted in an emergent need to seek
medical treatment. Indeed, Claimant was shocked by multiple wires energized
with 110 volts of current, was unable to break the electrical connection and was
shocked for greater than one minute before the electrical current was cut. As
noted, before the current was cut, Claimant lost consciousness and fell to the
floor injuring his back. He was tachycardic, hypertensive and complaining of
chest pain and shortness of breath upon examination in the ED, raising concern
for cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial injury, rhabdomyolysis, internal burns/tissue
1 The exception is not limited to situations where life is threatened. Bunch v. Industrial Claim
Appeals Office of State of Colorado, 148 P.3d 381 (Colo.App.2006).
5

damage and neurologic injury as potential critical diagnoses. (CHE 2, p. 7). For
these reasons, the ALJ is convinced that Claimant suffered a bona fide medical
emergency and that the initial treatment rendered in the ED was reasonable and
necessary to evaluate the extent of damage caused by Claimant’s prolonged
electrical shock. Consequently, Claimant was not required to obtain prior
authorization from Respondent-Employer for this treatment.
H. Concerning the remainder of Claimant’s treatment, § 8-43-404(5) (a) (I)
(A), C.R.S. 2025, gives the employer has the right in the first instance to
designate the authorized provider to treat the claimant's compensable condition.
The rationale for this principle is that the employer and the employer’s insurance
carrier (respondents) may ultimately be liable for the claimant's medical bills and,
therefore, have an interest in knowing what treatment is being provided. Andrade
v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 121 P.3d 328 (Colo. App. 2005). The statute
requires the employer or insurer to "provide a list of at least four physicians . . .
in the first instance, from which list an injured employee may select the
physician who attends said injured employee." Similarly, Workers' Compensation
Rules of Procedure, Rule 8-2(A), 7 Code Colo. Reg. 1101-3, states that "[w]hen
an employer has notice of an on-the-job injury, the employer or insurer shall
provide the injured worker with a written list” of providers. In order to maintain
the right to designate a provider in the first instance, the employer has an
obligation to name the treating physician forthwith upon receiving notice of the
compensable injury. See Rogers v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 746 P.2d
545 (Colo. App. 1987). The failure to tender the "services of a physician . . . at
the time of injury" gives the employee "the right to select a physician or
chiropractor."
I. An employer's duty to designate is triggered once the employer or
insurer has some knowledge of facts that would lead a reasonably
conscientious manager to believe the case may involve a claim for
6

compensation. Bunch v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 148 P.3d 381 (Colo.
App. 2006); Jones v. Adolph Coors Co., 689 P.2d 681 (Colo. App. 1984);
Gutierrez v. Premium Pet Foods, LLC, W.C. No. 4-834-947 (ICAO, September 6,
2011). In this case, the evidence presented persuades the ALJ that Mr. Moyers
was present on the job site when Claimant was shocked, that he cut the power to
prevent further injury/death to Claimant and that he helped revive Claimant
before he was taken to the hospital for treatment. Accordingly, the ALJ is
convinced that Mr. Moyers was aware of Claimant’s accident and the work-
related nature of his injuries. The ALJ is also convinced that Mr. Moyers took no
action to designate a provider to attend to Claimant’s injuries following his initial
treatment in the ED at Parkview Pueblo West Hospital. Accordingly, the ALJ
concludes that the right to select a provider to treat Claimant’s injuries passed to
him. Based on the evidence presented, the ALJ finds that Claimant exercised
that right by initiating treatment with the providers at UCHealth Aspen Creek
Medical Center. As noted, authorized providers include those medical personnel
to whom the claimant is directly referred by an authorized provider in the normal
progression of care. Town of Ignacio v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, supra.
Thus, Dr. Craig Lance and those providers who performed diagnostic testing to
help delineate Claimant’s diagnosis are also authorized to treat Claimant. Based
on the evidence presented, the ALJ concludes that Respondent-Employer (Mr.
Moyers) is liable for the costs of any treatment rendered to Claimant by the
aforementioned providers, including the costs for any diagnostic testing based
upon the referrals of Drs. Russo, Rodgers, Ravin, Farkas, and Lance. Payment
shall be made in accordance with the Colorado Workers’ Compensation Medical
Benefits Fee Schedule. The Colorado Division of Workers’ Compensation can
help Employer calculate medical payments owed under the fee schedule.
Claimant’s Entitlement to Temporary Disability Benefits
7

J. To receive temporary disability benefits, Claimant must prove that his
injuries caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, that he left work
as a result of the disability, and that the disability resulted in an actual wage loss.
PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542 (Colo. 1995); City of Colorado
Springs v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 954 P.2d 637 (Colo. App. 1997).
Section 8-42-103(1), C.R.S. 2001; PDM Molding, Inc. v. Stanberg, 898 P.2d 542
(Colo. 1995). As stated in PDM, the term "disability" refers to the claimant's
physical inability to perform regular employment. See also McKinley v. Bronco
Billy's, 903 P.2d 1239 (Colo. App. 1995). Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S., requires
Claimant to establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a
subsequent wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. PDM Molding, Inc. v.
Stanberg, supra. The term disability connotes two elements: (1) Medical
incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily function; and (2) Impairment
of wage-earning capacity as demonstrated by Claimant's inability to resume his
prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of
the earning capacity element of disability may be evidenced by a complete
inability to work, or by restrictions which impair the claimant's ability to effectively
and properly perform his/her regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy &
Co., 964 P.2d 595 (Colo. App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a
claimant must produce evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony
alone is sufficient to demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952
P.2d 831, 833 (Colo. App. 1997).
K. In this case, Claimant testified that he has not been returned to work by
his treating providers since being shocked on July 22, 2025. The ALJ credits
Claimant’s testimony to find and conclude that he last worked on July 22, 2025,
that he has not been released to work by his medical providers and that his
complete inability to work has resulted in an actual wage loss lasting more than
three work shifts. Based upon the evidence presented, the ALJ is persuaded
that Claimant has been “disabled” within the meaning of section 8-42-105, C.R.S.
8

beginning July 22, 2025. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971 P.2d 641 (Colo. 1999);
Hendricks v. Keebler Company, W.C. No. 4-373-392 (ICAO, June 11, 1999).
Thus, he is entitled to TTD benefits. Because the period of disability lasted
longer than two weeks from the day Claimant left work as a consequence of the
injury, he is entitled to recover disability benefits from the day he left work in this
case. See § 8-42-103(1)(b), C.R.S.
L. TTD benefits shall continue until the employee reaches maximum medical
improvement, returns to regular or modified-duty employment, is given a written
release by his attending physician to return to regular work or is given a written
release to modified duty and such modified duty is offered to Claimant, in writing,
and Claimant fails to begin such employment. See § 8-42-105 (3). Here, the
evidence presented supports the conclusion that none of the aforementioned
factors have been satisfied. Consequently, Respondent-Employer shall pay TTD
in accordance with C.R.S. § 8-42-105 (1) until such time that these benefits can
be terminated pursuant to statute. See § 8-42-105 (3) (a-d).
Claimant’s Average Weekly Wage and Concurrent Employment
M. The overall purpose of the average weekly wage (AWW) statute is to arrive
at a fair approximation of a claimant’s wage loss and diminished earning capacity
resulting from the industrial injury. See Campbell v. IBM Corp., 867 P.2d 77 (Colo.
App. 1993)2; National Fruit Prod. v. Crespin, 952 P.2d 1207 (Colo. App. 1997).
2 The claimant in Campbell suffered three periods of temporary disability and for each subsequent
period was earning a higher average weekly wage. The question resolved was whether Ms.
Campbell was entitled to temporary disability benefits based on the higher AWW she was earning
during each successive period of temporary disability. The Court held that it would be unjust to
calculate her disability benefits in 1986 and 1989 on her substantially lower earnings she was
making in 1979.
9

N. The best evidence of Claimant’s actual wage loss and therefore a fair
approximation of his diminished earning capacity at the time of his industrial
injury comes from his testimony at hearing. Claimant testified that at the time of
his work-related accident he was working 9 hours per day, 5 days a week for a
total of 45 hours. He noted that he was paid $28 per hour which equates to an
average weekly wage of $1,350. ($28/hr. x 45 hour/week = $1,350/week). The
ALJ credits Claimant’s testimony to find that this $1,350 figure most closely
approximates Claimant’s wage loss and diminished earning capacity at the time
of his July 22, 2025, work-related injury.
Penalties
O. Claimant seeks penalties against Respondent-Employer for failing to carry
Worker’s Compensation insurance pursuant to C.R.S. § 8-43-408. Section 8-43-
408(5), C.R.S. provides:
In addition to any compensation paid or ordered . . . an
employer who is not in compliance with the insurance provisions
of [the Act] at the time an employee suffers a compensable
injury, or occupational disease shall pay an amount equal to
twenty-five percent of the compensation or benefits to which the
employee is entitled to the Colorado uninsured employer fund
created in section 8-67-105.
P. Based upon the evidence presented, including Claimant’s testimony
surrounding Respondent-Employer’s actions of paying some lost wage benefits
after Claimant’s accident persuades the ALJ that Respondent-Employer was not
insured for workers’ compensation injuries on July 22, 2025. The penalty for
failure to insure only applies to indemnity benefits; it does not apply to medical
benefits. Industrial Commission v. Hammond, 77 Colo. 414, 236 P. 1006 (1925);
Jacobson v. Doan, 319 P.2d 975 (Colo. 1957); Wolford v. Support, Inc., W.C. No.
4-155- 231 (February 13, 1998). Although the ALJ is not aware of a case directly
10

on point, statutory interest is not properly considered “compensation or benefits”
within the meaning of § 8-43-408 (5). Interest is a statutory right intended to
secure claimants the present value of benefits to which they are entitled by
creating an equitable remedy for the lost time value of money during the accrual
period. Subsequent Injury Fund v. Trevethan, 809 P.2d 1098 (Colo. App. 1991).
Accordingly, interest is not included in the “penalty” amount Respondent-
Employer is ordered to pay pursuant to C.R.S. § 8-43-408 (5).
Q. Claimant is entitled to $900 in weekly or $128.57 in daily TTD benefits
beginning July 22, 2025, and continuing until such time that the TTD benefits can
be terminated in accordance with statute. See § 8-42-105 (3) (a-d). As of the
issuance of this order, Claimant is entitled to 288 days of TTD benefits for a total
TTD award of $37,028.16. ($128.57/day x 288 days = $37,028.16). Twenty- five
percent (25%) of the compensation awarded is $9,257.04, which sum shall be
sent to the Division of Workers’ Compensation Revenue Assessment Unit, 633
17th Street, Suite 400, Denver, CO 80202.
R. As Respondent-Employer was not insured for workers’ compensation liability
at the time of Claimant’s injury, § 8-43-408(2) of the Workers’ Compensation Act
requires Employer to pay to the trustee of the Division of Workers’ Compensation
(“Division”) an amount equal to the present value of all unpaid compensation or
benefits, computed at 4% per annum. In the alternative, Employer may file a
bond with the Division signed by two or more responsible sureties approved by
the Director or by some surety company authorized to do business in Colorado.
Employer may contact the Division Trustee for assistance with his obligations in
this regard. The Division Trustee may be contacted through the Division’s
customer service line at 303-318-8700 or by email to Mariya Cassin
mariya.cassin@state.co.us.
S. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
11

NOTE: This decision is final and not subject to appeal unless a full order is
requested. The request shall be made at the Office of Administrative Courts,
2864. S. Circle Drive, Suite 810, Colorado Springs, CO 80906 within ten (10)
working days of the date of service of this Summary Order. Section 8-43-215 (1),

If a party makes a request for a full order both parties shall submit a

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-283-790-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-283-790-001
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence he is entitled to
⮚
temporary total disability (TTD) benefits from March 13, 2025 to February 11,
2026.
Whether Respondents proved by a preponderance of the evidence Claimant is
⮚
responsible for his termination from employment and thus not entitled to TTD.
Whether Claimant is entitled to an award of disfigurement benefits.
⮚
Stipulations
At hearing, the ALJ accepted the following stipulations of the parties:
1. Claimant was placed at maximum medical improvement (MMI) by Dr. Scott
Primack on February 11, 2026.
2. The contract term that Claimant was playing under at the time of injury was for
the 2024/2025 season where he earned $1,055,000. His average weekly wage
(AWW) is $20,288.
3. Respondent paid salary continuation from the date of injury (7/31/2024) to March
12, 2025.
4. The claimed wage loss period is from March 13, 2025 to February 11, 2026.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant is 31 years old. Claimant was employed by Employer, a National
Football League Team (NFL) team, as a professional football player.
1

2. On July 31, 2024, Claimant suffered an admitted industrial injury while
participating in team practice. Claimant sustained a right ankle Maisonneuve
fracture and dislocation.
3. At the time of the industrial injury Claimant was under contract with Employer for
one football season. Claimant’s NFL Player Contract, executed on March 6,
2024, provided that the contract term covered one football season, beginning on
the date of execution and ending the last day of the 2024 League Year, unless
extended or renewed.
4. As a result of the industrial injury, Employer placed Claimant on injured reserve
on August 1, 2024. The injury was classified by Employer as “major,” with an
estimated time loss of six to nine months from the date of injury.
5. Claimant underwent multiple surgeries for the industrial injury performed by
authorized treating physician (ATP) Joshua Metzl, MD, including a right ankle
arthroscopic debridement with syndesmotic open reduction and internal fixation
repair and deltoid ligament repair on August 7, 2024, and hardware removals on
September 30, 2024 and October 24, 2024. Claimant attended multiple post-
operative physical therapy sessions.
6. On January 13, 2025, Dr. Metzl conducted Claimant’s end of season physical for
Employer. On examination, Dr. Metzl noted mild ankle swelling with no pain
through ankle range of motion. Dr. Metzl determined that Claimant failed the
physical exam, noting that Claimant would have to wait for clearance for another
eight weeks as physical therapy progressed. Claimant testified that he did not
return to Dr. Metzel in eight weeks because his contract with Employer
subsequently ended and he thus did not have access to see Dr. Metzel at that
time.
7. Claimant continued physical therapy and rehabilitation with Employer’s provider,
attending sessions 5 days/week every week until March 11, 2025. Claimant
ceased attending physical therapy and rehabilitation with Employer’s provider
because he became a free agent upon expiration of his contract. The team’s
2

provider noted, “[Claimant] reported today that he would be foregoing the last two
days of rehab as he will become a free agent after Wednesday. [Claimant] and I
discussed continued therapy and we have help set him up with NextLevel
Physical Therapy where he will continue his rehab on Thursday 3/13/25.” [RHE
B, p. 67].
8. Claimant did not play the entire 2024 football season due to his industrial injury.
Employer paid Claimant salary continuation through March 12, 2025, as provided
under Claimant’s contract. Claimant’s contract with Employer ended by its own
terms on March 12, 2025 at the conclusion of the 2024 football season.
9. On March 13, 2025, Claimant presented to Next Level Physical Therapy (Next
Level) for continued care of his right ankle injury. The physical therapist noted
that Claimant was advancing in strength, running, jumping and light field work,
but continued to have limitations with dorsiflexion, swelling, stiffness, joint
mobility restriction and altered movement. The physical therapist remarked that
Claimant would “need focused intervention to aide in his ability to return to
professional football.” CHE 4, p. 9. Claimant was to attend physical therapy 4
days/week for 12 weeks.
10. Claimant continued to attend physical therapy at NextLevel, as well as at
UCHealth Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation Clinic. On September 22 and
October 6, 2025, the physical therapist noted that Claimant presented with
impaired ankle range of motion, swelling, pain and mobility. It was noted that
physical therapy was required for Claimant to address these impairments and to
safely return to playing professional football.
11. In October 2025, despite not being cleared to return to play football or released
from care, Claimant participated in a tryout for Employer in hopes of getting re-
signed by the team and returning to play as an offensive lineman. Claimant
executed Employer’s Release and Waiver on October 13, 2025 representing, in
part, “…that I am in good health and sound physical condition, and that I have no
physical defects, conditions or injuries, latent or patent that would endanger my
3

health or that may be aggravated or exacerbated by the tryout…” [RHE F, p.
329].
12. Claimant credibly testified at hearing. Claimant testified that he signed the waiver
and attended the tryout because, prior to the tryout, he felt good and believed
that he was able to play. However, during the tryout, he experienced continued
issues with ankle range of motion and load bearing and realized that he was
unable to participate in professional football activities at that time.
13. Respondent did not offer Claimant a contract after the tryout.
14. On January 6, 2026, Claimant returned to Dr. Metzl on the referral of his primary
care physician at UC Health. Dr. Metzl noted that Claimant overall had steady
improvement since his surgeries and continued to train for a potential return to
the NFL. Claimant reported experiencing daily pain and stiffness in his ankle. Dr.
Metzl noted radiographic signs of anterior impingement with posttraumatic ankle
arthrosis. Dr. Metzl wrote, “We discussed that he will continue training and if the
pain is persistent he would be a good candidate for arthroscopy with anterior
decompression. He expressed understanding and will see me back on a [sic] as
needed basis.” [CHE 7, p. 41].
15. On February 11, 2026, Scott Primack, DO, conducted an Independent Medical
Examination (IME) at request of Respondent. Claimant reported persistent ankle
stiffness. Dr. Primack placed Claimant at MMI as of the date of his IME and
assigned a 12% lower extremity impairment rating. Dr. Primack remarked,
“[Claimant] certainly can perform the essential functions of a job in many
positions; however, it is fairly obvious that he would not be able to adequately
perform the essential functions of the job as an offensive lineman in the National
Football League given his residual stiffness.” [CHE 8, p. 46].
16. Dr. Primack credibly testified at hearing on behalf of Respondents. Dr. Primack
testified as a Level II accredited expert in physical medicine and rehabilitation
and occupational medicine. Dr. Primack testified consistent with his IME report.
He testified that, at the time of his IME, he was unaware that Claimant had
4

participated in team tryouts in October 2025; however, such knowledge did not
change any of his opinions.
17. Claimant and Employer entered multiple Practice Player and NFL Player
contracts over the course of approximately six football seasons. Employer has a
history of offering new contracts to Claimant despite terminating his contracts for
purported unsatisfactory skill or performance. On September 1, 2019, Employer
terminated Claimant’s 2019-2021 contract citing the following reason: “In the
judgment of the Club, your skill or performance has been unsatisfactory as
compared with that of other players competing for positions on the Club’s roster.”
[RHE F, p.197]. Employer cited the same reason when terminating Claimant’s
2020-2021 contract on September 6, 2020, Claimant’s 2021-2022 contract on
September 1, 2021, Claimant’s 2022-2023 contract on August 31, 2022,
Claimant’s 2022-2023 contract on December 7, 2022, and Claimant’s 2023-2024
contract on August 29, 2023.
18. Claimant testified that when he signed his 2024 contract, his plan at the
expiration of the contract was to continue playing in the NFL. Claimant testified
he would have liked to continue playing for Employer, but understood there was
no guarantee, as he was set to become an unrestricted free agent at the
expiration of his 2024 contract. Claimant testified that he failed Employer’s end of
season physical, which meant he was neither cleared to play nor able to play at
the time. Claimant explained that his position as an offensive lineman required,
among other things, bracing, impact, pushing, and running. Claimant testified that
the industrial injury resulted in decreased stability, strength, and range of motion
that affected his ability to effectively run, bend, and produce explosive
movements as required of his position. Claimant testified that, at the time his
2024 contract expired, he was unable to perform his offensive lineman duties due
to the industrial injury but continued with treatment in hopes of continuing to play
and re-signing with Employer.
5

19. Respondent’s Vice President of Football Administration, Rich Hurtado, credibly
testified at hearing on behalf of Employer. Mr. Hurtado’s role involves negotiating
player contracts, managing the club’s salary cap, and strategic planning with the
general manager regarding player acquisition and roster construction. Mr.
Hurtado explained that the employment relationship between Employer and the
players is governed by a collective bargaining agreement. Mr. Hurtado engaged
in contract negotiations with Claimant’s agent on multiple contracts, including
Claimant’s 2024-2025 contract. Mr. Hurtado testified that Claimant’s agent
negotiated a one-year term, as Claimant was set to become an unrestricted free
agent at the end of the 2024-2025 football season. Mr. Hurtado explained that an
unrestricted free agent is where the team would have, “no right to keep the player
unless he’s really, really talented and we can place what’s called a franchiser
transition tag.” [Hr. Tr. p. 49, l. 15-18]. Mr. Hurtado testified that, at the time of
Claimant’s 2024 contract negotiations, the team did not intend to keep Claimant
as a franchise player.
20. Mr. further Hurtado testified that Claimant’s 2024 contract expired and the team
decided not to re-sign Claimant. Mr. Hurtado testified that he was involved in
Employer’s decision not to offer Claimant a new contract at the end of the 2024
football season. Mr. Hurtado acknowledged that a player’s availability and health
are factors in remaining competitive but testified that Claimant’s industrial injury
was not the reason Employer did not re-sign Claimant. Mr. Hurtado testified that,
at the time, the team already had 12 good lineman and decided to look towards
the draft and college free agency to further enhance the offensive line. Mr.
Hurtado testified that Claimant was not competitive with the other players the
team was considering for the offensive lineman positions and that other players
were better alternatives.
21. Claimant has not returned to playing professional football. Claimant has not
earned any wages since March 13, 2025.
6

22. Claimant proved it is more probably true than not he is entitled to TTD benefits
March 13, 2025 to February 11, 2026. The July 31, 2024 industrial injury to
caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts. As a result of the
disability, Claimant left work and sustained wage loss.
23. Respondents failed to prove it is more probably true than not Claimant was
responsible for the termination of employment. The termination of employment
was the result of the natural expiration of the fixed term of Claimant’s 2024
contract. Claimant intended to continue working as an offensive lineman in the
NFL upon expiration of the fixed term of the contract.
24. The ALJ observed Claimant’s right ankle at hearing and viewed photographs of
Claimant’s right ankle contained in Claimant’s Exhibit 12. As a result of his July
31, 2024 industrial injury, Claimant has a visible disfigurement consisting of the
following:
(1) A scar on Claimant’s inner right ankle measuring approximately 2.5 inches
in length and .5 inches in width. The scar is significantly darker in color than
the surrounding skin and textured. Suture scars are perceptible along the
length of the scar.
(2) A scar on Claimant’s inner right ankle measuring approximately 1 inch in
length and width. The scar is significantly darker in color than the surrounding
skin and textured. Suture scars perceptible along the length of the scar.
(3) A scar on the front of Claimant’s right ankle. The scar measures
approximately .5 inches in length and width and is darker in color than the
surrounding skin with minimal texture.
(4) A scar on Claimant’s outer right ankle measuring approximately 3 inches
in length and 1.25 inches in width. The scar is significantly darker in color
than the surrounding skin and textured, with suture scars perceptible along
the length of the scar.
7

25. Claimant has sustained a serious permanent disfigurement to areas of the body
normally expos and shall be awarded $3,750.00.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
8

Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
TTD Benefits
D. To prove entitlement to TTD benefits, a claimant must prove that the industrial
injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he left work as a
result of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss. See §§8-
42-(1)(g) & 8-42-105(4), C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102 P.3d 323
(Colo. 2004); City of Colorado Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d
637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S. requires the claimant to
establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent
wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. The term “disability” connotes two
elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily
function; and (2) impairment of wage earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971
P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her
regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo.
App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce
evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to
demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo.
App. 1997).
9

E. TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence of any of the following: (1)
the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to regular or modified
employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a written release to
return to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the employee
a written release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered in
writing and the employee fails to begin the employment. §8-42-105(3)(a)-(d),
C.R.S.; see Chavez v. Costco Wholesale, Inc., WC 5-096-055-003 (ICAO, Feb.
4, 2022) (noting that, where TTD benefits had not commenced, they could not be
terminated based on the ATP’s MMI determination).
F. As found, Claimant proved it is more probable than not he is entitled to TTD
benefits from March 13, 2025 to February 11, 2026. The July 31, 2024 industrial
injury to Claimant’s right ankle caused disability both in the form of loss and
restriction of Claimant’s bodily function and impairment of his wage earning
capacity. As credibly and persuasively testified to by Claimant and documented
in the medical records, the industrial injury caused deficits in range of motion and
persistent stiffness, which impaired his ability to effectively and properly perform
as an offensive lineman. As a result of the industrial injury, Claimant was placed
on injured reserve and was unable to play the entire 2024 season. Subsequent to
the expiration of his contract, Claimant remained unable to adequately perform
his duties as an offensive lineman as a result of the effects of the industrial injury.
Claimant continued treatment for the industrial injury yet was not cleared by any
physician to return to his regular work activities as an offensive lineman. The
industrial injury impaired Claimant’s wage earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his prior work, resulting in actual wage loss for
Claimant. Claimant therefore is entitled to TTD benefits from March 13, 2025 to
February 11, 2026, the date of MMI.
Responsibility for Termination
G. Under the termination statutes in §§8-42-105(4) & 8-42-103(1)(g) C.R.S. a
claimant who is responsible for his or her termination from regular or modified
10

employment is not entitled to TTD benefits absent a worsening of condition that
reestablishes the causal connection between the industrial injury and wage loss.
Gilmore v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 187 P.3d 1129, 1131 (Colo. App. 2008).
The termination statutes provide that, in cases where an employee is responsible
for her termination, the resulting wage loss is not attributable to the industrial
injury. In re of Davis, WC 4-631-681 (ICAO, Apr. 24, 2006). A claimant does not
act “volitionally” or exercise control over the circumstances leading to her
termination if the effects of the injury prevent her from performing her assigned
duties and cause the termination. In re of Eskridge, WC 4-651-260 (ICAO, Apr.
21, 2006). Therefore, to establish that Claimant was responsible for their
termination, respondents must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence
that the claimant committed a volitional act or exercised some control over their
termination under the totality of the circumstances. See Padilla v. Digital
Equipment, 902 P.2d 414, 416 (Colo. App. 1994). An employee is thus
“responsible” if they precipitated the employment termination by a volitional act
that they would reasonably expect to cause the loss of employment. Patchek v.
Dep’t of Public Safety, WC 4-432-301 (ICAO, Sept. 27, 2001).
H. Respondents acknowledge that Claimant’s employment ended because his
contract expired by its own terms at the conclusion of the football season.
Respondents argue, however, that by voluntarily entering a negotiated fixed term
contract, Claimant exercised a degree of control over the duration of his
employment and the circumstances under which his employment would end, and
thus is responsible for the termination of employment. The ALJ disagrees.
I. The concept of “fault” as it is used in the unemployment insurance context is
instructive for purposes of the termination statutes. See Kaufman v. Noffsinger
Manufacturing, W.C. No. 4-608-836 (April 18, 2005). The Court of Appeals has
previously held in unemployment insurance cases that the mere fact parties
agreed and understood employment would end at the expiration of a fixed term is
not a basis for denying unemployment insurance benefits. In re Interrogatories by
11

Indus. Comm'n, 496 P.2d 1064 (Colo. App. 1972); Intermountain Jewish News,
Inc. v. Indus. Comm'n, 564 P.2d 132 (Colo. App. 1977). Thus, when the
separation from employment occurs solely as a result of the expiration of an
agreed upon fixed term, the claimant is not deemed at fault merely because he
agreed to the fixed term of employment.
J. The Panel has previously addressed Respondents’ argument in the context of
seasonal employment in Judd v. Antarctic Support Svcs., WC 4-457-362 (ICAO
June 2, 2003). In Judd, the claimant was employed on a seasonal basis and
entered into a series of seven-month contracts with the employer. The ALJ
awarded the claimant TTD benefits for a period of time after the expiration of his
last contract. The respondents argued that the claimant was responsible for
termination of employment because he engaged in a volitional act leading to his
unemployment by voluntarily entering a fixed term contract. The Panel agreed
with the ALJ that, “the respondents’ proposed interpretation of the word
responsible ‘would bring about quite unreasonable, and unjust, results.” Id. The
Panel concluded that the loss of seasonal employment does not automatically
disqualify a claimant from receiving subsequent temporary disability benefits.
Rather, the question of whether the claimant's post-termination wage loss was
caused by the injury was one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Id. The Panel
cited City of Aurora v. Dortch, 799 P.2d 461 (Colo. App. 1990), where the court
concluded that a claimant's seasonal employment, which would have expired in
the month following her injury regardless of disability, did not preclude an award
of TTD benefits. The court emphasized that the evidence did not establish the
wage loss was either voluntary or due solely to the fact that her seasonal
employment would have expired. Id. at 462-63. The Panel in Judd stated,
Inherent in the Dortch decision is the court’s recognition
that seasonal employment is a common fact of economic life, and that the
conclusion of a particular period of seasonal employment should not
automatically be viewed as the permanent end to the employment
12

relationship or evidence of the claimant's “voluntary” decision to become
unemployed. Indeed, in many cases the end of seasonal employment is
best viewed as resulting from the unavailability of further work, an economic
factor for which the claimant is not at “fault.” In our opinion, it would be
contrary to the underlying purpose of the statutory scheme to hold, as a
matter of law, that termination of employment resulting from the conclusion
of a contract for seasonal work automatically disqualifies the claimant from
receiving subsequent TTD benefits. Cf. J.D. Lunsford v. Sawatsky, 780 P.2d
76 (Colo. App. 1989) (if claimant loses job because of economic factors and
is not at fault for the termination, claimant is entitled to TTD benefits). The
fact that the claimant knows the seasonal employment will end at a fixed
point in time does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that he is
responsible for the termination. City of Aurora v. Dortch, supra.
Judd v. Antarctic Support Svcs, supra.
K. While Claimant’s employment was not seasonal in the same exact sense, the
reasoning applies with respect to employment for an agreed upon fixed term. The
courts have also recognized that the result might be different if the ALJ were to
find the claimant selected a fixed period of seasonal employment with the intent
of remaining unemployed throughout a portion of the year, or permanently. See
El Paso County Department of Social Services v. Donn, 865 P.2d 877 (Colo.
App. 1986); Judd v. Antarctic Support Svcs, supra. The ALJ has made no such
finding in Claimant’s case. Claimant credibly and persuasively testified that, when
he signed his 2024 contract, his plan at the expiration of the contract was to
continue playing in the NFL and that he would have liked to continue playing for
Employer. As credibly and persuasively testified to by Claimant and documented
by providers, Claimant underwent extensive rehabilitation and training with the
intention of continuing to play NFL football. Despite not receiving physician
clearance, Claimant even participated in tryouts for Employer in October 2025 in
hopes of continuing his employment with the NFL. The evidence demonstrates
13

Claimant intended to continue working as an NFL player when he agreed to, and
upon the expiration of, his fixed term contract.
L. Claimant and Employer entered into multiple contracts over the course of six
seasons, with Employer citing unsatisfactory skill or performance as compared
with other players as the reason for termination of the contracts. Mr. Hurtado
testified that Employer’s decision not to offer Claimant a new contract in 2025
was based on Claimant’s performance compared to other players and not
Claimant’s industrial injury. While there was no guarantee Employer would offer
Claimant a new contract for the 2025 season upon the expiration of his 2024
contract, the evidence clearly demonstrates that the effects of the industrial injury
impaired Claimant’s ability to participate in professional football activities and
adequately perform his regular job duties, thus impairing his wage earning
capacity. As a result of the industrial injury, Claimant was unable to play the
entire 2024 season. He remained unable to play at the expiration of his contract
and no evidence was offered demonstrating Claimant was subsequently cleared
to play. Even when Claimant attempted to play during tryouts in October 2025,
he experienced continuing right ankle issues which impaired his ability to
adequately participate in professional football activities. Dr. Primack credibly
opined that, due to the residual effects of the industrial injury, it is “obvious”
Claimant would not be able to adequately perform the essential functions of the
job as an offensive lineman in the NFL.
M. In light of the totality of the circumstances of this case, the fact that Claimant’s
employment ended at the expiration of an agreed upon fixed term does not
render Claimant responsible for the termination of the employment and the
resulting wage loss.
Disfigurement
N. Section 8-42-108(1), C.R.S. provides that a claimant is entitled to additional
compensation if he is “seriously, permanently disfigured about the head, face, or
parts of the body normally exposed to public view.”
14

O. As found, Claimant sustained a serious permanent disfigurement to areas of the
body normally exposed to public view. Respondents shall pay Claimant
$3.750.00 for his disfigurement.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that he is entitled to TTD
benefits from March 13, 2025, through February 11, 2026.
2. Respondents failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence Claimant is
responsible for his termination from employment.
3. Respondents shall pay Claimant TTD benefits from March 13, 2025 to February
11, 2026.
4. Respondents shall pay Claimant $3,750.00 for his disfigurement.
5. Respondents shall pay statutory interest at a rate of 8% per annum on
compensation benefits not paid when due.
6. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20), days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the

aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
15

by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
