title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-026-826-003
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-026-826-003
Issues
Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that his
⮚
claim should be reopened pursuant to Section 8-43-303?
Whether Respondents have proven by a preponderance of the evidence
⮚
that they are entitled to a repayment of the overpayment of benefits provided to
Claimant?
Whether Respondents have proven by a preponderance of the evidence
⮚
that Claimant is subject to penalties pursuant to Section 8-43-304(1), C.R.S. for failing
to comply with a prehearing conference order compelling additional answers to
discovery dated January 7, 2026?
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant sustained an admitted injury to his left foot arising out of and in
the course and scope of his employment with Employer on July 5, 2016. Claimant
reported the injury to Employer and an Employer’s First Report of Injury was filed with
the Division of Workers’ Compensation on October 27, 2016. Respondents eventually
filed a general admission of liability (“GAL”) admitting for temporary total disability
(“TTD”) benefits on December 9, 2016. The TTD benefits commenced on November 3,
2016 according to the GAL.
2. Claimant was referred to Dr. Zyzda for medical treatment. Dr. Zyzda
referred Claimant for a magnetic resonance image (“MRI”) of the left foot on November
10, 2016. The MRI showed a second web space neuroma. Dr. Zyzda provided
Claimant with an injection into his foot. Claimant testified that his pain increased after
the injection.
1

3. Claimant testified at hearing that Dr. Zyzda included in one of his reports
incorrect information regarding Claimant’s drug and alcohol use which resulted in
Claimant and Dr. Zyzda terminating their doctor-patient relationship.
4. Claimant’s medical care was then transferred to Dr. Lugliani with Health
One Occupational Medicine. Dr. Lugliani initially examined Claimant on December 14,
2016. Dr. Lugliani reviewed Claimant’s MRI scan and noted the presence of a Morton
neuroma at the second interspace at the metatarsal phalangeal joint. Claimant reported
consistent pain at an 8/10 level that he described as achy, burning and stabbing in
nature, with numbness and tingling into his toe. Claimant reported prolonged standing
made his symptoms worse. Dr. Lugliani diagnosed Claimant with left foot pain
secondary to neuroma and recommended a referral to orthopedics for further evaluation
and treatment. Claimant was provided with work restrictions for seated work only and
provided with an orthotic boot.
5. Claimant returned to Dr. Lugliani on January 23, 2017. Dr. Lugliani noted
Claimant had an appointment with Dr. Myers, for an orthopedic evaluation on January
24. Dr. Lugliani continued Claimant’s work restrictions and instructed Claimant to return
on January 30, 2017 after his consultation with Dr. Myers.
6. Dr. Myers evaluated Claimant on January 24, 2017. Dr. Myers noted
complained of forefoot pain on examination and Dr. Zyzda had performed an injection
into the second web space. Dr. Myers reviewed the MRI and performed a physical
examination. Dr. Myers noted that Claimant had treatment options for his neuroma
which included topical analgesic cream, serial alcohol injections or surgical excision.
With regard to causation, Dr. Myers opined that Claimant’s neuroma developed post
injury and therefore, the pain and associated symptoms were “resulted from the injury.”
Dr. Myers noted that he did not believe it to be possible to determine the existence of
the neuroma prior to the injury. Claimant was instructed to return back to Dr. Myers in
three weeks.
2

7. Claimant testified he moved to Georgia in February 2017 and came under
the care of Dr. Armenia. Claimant was evaluated by Dr. Armenia on March 22, 2017.
Dr. Armenia recommended a referral to an orthopedic foot specialist.
8. Respondents wrote a letter to Dr. Lugliani on March 7, 2017 requesting he
answer questions regarding the causation of Claimant’s neuroma. The letter indicates
Claimant was carbon copied (“cc’d”) on the letter, but Claimant at hearing took issue
with the communication between Respondents and the physicians in this case. Dr.
Lugliani responded to the letter on March 13, 2017 in a confusing manner insofar as he
agreed with a statement that the neuroma was pre-existing but opined that Claimant
was not at MMI for his work injury because he would need surgery. Claimant’s surgery
was then denied as a compensable component of his work injury for a period of time
while Respondents sought an opinion in an attempt to determine that causal connection
of the surgery to the work injury.
9. Respondents arranged for an independent medical examination (“IME”) of
Claimant with Dr. Lahiji in Atlanta, Georgia on August 28, 2017. Dr. Lahiji reviewed
Claimant’s medical records, obtained a medical history and performed a physical
examination in connection with his IME. Dr. Lahiji opined in his report that Claimant’s
complaints appeared to be consistent with a neuroma involving the 2-3 intermetatarsal
nerve of the left forefoot. Dr. Lahiji opined that the cause of the nerve irritation could be
related to his work activities. Dr. Lahiji recommended surgical intervention to treat the
neuroma.
10. Claimant testified that the surgery at this point was still not authorized and
he emailed the adjuster on the claim and asked the adjuster to deny the claim.
Claimant testified the adjuster told Claimant to have his private insurance pay for the
claim.
11. Claimant testified that on June 11, 2018, Respondents sent Claimant
notice of a demand appointment with Dr. Luigiani. Claimant returned to Dr. Lugiani on
July 11, 2018. Dr. Lugiani issued a report following his examination of Claimant that
stated that he agreed with Dr. Myers that Claimant’s condition was related to his work
3

injury and that Claimant required surgery. Dr. Lugiani opined in his report that Claimant
should continue with work restrictions that included seated work only.
12. At hearing, Claimant took issue with the letter written by the adjuster to Dr.
Lugiani prior to the one-time evaluation. Claimant testified at hearing that he was
shown the letter by Dr. Lugiani when he arrived for the appointment. However, the
exhibit entered into evidence by Claimant representing the letter from the adjuster to Dr.
Lugiani is incomplete as it is a photo of the letter and cuts off the bottom part of the
letter so the ALJ can not ascertain from the exhibit whether Claimant was included on
the letter or not. Even assuming, arguendo, that this letter represented some type of
improper communication with Dr. Lugiani, the ALJ notes that no issues were raised with
regard to the letter until the hearing, which took place over seven years after the letter
was authored. Therefore, the ALJ finds that there is no legal remedy that the court
could apply in this case even if the letter represented improper communication with Dr.
Lugiani. The ALJ further concludes that the communication does not rise to the level of
fraud that would justify reopening Claimant’s claim.
13. Claimant eventually underwent surgery under the auspices of Dr. Johnson
on June 26, 2019. The surgery consisted of the excision of a digital nerve in his left
foot. Following Claimant’s surgery he continued to treat with Dr. Johnson. Dr. Johnson
evaluated Claimant on August 3, 2020. Dr. Johnson noted that on his previous
examination (which was six months post operation), Claimant was complaining of back
pain and right foot pain along with some knee pain that he attributed to his left foot
injury. Dr. Johnson noted that Claimant indicated that he did not feet he would be 100%
able to do a functional capacity evaluation (“FCE”). Dr. Johnson noted that Claimant
was now saying that his left foot is not improved and his right foot pain was related to
his left foot injury. Dr. Johnson noted that the FCE did not take place yet. Dr. Johnson
noted that with regard to Claimant’s workers’ compensation injury, he did not need
additional intervention, but could use some good formal orthotic, semi-accommodative
total-contact insert, and metatarsal posting. Dr. Johnson recommended seeing if they
could get Claimant the inserts and set him up for the final FCE and rating. Claimant
4

testified at hearing that he could not complete the FCE because he had other issues
with his right foot and lower back pain and was told that if he had issues that would
impact his ability to complete an FCE, he should not undergo an FCE.
14. Claimant returned to Dr. Johnson on March 4, 2021 at which time Dr.
Johnson noted that Claimant had not yet completed the FCE. Dr. Johnson noted that
Claimant was at maximum medical improvement (“MMI”) and he needed to be set up
with an FCE, PIR (“personal impairment rating). Dr. Johnson noted that there was no
further intervention that needed to be done for his condition and that barring the ability
to get some kind of objective measure of what Claimant could do functionally, he could
be released to full duty without restrictions.
15. Respondents issued a letter to Dr. Johnson on April 13, 2021 inquiring as
to Claimant’s status regarding MMI and permanent impairment. In response to the
inquiry, Dr. Johnson marked the box that Claimant was at MMI and initially issued an
MMI date of April 8, 2021, before crossing out that date and writing March 4, 2021 and
initialing the change. Dr. Johnson also marked the box that indicated Claimant did not
sustain any permanent impairment and did not need any post MMI medical treatment.
Dr. Johnson dated the report May 3, 2021.
16. After receiving the May 3, 2021 report from Dr. Johnson, Respondents
attempted to get an additional physician to evaluate Claimant. Claimant testified that
Dr. White had initially refused to evaluate Claimant, but then after a phone call from
Claimant, agreed to evaluate him.
17. Respondents eventually filed a final admission of liability (“FAL”) on
December 11, 2023 attaching the May 3, 2021 report from Dr. Johnson and admitting
for TTD benefits for the period of November 3, 2016 through March 3, 2021 for a total of
$54,841.86. The FAL admitted for 0% permanent impairment and claimed an
overpayment of TTD benefits in the amount of $33,668.64.
18. Claimant emailed an objection to the FAL to the Division of Workers’
Compensation on January 5, 2024, but did not file an application for hearing. In the
objection to the FAL, Claimant checked the box indicating that he would mail or deliver
5

an Application for Hearing form on disputed issues to the Office of Administrative Courts
within 30 calendar days of the FAL.
19. Claimant eventually filed an Application for Expedited Hearing on January
22, 2024 indicating on the form that Respondents had filed a Petition to Suspend,
Modify or Terminate Compensation on December 11, 2023 and Claimant filed an
objection to the petition on January 5, 2024. The ALJ notes that the Expedited
Application for Hearing was filed 42 days after the filing of the December 11, 2023 FAL.
20. The parties proceeded to a prehearing conference before PALJ Eley on
February 21, 2024. PALJ Eley issued an Order following the prehearing conference
that struck Claimant’s Expedited Application for Hearing as there was no Petition to
Suspend Benefits that was filed by Respondents in this case. In the prehearing
conference order, PALJ Eley noted that Claimant was not contesting the finding of MMI
or the permanent impairment rating, but was contesting the date of MMI and maintained
that the FAL was fraudulent. PALJ Eley agreed in his order with Respondents
contention that the issues listed on the Application for Expedited Hearing were not ripe
for hearing as no Petition to Suspend, Modify or Terminate Compensation had been
filed and struck the Application for Expedited Hearing and vacated the hearing that was
scheduled to proceed on April 9, 2024.
21. Claimant subsequently filed a new Application for Hearing on September
12, 2025 endorsing the issues of temporary total disability benefits, petition to reopen
and alleging violations of rules, fraud and unethical conduct. Claimant attached an
addendum to the Application for Hearing listing the issues he had with regard to the
handling of the claim, which included, but was not limited to, failing to timely file a first
report of injury, failing to provide Claimant with a choice of physicians at the outset of
the claim, failure to pay the proper period of TTD benefits, failure to attend a December
12, 2016 prehearing conference, improper denial of recommended medical treatment,
failure to record IME examinations, discovery violations, improper communications with
treating physicians, and fraudulent filing of a final admission of liability. Respondents
6

filed a Response to the Application for Hearing on October 10, 2025 endorsing the
issues of statute of limitations, offset, overpayments and credits among other issues.
22. The first issue the ALJ must address is whether Claimant’s case is closed
by virtue of the December 11, 2023 FAL. The FAL filed in this case attached the May 3,
2021 report from Dr. Johnson placing Claimant at MMI and providing an opinion that no
permanent impairment and no maintenance medical treatment was necessary.
Claimant does not argue that the Respondents were not allowed to rely on the May 3,
2021 report from Dr. Johnson other than arguing that after they received the report, they
referred Claimant for additional medical evaluations with Dr. White and did not file the
FAL until December 11, 2023. However, the ALJ finds that the FAL with the report from
Dr. Johnson is in compliance with the statute and the rules insofar as Dr. Johnson
provides an opinion regarding MMI, permanent impairment and the need for ongoing
medical treatment.
23. Insofar as Claimant had an issue with regard to the FAL and the finding of
MMI or the delay in Respondents filing of the FAL after receiving the report from Dr.
Johnson, Claimant had thirty (30) days from the date of the filing of the FAL to raise
issues involving the FAL pursuant to Section 8-43-203(2)(b)(II), C.R.S. Because
Claimant failed to timely file an application for hearing with the Office of Administrative
Courts within 30 days of the filing of the FAL, the ALJ determines that Claimant’s case
is closed as a matter of law.
24. Section 8-43-303 provides that if a case is closed as a matter of law,
Claimant may reopen the case based on the ground of fraud, an overpayment involving
the circumstances described in section 8-42-113.5, an error, a mistake, or a change of
condition, if the reopening is brought within six years of the date of injury, or two years
from the date the last temporary or permanent disability benefits become due or
payable. The claim may also be reopened for medical benefits if the petition to reopen is
filed within two years after the date the last medical benefits become due or payable.
25. In this case, Claimant’s Application for Hearing on September 12, 2025
was filed more than six years from the date of injury. Additionally, the FAL filed in this
7

case admitted for TTD benefits through March 3, 2021, so the Application for Hearing
was not filed within two years of the date temporary or permanent disability benefits
became due or payable. Claimant has additionally failed to present credible evidence
that the Application for Hearing was filed within two years after the date the last medical
benefits become due or payable. Therefore, the ALJ determines that Claimant’s
request to reopen his claim at this point is barred by the statute of limitations.
26. The ALJ notes however, that Respondents bear the burden of proof to
establish that Claimant’s claim for reopening is barred by the statute of limitations.
Respondents therefore must establish that Claimant’s request to reopen his claim came
more than two years after the date the last temporary or permanent disability benefits
became due or payable. In this case, based on the overpayment alleged by
Respondents, the payment of temporary disability benefits may have continued until
December 2025 when the FAL was filed. In that case, Claimant’s request to reopen
would be within the 2 year statute of limitations and would not be barred by the time
constraints set forth in Section 8-43-303.
27. However, assuming Claimant’s request to reopen his claim for benefits
was timely, Claimant has failed to present credible evidence that his case should be
reopened based on a claim of fraud, error, mistake, or a worsening of his condition.
Claimant’s arguments involving the conduct of Respondents in handling this case do not
rise to the level of fraud to allow for a reopening of his claim. The mere fact that
Respondents did not file a timely FAL after receiving the May 3, 2021 report from Dr.
Johnson does not establish that there was any fraud, error or mistake on behalf of
Respondents in handling Claimant’s claim. Moreover, Claimant’s issues with regard to
the communication between Respondents’, their counsel, and Claimant’s treating
physicians do not rise to the level of fraud. Based on the evidence entered at hearing,
there is insufficient evidence to establish that any of the communication was ex parte,
let alone fraudulent. Therefore, based upon the evidence presented at hearing,
Claimant’s Petition to Reopen is denied.
8

28. Respondents have requested an order requiring Claimant to repay the
overpayment of $33,668.64 listed on the FAL. However, Section 8-42-113.5(b.5)(I)
provides that after the filing of an FAL, except in cases of fraud, any attempt to recover
an overpayment shall be asserted within one year after the time the requester knew of
the existence of the overpayment. In this case, the ALJ finds that the FAL was filed by
Respondents on December 11, 2023. Respondents did not assert the attempt to
recover the overpayment until the Response to Claimant’s Application for Hearing was
filed on October 10, 2025. Therefore, the request to recover the overpayment is barred
by the limitations set forth under Section 8-42-113.5(b.5)(I).
29. Respondents also seek an Order issuing penalties against Claimant for
failing to comply with the PHC Order of PALJ Eidsmoe dated January 7, 2026 that
required Claimant to provide a complete answer regarding any sources of income
Claimant has received since his date of injury. The PHC Order was issued by PALJ
Eidsmoe following a prehearing conference that took place on January 6, 2026.
Following the issuance of the PHC Order, Claimant issued Supplemental Answers to
Interrogatories in which he denied receiving any wages or earnings from employment
during the relevant periods of time. Respondents at no point raised an issue with the
Supplemental Answers to Interrogatories, requesting more specific answers or objecting
to the Supplemental Answers to Interrogatories and requesting an additional prehearing
conference to argue the deficiency of the supplemental answers, other than to raise the
issue of penalties with regard to the supplemental answers at hearing.
30. The ALJ finds that the supplemental answers to interrogatories are not so

A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101,
et seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of
litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving
entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A
preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all
of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592
P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted
neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of
respondents; and a workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-

Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-

43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceeding is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo.
App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary
inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility
determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When
determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other things, the
consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been
contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony
is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Industrial Claim Appeals
Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to
conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none
of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Industrial Commission, 441 P.2d
21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Engineering, Inc. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App.
2000).
Compensability

D. Under the Workers’ Compensation Act, an employee is entitled to compensation
where the injury or death is proximately caused by an injury or occupational
disease arising out of and in the course of the employee’s employment. Section
8-41-301(1), C.R.S. The phrases “arising out of” and “in the course of” are not
synonymous and a claimant must meet both requirements. Younger v. City &
County of Denver, 810 P.2d 647, 649 (Colo. 1991); In re Question Submitted by
U.S. Court of Appeals, 759 P.2d 17, 20 (Colo. 1988). The “in the course of”
requirement refers to the time, place, and circumstances under which a work-
related injury occurs. Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 383 (Colo. 1991). Thus,
an injury occurs “in the course of” employment when it takes place within the time
and place limits of the employment relationship and during an activity connected
with the employee’s job-related functions. In re Question Submitted by U.S. Court
of Appeals, supra; Deterts v. Times Publ’g Co., 38 Colo. App. 48, 51, 552 P.2d
1033, 1036 (1976).
E. The term “arises out of” refers to the origin or cause of an injury. Deterts v. Times
Publ’g Co., supra. There must be a causal connection between the injury and the
work conditions for the injury to arise out of employment. Younger v. City &
County of Denver, supra. An injury “arises out of” employment when it has its
origin in an employee’s work-related functions and is sufficiently related to those
functions to be considered part of the employee’s employment contract.
Popovich v. Irlando, supra. Where the claimant’s entitlement to benefits is
disputed, the claimant has the burden to prove, by a preponderance of the
evidence, a causal relationship between the work injury and the condition for
which benefits are sought. Snyder v. Indus. Claim Apps. Office, 942 P.2d 1337
(Colo. App. 1997). The question of whether the claimant met the burden of proof
to establish that his injury arose out of and in the course of his employment is
one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Jefferson County Public Schools v.
Dragoo, 765 P.2d 636 (Colo. App. 1988). As found, Claimant proved by a
preponderance of the evidence that on October 29, 2024, he sustained a
compensable left knee injury arising out of and in the course of his employment
with the Employer.

Employment Status
F. A claimant is required to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that at the
time of the injury, both he and the employer were subject to the provisions of the
Workers’ Compensation Act, that he was performing service arising out of and in
the course of his employment, and that the injury was proximately caused by the
performance of such service. Section 8-41-301(1)(a) through (c), C.R.S. The
question of whether a claimant meets the burden of proof is one of fact for
determination by the ALJ. City of Boulder v. Streeb, 706 P.2d 786 (Colo. 1985);
Faulkner v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 12 P.3d 844 (Colo. App. 2000).
G. The term “employer” is defined to include every person, firm or corporation “who
has one or more persons engaged in the same business or employment, except
as expressly provided in articles 40 to 47 of this title, in service under any
contract of hire, express or implied.” Section 8-40-203(1)(b), C.R.S. Similarly, the
term “employee” is defined as including any person in the service of any person
or corporation “under any contract of hire, express or implied.” Section 8-40-
202(1)(b), C.R.S. The definition of “employer” in this section should be broadly or
liberally construed, in order to effectuate the purpose of the legislation. Conover
v. Indus. Comm’n, 125 Colo. 388, 244 P.2d 875 (1952). Consequently, the
Workers’ Compensation Act extends the concept of “employer” far beyond the
meaning of that term at common law. Doyle v. Missouri Valley Constructors, Inc.,
288 F. Supp. 121 (D. Colo. 1968).
H. Pursuant to § 8-40-202(2)(a), C.R.S., “any individual who performs services for
pay for another shall be deemed to be an employee” unless the person “is free
from control and direction in the performance of the services, both under the
contract for performance of service and in fact and such individual is customarily
engaged in an independent . . . business related to the service performed.”
Whether a worker is an independent contractor "is a factual determination for
resolution by the ALJ." Nelson v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 981 P.2d 210, 213
(Colo. App. 1998). If a claimant establishes he performed services for pay, the
burden shifts to the employer to prove the claimant was an independent
contractor. Stampados v. Colorado D & S Enterprises, 833 P.2d 815 (Colo. App.

1992); Almanza v. W.Y.B. d/b/a What’s Your Beef, W.C. No. 4-489-774 (April 16,
2002). As found, Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that on
October 29, 2024, he was an employee of the Employer.
Medical Benefits
I. The Employer is liable for medical treatment reasonably necessary to cure or
relieve the employee from the effects of the injury. Section 8-42-101, C.R.S.
Nevertheless, the right to workers’ compensation benefits, including medical
benefits, arises only when an injured employee establishes by a preponderance
of the evidence that the need for medical treatment was proximately caused by
an injury arising out of and in the course of the employment. § 8-41-301(1),
C.R.S.; Faulkner v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 12 P.3d 844, 846 (Colo. App.
2000). Claimant must establish the causal connection with reasonable probability
but need not establish it with reasonable medical certainty. Ringsby Truck Lines,
Inc. v. Indus. Comm’n, 491 P.2d 106 (Colo. App. 1971); Indus. Comm’n v. Royal
Indemnity Co., 236 P.2d 293. A causal connection may be established by
circumstantial evidence and expert medical testimony is not necessarily required.
Indus. Comm’n v. Jones, 688 P.2d 1116 (Colo. 1984); Indus. Comm’n v. Royal
Indemnity Co., supra, 236 P.2d at 295-296. All results flowing proximately and
naturally from an industrial injury are compensable. See Standard Metals Corp.
v. Ball, 172 Colo. 510, 474 P.2d 622 (1970). Where the claimant’s entitlement to
benefits is disputed, the claimant has the burden to prove, by a preponderance of
the evidence, a causal relationship between the work injury and the condition for
which benefits are sought. Snyder v. Indus. Claim Apps. Off., 942 P.2d 1337
(Colo. App. 1997).
J. When determining the issue of whether proposed medical treatment is
reasonable and necessary the ALJ may consider the provisions and treatment
protocols of the MTG because they represent the accepted standards of practice
in workers’ compensation cases and were adopted pursuant to an express grant
of statutory authority. However, evidence of compliance or non-compliance with
the treatment criteria of the MTG is not dispositive of the question of whether

medical treatment is reasonable and necessary. Rather the ALJ may give
evidence regarding compliance with the MTG such weight as he determines it is
entitled to considering the totality of the evidence. See Adame v. SSC Berthoud
Operating Co., LLC, WC 4-784-709 (January 25, 2012); Thomas v. Four Corners
Health Care, WC 4-484-220 (April 27, 2009); Stamey v. C2 Utility Contractors,
Inc., WC 4-503-974 (August 21, 2008). As found, Claimant is entitled to
reasonable and necessary medical benefits related to his work injury.
Right of Selection
K. Under § 8-43-404(5), C.R.S., the employer has the right to choose the treating
physician in the first instance. The employer must tender medical treatment
“forthwith,” or the right of selection passes to the claimant. Rogers v. Indus.
Claim Apps. Off., 746 P.2d 565 (Colo. App. 1987). To properly exercise its right
of selection, the employer must give the claimant a list of at least four providers
from which he can choose. Section 8-43- 404(5)(a)(I)(A). The ALJ may consider
factors such as the nature of the notice given by the employer, how recently the
notice was provided, and the claimant’s individual capacity to recall the notice.
Jones v. Weld County Government, W.C. No. 4- 176-234 (December 8, 1996).
L. In this instance, Employer failed to provide Claimant with a designated provider
list. Therefore, the right of selection passed to Claimant. In situations where the
claimant has signified “by words or conduct that he has chosen a physician to
treat the industrial injury,” they have made a physician “selection.” Murphy-
Tafoya v. Safeway Inc, W.C. No. 5-153-600-001 at *4 (Sept. 1, 2021). As found,
Claimant selected, through his conduct, Denver Health as his authorized
provider.
Average Weekly Wage
M. Section 8-42-102(2), C.R.S., requires the ALJ to calculate Claimant’s average
weekly wage (AWW) based on the earnings at the time of injury as measured by
the Claimant’s monthly, weekly, daily, hourly, or other earnings. However, if for
any reason, the ALJ determines the default method will not fairly calculate the

AWW, § 8-42-102(3), C.R.S., affords the ALJ discretion to determine the AWW in
such other manner as will fairly determine the wage. § 8-42-102(3), C.R.S.
establishes the so-called “discretionary exception”. Benchmark/Elite, Inc. v.
Simpson, 232 P.3d 777 (Colo. 2010); Campbell v. IBM Corp., 867 P.2d 77 (Colo.
App. 1993). The overall objective in calculating the AWW is to arrive at a fair
approximation of Claimant’s wage loss and diminished earning capacity.
Campbell v. IBM Corp., supra; Avalanche Indus. V. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
166 P.3d 147 (Colo. App. 2007). For the reasons set forth above, the Court
concludes that a fair approximation of Claimant’s average weekly wage at the
time of injury is $1,000.
TTD Benefits
N. To prove entitlement to TTD benefits, a claimant must prove that the industrial
injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he left work as a
result of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss. See §§
8-42-(1)(g) & 8-42-105(4), C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102 P.3d 323
(Colo. 2004); City of Colorado Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 954 P.2d
637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S., requires the claimant to
establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent
wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. The term “disability” connotes two
elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily
function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971
P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her
regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo.
App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce
evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to
demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo.
App. 1997). TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence of any of the

following: (1) the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to regular or
modified employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a written
release to return to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the
employee a written release to return to modified employment, the employment is
offered in writing and the employee fails to begin the employment. Section 8-42-
105(3)(a)-(d), C.R.S.
O. As found, Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that he is entitled
to ongoing TTD benefits effective October 30, 2024. Claimant proved both
medical incapacity and impairment of wage-earning capacity resulting from the
industrial injury. Claimant sustained traumatic injuries to his left knee, including
multiple ligament and meniscal tears, after a trench collapse at work. Following
the injury, Claimant required emergency treatment, prolonged use of crutches
and bracing, physical therapy, and ongoing orthopedic care, with treating
physicians repeatedly recommending surgical intervention. Claimant credibly
testified that he has been unable to return to any employment since the injury
because of persistent pain, instability, weakness, and functional limitations
affecting his ability to stand, walk, lift, push, pull, carry, and perform the physical
duties required by his prior employment. Dr. Drumright further opined that
Claimant was unable to engage in “substantial gainful activity” because of his left
knee condition. The Court finds this evidence sufficient to prove that Claimant’s
industrial injury caused a disability resulting in actual wage loss. There is no
credible evidence that Claimant has reached maximum medical improvement,
returned to employment, or been released to regular or modified work.
Accordingly, Claimant is entitled to temporary total disability benefits
commencing October 30, 2024, and continuing until terminated by law.
Uninsured Employer
P. Pursuant to § 8-43-408(2), C.R.S, “In all cases where compensation is awarded
under the terms of this section, the director or an administrative law judge of the
division shall compute and require the employer to pay to a trustee designated by
the director or administrative law judge an amount equal to the present value of

all unpaid compensation or benefits computed at the rate of four percent per
annum; or, in lieu thereof, such employer, within ten days after the date of such
order, shall file a bond with the director or administrative law judge signed by two
or more responsible sureties to be approved by the director or by some surety
company authorized to do business within the state of Colorado. The bond shall
be in such form and amount as prescribed and fixed by the director and shall
guarantee the payment of the compensation or benefits as awarded. The filing of
any appeal, including a petition for review, shall not relieve the employer of the
obligation under this subsection (2) to pay the designated sum to a trustee or to
file a bond with the director or administrative law judge.” The term
“compensation” refers to disability benefits. Shier v. Four Points Medical Center,
W.C. No. 4-573-910 (Dec. 15, 2005). Because Employer was uninsured at the
time of Claimant’s injury, the provisions of § 8-43-408(2), C.R.S., are mandatory.
Q. With respect to TTD Benefits, Employer shall pay the CUE Fund the cost of
benefits stemming from October 29, 2024, through present date plus interest at
the rate of 4% per annum. As noted above, the record contains insufficient
evidence to permit the Court to determine the monetary value of Employer’s
liability for medical benefits. This issue is preserved for future determination, and
either party may file an Application for Hearing to resolve this issue.
Penalties
R. With respect to penalties, § 8-43-408(5), C.R.S., provides, “In addition to any
compensation paid or ordered in accordance with this section or articles 40 to 47
of this title 8, an employer who is not in compliance with the insurance provisions
of those articles at the time an employee suffers a compensable injury or
occupational disease shall pay an amount equal to twenty-five percent of the
compensation or benefits to which the employee is entitled to the Colorado
Uninsured Employer Fund created in section § 8-67-105, C.R.S.
S. Employer did not have workers’ compensation coverage at the time of Claimant’s
work injury. For its failure to obtain and maintain workers’ compensation

insurance, Employer shall pay penalties to the CUE Fund in an amount equal to
25% of the total unpaid TTD benefits owed as of present date.
T. Because the record contains insufficient evidence of the amount of medical bills
incurred by Claimant for injury-related treatment, the Court is unable to calculate
any penalty to be assessed as a percentage of medical bills. Consequently, the
amount of any penalty based on medical benefits is reserved for future
determination.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. On October 29, 2024, Claimant sustained a compensable
injury arising out of and in the course of his employment with
the Employer.
2. At the time of his October 29, 2024, injury, Claimant was an
employee of Employer.
3. On October 29, 2024, the Employer failed to possess workers’
compensation insurance.
4. Claimant is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical
benefits to cure or relieve the effects of his October 29, 2024,
injury. Claimant’s injury-related treatment received to date is
reasonable and necessary.
5. The right of selection of the authorized provider passed to
Claimant and Claimant selected by his conduct Denver
Health.
6. Claimant’s Average Weekly Wage is $1,000, with a
corresponding TTD rate of $666.67.
7. Employer is liable for ongoing TTD payments beginning
October 30, 2024 and continuing until terminated by law.
8. Employer is liable for payment of Claimant’s medical
expenses pursuant to the Division of Workers’ Compensation

Medical Fee Schedule. The monetary amount of past medical
benefits is reserved for future determination. Because the
Employer is liable for payment of Claimant’s medical costs
associated with his work injury, no medical provider shall seek
to recover such costs from Claimant, pursuant to § 8-42-
101(4), C.R.S.
9. Employer is subject to penalties for failure to maintain
workers’ compensation insurance. The Employer shall pay to
the CUE Fund a penalty equal to 25% of the TTD benefits
awarded.
10. In lieu of payment of the above compensation and benefits to
the Claimant, the Employer shall:
a. Deposit the sum of the TTD payments with the Division of
Workers’ Compensation as trustee, to secure the payment
of all unpaid TTD benefits awarded. The check shall be
payable to and sent to the Division of Workers;
Compensation Division Trustee, c/o Mariya Cassin, 633
17th Street, Suite 400, Denver, CO 80202; or
b. File a bond in the sum of the TTD payments with the
Division of Workers’ Compensation within ten (10) days of
the date of this order:
i. Signed by two or more responsible sureties who
have received prior approval of the Division of
Workers’ Compensation; or
ii. Issued by a surety company authorized to do
business in Colorado.
iii. The bond shall guarantee payment of the
compensation and benefit awarded.
11. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future
determination.

If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
