title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-237-161-002
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-237-161-002
Issues
Whether Claimant established by a preponderance of the evidence that the hip
⮚
surgery recommended by Dr. Snyder is reasonably necessary and related to his
work injury.
Stipulations
The parties stipulated, and the ALJ accepts, that this is an admitted claim for
injuries sustained on April 17, 2023, while Claimant was acting in the course and scope
of his employment.
Respondents do not dispute that the recommended left hip surgery is reasonable
and necessary; the only contested issue is whether the hip injury and need for the
surgery is causally related to the April 17, 2023, work incident.
Findings of Fact
Background and Employment
1. On April 17, 2023, Claimant was employed with the Logan County Sheriff's Office. At
the time of the injury, he was working as a patrol deputy.
The April 17, 2023, Work Incident
2. On April 17, 2023, Claimant responded to a single-vehicle motor-vehicle accident
involving a driver trapped in a burning car. The vehicle had lost control and ultimately
came to rest wedged between a concrete embankment and a concrete overpass.
3. To reach the burning vehicle, Claimant initially attempted to climb up the steep concrete
embankment under the overpass but was unable to do so. He then ran up a steep soft
1

dirt portion of the embankment with a fire extinguisher to reach the burning car.
Because of the narrow space between the overpass and embankment, he was on his
hands, knees, and abdomen attempting to reach the car. He backed out, ran further up
the embankment, climbed over a guardrail, crossed the highway and climbed over a
second guardrail, ran back down the embankment, and crawled approximately ten feet
into the space beneath the overpass to attempt to access the car from the other side.
4. Claimant attempted to extinguish the fire with a fire extinguisher and while doing so, he
inhaled a significant amount of smoke. While Claimant was attempting to extinguish the
fire, the car exploded. Due to the explosion, Claimant rotated to his left and fell back
onto his knees. He was overcome by thick, heavy smoke. He had difficulty breathing.
After exhausting two fire extinguishers, with a third extinguisher being brought to the
scene unsuccessfully, the fire department arrived and took over. Because of the heavy
smoke, Claimant was unable to walk out under his own power. EMS assisted him to an
ambulance, which transported him to Sterling Regional Medical Center.
5. The incident was recorded on Claimant's body-worn camera and is admitted as Exhibit
21. The body-camera footage corroborates the general sequence and physically
demanding nature of the rescue effort, including Claimant running up and down the
embankment, the constrained position underneath the overpass, his exposure to a
significant amount of smoke, the explosion, and his rotation to the left and fall onto his
knees following the explosion.
6. By the end of the rescue attempt, Claimant had developed left hip-region pain.
Pre-Injury Status
7. Claimant credibly testified that he had no left hip symptoms before the April 17, 2023,
work incident. He was working full duty as a patrol deputy with the Sheriff's Office.
Before April 17, 2023, Claimant had never treated for left hip or groin symptoms,
undergone imaging of the left hip, received a left hip injection, or received a
recommendation for left hip surgery. He had passed all required qualifications and
2

training for law enforcement. He had no functional limitations involving lifting his leg,
putting on shoes or socks, or walking.
Initial Hospital Treatment
10.Claimant was taken by ambulance to the Sterling Regional Medical Center after his
attempts to put out the fire and save the driver of the car. The emergency room records
reflect significant smoke inhalation and respiratory distress, and Claimant required
intubation. Because of his respiratory condition, he was unable to provide a detailed
history at the time. The records nevertheless document left-sided complaints, including
left lower quadrant pain and left flank pain. Due to pelvic pain, an x-ray was taken of his
pelvis and it was negative for a fracture. CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was
also performed and showed dependent atelectasis and possible consolidation but no
evidence of acute blunt-force traumatic injury.
11.Because of the seriousness of his exposure and injuries, Claimant was transported by
air to Swedish Hospital and admitted to the intensive care unit. He underwent CT
imaging of the cervical spine and head, which showed multilevel degenerative changes
without substantial osseous spinal narrowing and no acute findings. A bronchoscopy
was performed and was interpreted as "unimpressive." Claimant improved overnight
and was extubated.
12.The ALJ finds that pelvic pain, left flank pain, and left lower quadrant pain are
anatomically consistent with hip-region pain/injury, even though the providers have yet
to make a formal diagnosis of left hip labral pathology. The presence of pelvic, left flank,
and left lower quadrant complaints on the date of injury, which was sufficient to prompt
the ordering of pelvic imaging, is part of the relevant medical history and chronology in
determining whether Claimant injured his hip during the incident and requires surgery.
Treatment with Dr. Mackintosh
13.On April 21, 2023, just three days after being discharged from the hospital and just four
days after the accident, Claimant started treating with Adam Mackintosh, DO, a family-
medicine physician. Claimant reported being very sore on the left side from the blast.
3

Dr. Mackintosh diagnosed pain on the left side of the body, right wrist pain, and a
smoke-inhalation injury. Although the April 21, 2023, record does not identify left hip or
groin pain, the ALJ finds this unsurprising given that the visit occurred only four days
after a serious blast and smoke-inhalation, shortly after being discharged from the
hospital, and that the physician was attempting to assess a multi-system presentation.
14.On May 8, 2023, Claimant returned to Dr. Mackintosh for what appears to have been his
second medical appointment following his discharge from the hospital. This visit is
significant. Claimant continued to complain of left-sided body pain and reported deep
soreness in his core muscles when pulling his legs up to put on socks. He also reported
bruising, though the location was not identified in the record. Most importantly, Dr.
Mackintosh documented that Claimant had a mild limp.
15.The ALJ finds that Claimant’s reported difficulty pulling his legs up to put on socks,
together with Dr. Mackintosh’s observation of a limp, is consistent with symptoms
involving the left hip or groin. These symptoms were documented at what appears to
have been Claimant’s second post-discharge medical appointment, approximately three
weeks after the April 17, 2023, work incident. The fact that the symptoms were first
specifically documented on May 8 does not establish that they first began on that date;
it establishes only when they were first recorded by a medical provider. Given the
serious concerns of the initial blast and smoke-inhalation injury, Claimant’s recent
hospital discharge, and the broader focus of the early medical evaluations, the absence
of an earlier specific reference to “hip” or “groin” pain does not persuade the ALJ that
those symptoms were unrelated to the work incident or absent from the outset. Rather,
the May 8 record supports a finding that Claimant experienced symptoms consistent
with a left hip or groin injury following the April 17, 2023, rescue incident, and that those
symptoms became more identifiable as the evaluation and treatment of his work-related
injuries progressed.
16.Claimant returned to Dr. Mackintosh on June 7, 2023. At that visit, Dr. Mackintosh
documented groin pain when Claimant bent to put on his socks, stretching of the left hip
flexors, and continued left-sided pain. The ALJ finds this record significant because it
4

provides more specific documentation of the hip-region symptoms that were suggested
by the May 8 findings, including difficulty putting on socks and a mild limp. Although
June 7 appears to be the first specific documentation of groin pain, the record is better
understood as a further refinement of Claimant’s evolving symptom presentation and
the assessment of the injuries caused by the accident, not as evidence that the hip-
region symptoms began on that date. When considered with the earlier reports
documenting imaging of the pelvis due to pain right after the accident, left lower
quadrant pain, left flank pain, pelvic pain, left-sided body pain, difficulty lifting his legs to
put on socks, and a mild limp, the June 7 record supports a finding that Claimant’s left
hip-region symptoms were temporally related to the April 17, 2023, rescue incident and
became a more prominent focus of treatment as the evaluation of his work-related
injuries progressed.
17.Claimant returned to Dr. Mackintosh on June 26, 2023, due to ongoing pain. Because of
Claimant's ongoing complaints, Dr. Mackintosh considered a referral to a physical
medicine and rehabilitation physician.
18.On July 7, 2023, Claimant saw PA Hicks in Dr. Mackintosh's office. PA Hicks
documented increased pain, difficulty getting out of bed (taking ten minutes),
aggravation with movement and sitting, and an inability to lift the left foot to put on a
sock or shoe or to raise the foot or leg. Due to Claimant’s ongoing symptoms, PA Hicks
referred Claimant to Dr. Reichhardt, a physiatrist.
19.On August 7, 2023, Claimant saw Dr. Mackintosh. The notes from that visit indicate
Claimant had returned to work. However, Claimant continued to have left-sided pain at
6/10 after he worked at a fair while wearing his duty vest. He also had left leg pain and
an inability to lift his leg. Again, the ALJ finds these symptoms consistent with hip
pathology/injury.
Referral, Diagnostic Workup, and Surgical Recommendation
20.On September 12, 2023, Claimant was evaluated by Greg Reichhardt, M.D., a
physiatrist. Dr. Reichhardt documented left flank, chest wall, and groin pain following the
5

work injury. By this visit, Claimant’s primary pain complaint was left groin pain. Dr.
Reichhardt documented difficulty flexing the left hip, difficulty putting on socks, an
antalgic gait, i.e., an limp, favoring the left leg, decreased lumbar range of motion due to
groin pain, and tenderness over the periumbilical region without a palpable hernia.
Based on his evaluation, Dr. Reichhardt suspected a possible left hip labral tear and
also considered whether Claimant could have complications from a prior periumbilical or
inguinal hernia. He recommended an MR arthrogram of the left hip, a general surgery
consultation to rule out hernias, and MRI studies of the thoracic and lumbar spine. The
ALJ finds that Dr. Reichhardt’s evaluation is consistent with the prior medical
chronology. It reflects that Claimant’s left hip and groin symptoms had become the
primary, while providers continued to consider other possible explanations for
Claimant’s broader left-sided and abdominal complaints. Dr. Reichhardt’s
documentation of left groin pain, difficulty flexing the hip, difficulty putting on socks, and
an antalgic gait further supports the finding that Claimant’s post-injury symptoms
involved the left hip region and relate back to the April 17, 2023, work incident.
21.Claimant was evaluated by Alan Sears, M.D., a general surgeon, on October 2, 2023.
Dr. Sears determined that Claimant did not have a hernia causing his pain and
concluded that the pain was most likely musculoskeletal.
22.The MR arthrogram of the left hip was performed on June 7, 2024. The study revealed
hip morphology that can predispose to mixed femoral acetabular impingement, and a
non-displaced anterosuperior left acetabular labral tear.
23.Based on the continued focus on Claimant’s left hip and groin complaints, Dr.
Reichhardt’s physical examination findings, and the subsequent left hip imaging
findings, Claimant was referred to Joshua Snyder, M.D., an orthopedic surgeon. Dr.
Snyder evaluated Claimant on July 15, 2024. He noted Claimant’s history of left hip pain
since the work injury. On examination, Claimant had an antalgic gait, decreased range
of motion, positive impingement signs, a positive FABER test, and pain with resisted hip
flexion and abduction. Imaging showed a left center-edge angle of 50 degrees with
slightly decreased joint space at 4 mm and a right center-edge angle of 45 degrees. Dr.
6

Snyder recommended physical therapy and avoidance of deep flexion, internal rotation,
and external rotation. He further noted that, if Claimant did not improve, he would
recommend arthroscopic surgery, with possible microfracture, femoral neck
osteochondroplasty, acetabuloplasty, and capsular closure. The ALJ finds that Dr.
Snyder’s evaluation is consistent with the earlier medical chronology documenting left-
sided pain, difficulty putting on socks, groin pain, hip-flexor involvement, and an antalgic
gait. His evaluation further supports the finding that Claimant’s left hip condition was
part of the same continuum of symptoms that began with the April 17, 2023, work
incident and became a more prominent focus of treatment as the post-injury evaluations
continued.
Dr. O'Brien's IME
25.At Respondents' request, Timothy S. O'Brien, M.D., a board-certified orthopedic
surgeon, conducted an independent medical examination of Claimant on November 13,
2024. He issued a report dated November 25, 2024, and a supplemental report dated
January 14, 2025, addressing dry needling.
26.Dr. O'Brien diagnosed preexisting left hip femoral acetabular impingement and
underlying degenerative arthritis and chondromalacia. He opined that the April 17, 2023,
work incident did not result in a musculoskeletal injury and did not substantially
aggravate or accelerate beyond its normal rate of progression Claimant's preexisting left
hip femoral acetabular impingement and underlying degenerative arthritis. He opined
that the recommended left hip arthroscopic surgery, while reasonable, was not causally
related to the work incident.
27.Dr. O'Brien's stated reasons for his causation opinion included that there was no
mechanism of injury, that Claimant reported the explosion pushed him backward but did
not fall and did not twist; that an acute traumatic labral tear typically results from highly
traumatic and very energetic injuries such as hip dislocation; that more than 98% of
labral tears occur due to degeneration and day-to-day attritional tearing; that the MRI
showed chronic degenerative changes that were long-standing and a hypoplastic
7

labrum, which is a congenital condition predisposing to degenerative tearing; and that
Claimant did not complain of left groin pain until "nearly five months had passed."
Dr. O’Brien’s Testimony
28.Dr. O'Brien was deposed on March 20, 2026. Before his deposition, Dr. O'Brien
reviewed additional medical records from Dr. Mackintosh's office, the body-camera
footage of the incident, and the transcript of the February 26, 2026, hearing.
29.Dr. O'Brien testified that he met with Claimant on November 13, 2024, for the purpose
of determining whether the recommended hip surgery was indicated and causally
related to the April 17, 2023, incident. He confirmed that an accurate description of the
mechanism of injury and an accurate description of the onset and progression of
symptoms is important in determining causation.
30.With respect to the mechanism of injury, Dr. O'Brien testified that, at the time of the IME,
Claimant told him it was difficult to know exactly what happened at the time of the
incident because he lost consciousness and woke up in the emergency room. Dr.
O'Brien further testified that, at the IME, Claimant indicated most of his recollection of
what happened was from his own review of the body-camera footage, not from an
actual memory of what happened.
31.With respect to the medical-record chronology, Dr. O'Brien testified that the June 7,
2023, clinical note from Dr. Mackintosh was the first record to expressly mention left
groin pain. He asserted that the September 12, 2023, report from Dr. Reichhardt, which
stated Claimant had been having groin pain since April 17, 2023, was not accurate.
32.Dr. O'Brien testified that, in his opinion, the time gap between the April 17, 2023,
incident and what he characterized as the first sustained complaint of left hip pain in
September 2023 was a five-month gap that "excludes any temporal relationship
between the two." When asked whether his opinion would change if the onset of groin
pain was June 7, 2023, Dr. O'Brien testified that even if there had been "sustained
complaints of groin pain beginning on June 7th, I would still not have attributed those
sustained complaints of groin pain to the April 17th, 2023, incident. That's a long gap in
8

time, especially given the complaints that did exist between April and June 7th, which
were not groin related."
33.Dr. O'Brien testified that the April 17, 2023, incident "had no impact on the preexisting
condition. It didn't create an acceleration. It didn't create any type of aggravation. So the
April 17th, 2023, incident did not create any type of hip injury."
34.With respect to the imaging, Dr. O'Brien testified that the June 7, 2024, MRI showed
chronic degenerative changes that were long-standing, that some of the most significant
findings were congenital and that there was nothing acute on the MRI scan. He testified
that the vast majority of labral tears occur without trauma, that more than 95 percent of
the labral tears he has encountered clinically resulted from a congenital starting point
combined with the aging process, and that labral tears occur over the course of
thousands or millions of repetitions of hip motion and weight bearing. He compared the
development of a degenerative labral tear to "how the Grand Canyon was formed with a
little trickle of water over the course of, you know, hundreds of thousands of years."
35.Dr. O'Brien also testified about a CT scan obtained on the date of the incident. He
acknowledged that the CT scan documented the presence of mild degenerative
changes in both hips.
36.On cross-examination, Dr. O'Brien acknowledged each of the following with respect to
Claimant's pre-injury status: prior to April 17, 2023, Claimant was fully functional; was
not under any restrictions; was working full duty as a Logan County deputy; had passed
all required law-enforcement qualifications and trainings; had never treated for his left
hip; had never had an MRI of his left hip; had never had a recommendation for left hip
injections; had never had a surgical recommendation for the left hip; had never been
diagnosed with a labral tear of the left hip; and had never been diagnosed with chronic
degenerative changes of his left hip. He further acknowledged that Claimant has no
symptoms or functional issues in his right hip and has never been treated for his right
hip.
37.Dr. O'Brien further acknowledged on cross-examination that Claimant reported left flank
pain and pelvic pain in the emergency room on the date of injury. He also
9

acknowledged that, on May 8, 2023, Claimant reported he could not lift his leg to put his
socks on; that on June 7, 2023, Claimant reported he could not lift his leg to put his sock
on, with pain in the groin area; that Claimant reported difficulty lifting his leg and foot
toward him after April 17, 2023; and that Claimant reported difficulty getting up from a
seated position after April 17, 2023.
38.With respect to the basis for his causation opinion, Dr. O'Brien testified on redirect that
his opinion was not based on whether Claimant had pre-injury symptoms in his left hip,
was not based on whether Claimant had pre-injury treatment in his left hip, and was
instead based on his view that the left hip pain "occurred insidiously subsequent to April
17th, 2023."
39.Finally, Dr. O'Brien testified about his post-IME review of the body-camera footage. He
acknowledged that, after the explosion, Claimant "threw his arms up and turned to the
left and got up on his knees, walked a couple of steps and, kind of, went down to a knee
and his hands." Dr. O'Brien testified that, in his interpretation, "nothing happened after
the explosion had anything to do with falling."
Dr. Wilcox’s IME
40.At Claimant's request, Elizabeth Wilcox, M.D., M.P.H., F.A.C.O.E.M., a board-certified
occupational medicine physician, conducted an independent medical examination of
Claimant on May 19, 2025, and issued a report dated June 5, 2025. Dr. Wilcox reviewed
the medical records, the entire 30-minute body-camera footage of the rescue attempt,
Claimant's pre-injury status, and the progression of symptoms.
41.Dr. Wilcox diagnosed, among other conditions, "left hip labral tear with femoral
acetabular impingement, pre-existing, but permanently aggravated as a result of his
work injury." She opined to a reasonable degree of medical probability that the
symptomatic labral tear and femoral acetabular impingement is solely due to the work
injury. She explained that although Claimant may have had evidence of a labral tear and
impingement prior to his injury, he was asymptomatic, had never been treated for hip
pain or groin pain (outside of his prior unrelated hernia), and was working full duty in a
heavy-duty category without limitations.
10

42.Dr. Wilcox specifically rejected Dr. O'Brien's mechanism analysis. She stated: "Dr.
O'Brien is wrong in his opinion regarding the mechanism of injury. At the time of the
explosion, time stamp 3 minutes 47 seconds, it clearly showed Claimant falling back,
rotating to his left and landing on his hands and knees." She further explained that the
body-camera footage showed a clear mechanism for the symptomatic labral tear and
femoral acetabular impingement, including significant time on his hands, knees, and
abdomen attempting to reach the victim, climbing up and down a steep embankment,
and jumping over guardrails.
Credibility and Weight of the Evidence
43.The ALJ has considered the testimony, written reports, and the medical records and
makes the following credibility determinations.
Claimant’s Credibility
44.Claimant is found credible regarding his pre-injury asymptomatic status, the absence of
prior left hip symptoms or treatment, the physical exertion and physical requirements of
his rescue activities on April 17, 2023, his exposure to the vehicle explosion and the
effect it had on his body, and the presence of ongoing post-incident left hip-region
symptoms. His testimony on these points is corroborated by the body-camera footage,
the contemporaneous medical records, and the pattern of left-sided, pelvic, groin, and
hip-region complaints documented in the medical records after the work incident.
45.The ALJ does not find Claimant’s testimony reliable regarding the precise moment his
left hip pain began or regarding the assertion in his Answers to Interrogatories that his
left hip pain was 9/10 while he was running up the embankment and crawling toward the
burning vehicle. Claimant has reported that he lost consciousness or could not recall
portions of the incident, although the body-camera footage does not clearly show
Claimant passing out. In addition, the contemporaneous medical records from the date
of injury and the weeks that followed do not document an immediate complaint of 9/10
left hip or groin pain. The ALJ finds, however, that these inconsistencies do not reflect
an intentional misrepresentation by Claimant. Rather, Claimant’s later descriptions of
the precise onset, mechanism, and severity of his hip pain were influenced by the
11

passage of time, his incomplete recollection of the traumatic event, his review of the
body-camera footage, and his attempt to reconstruct the timing of symptoms during a
chaotic and traumatic rescue incident.
46.For these reasons, the ALJ does not rely on Claimant’s testimony to find that he
sustained a new acute traumatic labral tear with immediate disabling groin pain during
the incident. But the ALJ does rely on Claimant’s testimony to find that he did develop
hip and groin pain right after the accident, that such pain was continuous, and that those
symptoms are consistent with the aggravation of a preexisting condition. The ALJ also
relies on the contemporaneous medical records, the chronology of symptoms and care,
the body-camera evidence, Claimant’s pre-injury asymptomatic baseline, and the
medical opinions to the extent they are consistent with the record as a whole. Based on
that evidence, the ALJ finds that Claimant developed left hip-region pain, i.e., a hip
injury, during the April 17, 2023, rescue attempt and that the pain continued thereafter.
The early medical records’ lack of specific focus on the left hip does not undermine that
finding because Claimant was initially being evaluated and treated for multiple injuries
and conditions, including the more urgent smoke-inhalation injury.
Dr. O’Brien
47.After the IME and before his deposition, Dr. O’Brien reviewed the body-camera footage.
Confronted with that footage, he conceded that after the explosion Claimant “threw his
arms up and turned to the left and got up on his knees, walked a couple of steps and,
kind of, went down to a knee and his hands.” That description is materially different from
Dr. O’Brien’s pre-deposition characterization that the explosion “only served to push him
backward a small distance” and that Claimant “did not fall” and “did not twist.” Although
Dr. O’Brien continued to resist characterizing the movement as a fall, the physical
sequence he conceded that turning left, going to his knees, and then going to a knee
and his hands is substantially consistent with Dr. Wilcox’s description of Claimant falling
back, rotating left, and landing on his hands and knees. The ALJ finds that Dr. O’Brien’s
original mechanism description was materially inaccurate and that his later semantic
distinction did not cure the inaccuracy.
12

48.The ALJ credits Dr. O’Brien’s opinion only to the limited extent that the imaging reflects
preexisting degenerative pathology and that the surgery is reasonable and necessary.
The ALJ does not credit his broader causation opinion that the April 17, 2023, work
incident neither aggravated nor accelerated Claimant’s previously asymptomatic
degenerative left hip condition. The reasons for such findings are set forth below.
49.First, Dr. O'Brien appeared to primarily address a narrower question than the one
presented. He repeatedly focused on whether Claimant sustained a new acute
traumatic labral tear, emphasizing the absence of hip dislocation, fracture, immediate
profound groin pain, and inability to walk. But the issues in this case are not limited to
whether Claimant suffered a new traumatic labral tear. The issue also includes whether
the work incident aggravated or accelerated a previously asymptomatic preexisting
condition and caused the need for the surgery recommended by Dr. Snyder. While Dr.
O’Brien also concluded Claimant did not suffer an aggravation of a preexisting
condition, the ALJ finds that Dr. O'Brien did not meaningfully analyze that issue.
50.Dr. O'Brien's own testimony confirms this defect. He conceded that his causation
opinion was not based on whether Claimant had pre-injury symptoms and was not
based on whether Claimant had pre-injury treatment. Instead, he attributed the left hip
symptoms to an insidious onset after April 17, 2023. That concession is significant. In an
aggravation case, the asymptomatic pre-injury baseline is a central fact. By treating that
baseline as immaterial, Dr. O'Brien excluded from his analysis the very facts that can be
used to determine whether the work incident caused the preexisting condition to
become symptomatic and require surgery.
51.Second, Dr. O'Brien's temporal-gap analysis is not supported by the record or by his
own deposition testimony. In his report, he stated that the first complaint of left hip pain
occurred in September 2023, and that this gap excluded any temporal relationship to
the work incident. At deposition, however, Dr. O'Brien acknowledged that June 7, 2023,
was the first record expressly documenting left groin pain, and when asked to explain
his five-month-gap opinion, he conceded, "We've already established that there were
complaints of groin pain before this." He then discounted those earlier groin complaints
13

because, in his view, they were not "sustained" and were associated with bloating,
eating, abdominal complaints, or core musculature complaints.
52.His reframing is unpersuasive and outcome oriented. Once the record did not support
his report's premise of a five-month absence of hip-related complaints, Dr. O'Brien did
not meaningfully reassess his causation opinion. Instead, he moved the goalposts by
narrowing the category of symptoms he was willing to consider and requiring
"sustained" left hip or groin complaints be documented in terms he deemed sufficiently
specific. The June 7, 2023, record is significant not because it necessarily marks the
first time Claimant experienced groin pain, but because Dr. Mackintosh expressly
documented groin pain associated with bending or lifting the leg to put on socks, which
is the same functional activity already documented on May 8. Dr. O'Brien himself
acknowledged that the groin is the typical location of pain associated with labral
pathology. The June 7 record therefore documents a hip-consistent symptom
approximately seven weeks after the incident, not five months later. Dr. O'Brien's refusal
to give meaningful weight to these earlier symptoms reflects a selective reading of the
record that discounts the very symptoms most relevant to determining whether
Claimant’s left hip condition and need for surgery was proximately caused by the work
incident.
53.Third, Dr. O'Brien's report presents the evidence selectively in a manner inconsistent
with his own record summary. His report acknowledges that, on the date of injury,
treating providers ordered a pelvic x-ray, which the hospital records document was due
to pain. His report acknowledges that, on May 8, 2023, Claimant complained of
soreness when pulling his legs up to put on socks and had developed a mild limp. It
further acknowledges that, on June 7, 2023, Claimant reported specific groin pain when
he bends over to put his socks on and that Dr. Mackintosh stretched the left hip flexors.
And it acknowledges that, on July 7, 2023, Claimant could not lift his left foot to put on
his sock and could not raise his left foot or leg. Yet after summarizing those findings, Dr.
O'Brien still opined that there was no meaningful complaint of left hip pain until nearly
five months after the incident. An expert who acknowledges evidence in the record
14

review and then provides an opinion as though that evidence does not exist has not
engaged in an objective evaluation of the record.
54.Fourth, Dr. O'Brien's mechanism-of-injury analysis reflects the same selective approach.
His report stated that Claimant "did not fall to the ground" and that the explosion "only
served to push him backward a small distance." The body-camera footage contradicts
that characterization. Even Dr. O'Brien ultimately conceded that after the explosion
Claimant threw his arms up, turned to the left, got onto his knees, walked a few steps,
and went down to a knee and his hands. That sequence is materially different from the
minor, non-rotational event described in his report. Dr. O'Brien also failed to
meaningfully analyze the cumulative physical demands of the rescue activity, including
running up a steep embankment, climbing over guardrails, crossing the interstate on
foot, climbing down an embankment, crawling in a constrained position, and then being
blown back by the explosion while rotating left and going to his knees and hands.
Instead, he reduced the analysis to whether the explosion alone produced the type of
event he would accept as causing an acute traumatic labral tear, which again avoids the
framing aggravation question.
55.Fifth, Dr. O'Brien's presentation of the imaging evidence is overstated. Dr. O'Brien did
not credibly explain how the CT scan or MR arthrogram could distinguish a stable,
asymptomatic degenerative condition, from a degenerative condition rendered
symptomatic by Claimant's attempt to rescue the driver of the burning car, or from an
insidious onset, as he concluded. He presented the imaging as objective proof against
causation but never established that the imaging could actually resolve the aggravation
question presented. In doing so, he gave the imaging a causation role it was not shown
to be capable of serving.
56.Sixth, Dr. O'Brien's Grand Canyon analogy does not salvage his opinion. He testified
that degenerative labral tearing develops over time as the labrum is subjected to
repeated bony impingement and “ultimately fails over time as we age due to the trauma
that exists upon it.” He compared the process to “how the Grand Canyon was formed
with a little trickle of water over the course of, you know, hundreds of thousands of
15

years.” That analogy may explain why Claimant had a degenerative or vulnerable
preexisting condition, but it does not explain why that previously asymptomatic condition
became symptomatic after the April 17, 2023, work incident. If anything, the analogy
underscores the aggravation issue: a structure weakened and thinned over time may be
more susceptible, not less susceptible, to becoming symptomatic when subjected to
unusual mechanical stress. Dr. O'Brien used evidence of preexisting vulnerability to
deny causation, but that vulnerability is precisely why the aggravation analysis matters.
57.Seventh, the bilateral degenerative findings further weaken Dr. O'Brien's insidious onset
theory. The CT imaging taken on the date of injury documented mild degenerative
changes in both hips, and later imaging likewise documented bilateral findings. Yet
Claimant's symptoms, treatment, functional limitations, and surgical recommendation
involved the left hip, not the right. The bilateral imaging findings do not, standing alone,
explain the unilateral left-sided clinical presentation that developed after the work
incident. But that asymmetry is more consistent with a work-related aggravation of the
left hip than with a purely insidious degenerative process unrelated to work.
58.Thus, the ALJ rejects Dr. O'Brien's assertion that Claimant's left hip symptoms arose
insidiously and independently of the work incident. Before April 17, 2023, Claimant had
no left hip symptoms, no left hip treatment, no left hip restrictions, and no left hip
diagnosis. After the incident, he had pelvic pain, left-sided complaints, difficulty lifting his
leg to put on socks, a documented limp within weeks, continued difficulty raising the left
leg, and later specific groin pain. No intervening trauma or unrelated event explains that
progression. An insidious-onset theory that does not account for those facts is not
credible.
59.Taken together, the defects in Dr. O'Brien's opinion are not isolated errors. They reflect a
consistent pattern of advocacy rather than objective medical analysis. Dr. O'Brien
primarily answered the wrong question, treated Claimant’s asymptomatic baseline as
immaterial, relied on a temporal-gap premise contradicted by the record, moved the
goalposts when that premise could not be sustained, selectively credited only those
portions of the chronology that supported his conclusion, initially mischaracterized the
16

mechanism of injury, overstated the significance of the imaging, and used evidence of
preexisting vulnerability to deny rather than evaluate aggravation. His conclusion that
Claimant’s left hip condition and need for surgery are unrelated to the work incident
depends on a selective reconstruction of the record in which material contrary evidence
is narrowed, reclassified, minimized, or disregarded. The ALJ finds that Dr. O'Brien did
not apply the record to reach an opinion; he recast the record to support the opinion he
had already reached. For those reasons, the ALJ finds his causation opinion regarding
the cause of Claimant’s hip injury and need for surgery to be unreliable, result-oriented,
not credible, and entitled to no weight.
Dr. Wilcox
60.The ALJ gives greater weight to Dr. Wilcox's causation opinion. Dr. Wilcox's analysis is
more consistent with the medical-record chronology, including the absence of pre-injury
left hip symptoms or treatment, the mechanism of the rescue activity, the early left lower
quadrant, left flank, and pelvic complaints, the May 8, 2023, difficulty putting on socks
and a limp, the June 7, 2023, groin pain and hip-flexor findings, and the later objective
hip findings. Dr. Wilcox did not rely solely on Claimant's later recollection of immediate
severe hip pain. Her opinion accounts for the record as a whole which includes a review
of the entire body-camera footage, the pre-injury baseline, the early medical records,
and the progression of symptoms and reconciles that evidence rather than focusing only
on the absence of an early formal hip diagnosis as done by Dr. O’Brien.
Mechanism of Aggravation
61.The ALJ finds that the April 17, 2023, work incident involved a sufficient physical
mechanism to significantly and permanently aggravate a previously asymptomatic
degenerative left hip condition. Claimant ran, climbed, crawled, traversed guardrails,
worked in awkward and constrained positions on a steep embankment and beneath an
overpass, and was forcefully blown back by a vehicle explosion that caused him to fall
back, rotate to his left, and land on his hands and knees.
17

Ultimate Findings of Fact
62.Claimant had preexisting degenerative left hip pathology, including labral pathology and
femoral acetabular impingement. Before April 17, 2023, that condition was
asymptomatic and had not required medical treatment until the work incident.
63.The April 17, 2023 work activities, including Claimant’s efforts to reach the vehicle,
extinguish the fire, and rescue the driver, permanently and significantly aggravated and
accelerated Claimant’s previously asymptomatic degenerative left hip condition and
caused it to become symptomatic and require medical treatment.
64.The aggravation of his preexisting asymptomatic hip condition proximately caused the
Claimant’s need for medical treatment for his left hip - including the left hip surgery
recommended by Dr. Snyder.
65.The need for surgery is also found to be reasonably necessary to treat Claimant from
the effects of his work injury.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et seq.,
C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to
injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of litigation.
See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden of proving entitlement to
benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance
of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of the evidence,
to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo.
1979). The facts in a workers’ compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither
in favor of the rights of the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a
workers’ compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers' Compensation
proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge. University Park
Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App. 2001). Even if
18

other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary inference, it is for the ALJ
to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility determinations, and draw plausible
inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When determining credibility, the fact finder
should consider, among other things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's
testimony and actions; the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or
improbability) of the testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the
testimony has been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v.
Cline, 57 P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony is a
matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 55 P.3d
186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to conflicting
interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none of the
testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be dispositive
of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of evidence or every
inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has rejected evidence contrary
to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Whether Claimant established by a preponderance of the evidence
that the left hip surgery recommended by Dr. Snyder is reasonable,
necessary, and causally related to the admitted April 17, 2023, work
injury.
D. Respondents do not contest that the recommended left hip surgery is reasonable and
necessary. The sole contested issue is causation.
E. The purpose of the Workers' Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et seq.,
C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to
injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of litigation. §
8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant bears the burden of proving entitlement to benefits by a
preponderance of the evidence. § 8-43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is
19

that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact
is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a
workers' compensation case must be interpreted neutrally. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
F. Respondents are liable to provide medical treatment that is reasonable and necessary
to cure and relieve the effects of the industrial injury. Section 8-42-101(1)(a), C.R.S.
The question of whether the claimant proved treatment is reasonable and necessary is
one of fact for the ALJ. Kroupa v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 53 P.3d 1192 (Colo.
App. 2002).
G. To prove a compensable injury, a claimant must establish that the injury arose out of
and in the course of employment. § 8-41-301(1), C.R.S.; Madden v. Mountain West
Fabricators, 977 P.2d 861 (Colo. 1999). Where a claimant's entitlement to benefits is
disputed, the claimant also has the burden to prove a causal relationship between the
work-related injury and the condition for which benefits are sought. Snyder v. Industrial
Claim Appeals Office, 942 P.2d 1337 (Colo. App. 1997).
H. A pre-existing disease or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the
employment aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing disease or
infirmity to produce a disability or need for medical treatment. H & H Warehouse v.
Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167 (Colo. App. 1990); Duncan v. Industrial Claim Appeals Off., 107
P.3d 999 (Colo. App. 2004). The employer takes the claimant as it finds him, and the
existence of a preexisting condition does not preclude the existence of a compensable
injury. Where a claimant's preexisting condition places the claimant in a weakened
condition and makes the claimant more susceptible to injury, work activities that would
not injure a healthy person may nonetheless be compensable. H & H Warehouse v.
Vicory, 805 P.2d at 1167; Hard v. City of Westminster, WC 5-212-369-002 (July 11,
2024, affirmed by ICAO Nov. 7, 2024). The question is whether the work activity was
the proximate cause of the need for treatment, not whether the work activity would have
injured someone without the preexisting condition.
I. A claimant is not required to understand the exact mechanism of injury to prove a
compensable injury, nor is the claimant required to explain in medical, physiological, or
20

anatomical terms the way in which the accident resulted in the symptoms. In Re
Montoya, W.C. No. 4-633-835 (ICAO, April 26, 2006). Medical evidence is neither
required nor determinative of causation. Id.
J. Assessing the weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence is the exclusive domain of
the ALJ. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo.
App. 2001). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony is a matter within
the discretion of the ALJ, and where expert testimony is subject to conflicting
interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part, all, or none of the
testimony. Cordova v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002);
Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm'n, 441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
K. Applying these principles, Claimant has met his burden of proving by a preponderance
of the evidence that the recommended left hip surgery is causally related to the April 17,
2023, work injury under an aggravation theory.
L. The record establishes a previously asymptomatic preexisting left hip condition. Before
April 17, 2023, Claimant had no left hip symptoms, treatment, imaging, injections,
surgical recommendation, diagnosis, restrictions, or functional limitations. He was
working full duty as a patrol deputy and had passed all required law-enforcement
qualifications and training. The asymptomatic baseline is central to the aggravation
analysis.
M. The record establishes a sufficient work-related mechanism. On April 17, 2023,
Claimant engaged in physically demanding rescue activities, including running up a
steep embankment, crawling on his hands, knees, and abdomen beneath a concrete
overpass in a constrained position, climbing over guardrails, traversing the highway on
foot, and being forcefully displaced by a vehicle explosion while rotating to the left and
going to his hands and knees. The question is not whether those activities would have
injured a healthy person, but whether they were a proximate cause of the aggravation of
Claimant’s preexisting condition and proximately caused the need for treatment, i.e., the
surgery recommended by Dr. Snyder.
21

N. The contemporaneous medical record supports a progressive post-incident
development and identification of left-sided, pelvic, hip-region, and groin symptoms. On
the date of injury, Claimant had pelvic pain sufficient to prompt pelvic imaging, along
with left flank and left lower quadrant pain. Within three weeks, the medical records
documented that he had difficulty pulling his legs up to put on socks and exhibited a
limp. By June 7, 2023, a provider expressly documented groin pain with the same
functional activity, along with hip-flexor findings. Those records, considered with the
absence of intervening trauma or any unrelated explanation, support a causal
connection between the April 17, 2023 work activities and the later diagnosis of left hip
labral pathology and femoral acetabular impingement.
O. Dr. Wilcox’s credited causation opinion directly supports compensability. Dr. Wilcox
diagnosed a left hip labral tear with femoral acetabular impingement that was
preexisting but permanently aggravated by the work injury, and she opined to a
reasonable degree of medical probability that Claimant’s symptomatic left hip condition
was due to the work injury. Her opinion accounts for Claimant’s asymptomatic pre-injury
baseline, the Claimant’s development of hip pain after the incident, the work-related
mechanism documented by the body-camera footage, and the documentation of
symptoms in the contemporaneous medical record. The ALJ finds her opinion
persuasive for the reasons set forth in the findings of fact.
P. Dr. O’Brien’s contrary opinion does not defeat causation. As set forth in the findings of
fact, Dr. O’Brien primarily analyzed whether Claimant sustained a new acute traumatic
labral tear, rather than whether the work incident aggravated or accelerated a previously
asymptomatic preexisting condition. That was not the controlling causation question. Dr.
O’Brien also testified that his opinion was not based on Claimant’s asymptomatic pre-
injury baseline, although that baseline is central to the aggravation analysis. For the
reasons stated in the findings of fact, the ALJ finds Dr. O’Brien’s causation opinion
unreliable, not credible, and entitled to no weight.
Q. Claimant’s inability to pinpoint the precise moment his left hip condition became
symptomatic does not defeat causation. Causation may be established by the record as
22

a whole. Here, the asymptomatic pre-injury baseline, the physically demanding work-
related mechanism, the date-of-injury left-sided and pelvic complaints, the progressive
documentation of hip-region and groin symptoms, and Dr. Wilcox’s credited medical
opinion together establish that the April 17, 2023 work activities were the proximate
cause of Claimant’s left hip aggravation and resulting need for surgery.
R. As a result, the ALJ finds and concludes that Claimant has established by a
preponderance of the evidence that he sustained a compensable injury consisting of an
aggravation of his preexisting left hip condition because of the April 17, 2023 work
incident. Claimant has also established that the left hip surgery recommended by Dr.
Snyder is reasonable, necessary, and causally related to the April 17, 2023, work injury.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Respondents shall authorize and pay for the left hip surgery recommended by
Dr. Snyder, together with all reasonably necessary and related medical
treatment.
2. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
23

by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
