Peter J. Cannici
Administrative Law Judge

title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-310-234-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-310-234-001
Issues
I. Whether Claimant established, by a preponderance of the evidence, that she
sustained a work-related injury to her right foot and right wrist on June 27, 2025.
II. If Claimant established that she sustained a work-related injury, did she also
prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that she is entitled to reasonable,
necessary and related medical treatment to cure and relieve her of the effects of
this work-related injury.
III. If Claimant established that she sustained a work-related injury on June 27,
2025, did she also prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that she is
entitled to temporary disability benefits beginning June 27, 2025, and continuing
until these benefits can be terminated in accordance with law.
IV. If Claimant established that she sustained compensable injuries to her right foot
and wrist and is entitled to temporary disability benefits, did Respondents prove
that said TTD benefits are subject to offset for Claimant’s receipt of short-term
disability benefits.
V. If Claimant established that she sustained compensable injuries to her right foot
and right wrist, what was Claimant’s average weekly wage at the time of her
June 27, 2025, injury.
Because the ALJ finds/concludes that Claimant failed to establish that she
suffered a compensable injury to her right foot/wrist, this order does not address
issues II-V outlined above.
Findings of Fact
Based on the evidence presented at hearing, the ALJ enters the following
findings of fact:
1

Background and Claimant’s Alleged June 27, 2025, Slip and Fall
1. Claimant works for Employer as a customer service representative. She takes
in-bound service calls at Employer’s call center. She alleges that she suffered
injuries to her right foot and wrist during a fall in the company bathroom after
reporting to work on June 27, 2025.
2. Claimant testified that shortly after reporting to work on the morning of June 27,
2025, she went to the ladies’ room where she slipped and fell in a bathroom stall.
Claimant testified she felt scared and helpless after her fall and began calling out
for help. She was heard screaming by her Supervisor, Lisa Darensborug, who
responded to her location.
3. According to Employer’s incident report, Claimant was found sitting in the “toilet
room” at which time she reported that she “lost her balance and fell between the
toilet bowl and the door.” (RHE B, p. 19). Claimant reported that her right foot
and right wrist were bruised and she was in pain. Id.
4. Employer’s Human Resources Manager (HRM) Lanita Raney was contacted and
immediately responded to Claimant’s location. In a post-accident statement, Ms.
Raney noted that Claimant was found sitting on a toilet in the bathroom. (RHE B,
p. 23). Ms. Raney also noted that Claimant advised her that she was unsure
how she slipped and fell. Indeed, Claimant simply reported that she turned, that
her feet “just slipped from under her” and she fell to the floor. Id. In her post-
accident statement, Ms. Raney noted the floor to be free of moisture, wetness or
slippery substances. Id. Ms. Raney also observed that Claimant’s right foot was
“visibly bruised and discolored.” Id. Consequently, Ms. Raney asked Claimant if
she could take photographs of Claimant’s injuries, including her right foot, right
arm, right wrist and hand. Id. Because Claimant reported an inability to walk,
emergency medical technicians (EMTs) were summoned to her location. These
ENTs subsequently transported Claimant to Memorial Hospital by ambulance.
Claimant’s Medical Treatment
2

5. Upon arrival at the hospital, Claimant was evaluated in the emergency room by
Dr. Bradley Wallace, to whom she reported that she slipped in the restroom at
work. (RHE C, p. 28). She reported that she believed her right arm was caught
in the bar for the handhold and that she struck her head. Id. Claimant was able
to stand but complained or right foot and right wrist pain. Id. Examination
revealed a distal right wrist deformity. Id. Although Claimant reported hitting her
head, the physical examination findings are devoid of any cuts or bruises located
about the head. Nonetheless, a CT scan of the head was performed which was
reportedly negative for pathology. Id.
6. X-rays of the right foot and right wrist were obtained. X-rays of the right foot
revealed a “[m]inimally displaced fracture of the second metatarsal base with
widening of the Lisfranc interval” along with a “[s]uspected nondisplaced fracture
of the third metatarsal base and “[m]inimally displaced fractures of the third
through fifth toes proximal phalanx base with intra-articular extension.” (RHE C,
pp. 31-32). X-rays of the right wrist revealed a “[m]ildly displaced comminuted
fracture of the distal radius” and a “[m]ildly displaced fracture of the ulnar styloid.
Id. Claimant’s right foot injuries were consistent with a Lisfranc fracture.
7. An orthopedic consultation was requested, and Claimant was initially evaluated
by Physician Assistant (PA-C), Vincenzo Louis Paintanida. (RNE C, p. 32). PA
Paintanida noted that Claimant fell while at work when she “slipped off the toilet.”
Id. at 33. Following his review of Claimant’s x-rays, PA Paintanida consulted with
Dr. Rambau and Dr. Davidson regarding additional treatment recommendations.
Id. Claimant was ultimately admitted to the hospital, given non-weight bearing
restrictions and placed in a right lower extremity and right wrist splint and moved
to the orthopedic service.
8. Claimant underwent an open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) procedure for
her right foot Lisfranc fracture on July 3, 2025, and an ORIF procedure for the
distal radius fracture two days later on July 5, 2025. (RHE C, p. 44). Claimant
remained in the hospital until July 16, 2025, at which point she was discharged to
a skilled nursing facility for additional rehabilitation. (CHE 1, p. 51).
3

9. Claimant returned to the orthopedist for a repeat surgical procedure on July 27,
2025, where she underwent a revision right foot Lisfranc fixation and removal of
painful surgical hardware. (CHE 2, p. 95; CHE 4, p. 451; RHE A, p. 6). Because
there was concern for seeded infection in the joint, Claimant was started on a 6-
week course of intravenous antibiotics and transferred to a skilled nursing facility
for recovery and rehabilitation. (Healthcare Resort of Colorado Springs). She
remained in the nursing facility for several months, where she received in-patient
therapy, until she was discharged to independent living in her home.
10.Claimant continued in follow-up with the orthopedist Dr. Peter Daniel Fredericks
through the UC Health Orthopedics Clinic. On September 22, 2025, Dr.
Fredericks issued a letter stating that Claimant would be out of work through
October 20, 2025 (Ex. 3, 17p. 173). No subsequent treatment records were
offered into evidence.
Claimant’s Hearing Testimony
11.Claimant testified that she has a history of falls. Indeed, Claimant testified that
she had fallen several times prior to her June 27, 2025, fall at work. She fell at
home in 2024 breaking her right ankle, which fracture subsequently required
surgery. She informed Dr. John Burris, during an independent medical
examination, that she continued walking despite this fracture for an entire month
before pursuing treatment. Claimant testified that she has no residual effects
from her 2024 ankle injury but ambulates with a limp due to an unrelated right
knee condition, which she testified needs surgery.
12.Claimant also testified that after her June 27, 2025, fall at work, she slipped and
fell in her bathroom fracturing her hip. Claimant testified that she is currently
waiting for an orthopedic evaluation concerning this alleged injury. Despite her
history of falls, Claimant testified that she has never suffered any injuries to her
right foot or wrist prior to June 27, 2025. Claimant further testified that her right
4

foot is numb since her surgeries and that she has difficulty lifting with her right
arm as well as weekly dull throbbing pain lasting up to two hours.
13.On cross-examination, Claimant acknowledged that she has taken a significant
amount of personal time off work since beginning her employment with
Employer. She reported that she suffers from emotional problems, depression
and anxiety. She admitted that she has missed work for these conditions and
has requested accommodation due to suffering from a generalized anxiety
disorder.
14.Claimant also testified that she received approximately $9,000 after taxes from
short term disability due to her June 27, 2025, right foot and wrist conditions.
The Testimony of Lanita Raney
15.Ms. Raney testified that she was working as Employer’s Human Resources
Manager on June 27, 2025, and that she was moved into that position due to her
background in safety and experience surrounding leave of absence issues. Ms.
Raney testified that she became acquainted with Claimant as part of Claimant’s
routine intake with her HR generalist. Ms. Raney asked to attend the meeting
with Claimant and the HR Generalist because Claimant had taken extensive
leave and Employer was working to help employees in her situation in returning
to work.
16.Ms. Raney testified that she first became aware of Claimant’s injuries when it
was reported to her that Claimant had fallen in the bathroom stall by one of her
supervisors. Ms. Raney testified that the incident, i.e. Claimant’s alleged fall,
occurred within minutes of Claimant clocking into work. According to Ms. Raney,
Claimant clocked in at 10:57 a.m. and the incident occurred at approximately
11:00 a.m. Claimant stated in her testimony that this was not her regular shift but
claimed she had volunteered to work extra hours.
17.Ms. Raney testified that after being advised of Claimant’s fall, she proceeded
directly to the ladies’ room where she found Claimant sitting on the floor. Ms.
5

Raney testified that Claimant advised her that she had fallen but did not know
what had caused her to fall. Ms. Raney testified that the bathroom floor was
clean and dry. Because Claimant was reportedly unable to stand, Ms. Raney
testified that she assisted Claimant off the floor to a seated position on the toilet.
Ms. Raney then asked Claimant if she could take photos of her injured foot and
wrist, i.e. her injuries, which she testified was a normal part of her accident
investigation process. Claimant then consented to being photographed.
18.Ms. Raney testified that while the photographs were taken within minutes of the
incident, she observed that the bruising on the foot was already black and blue.
During cross-examination, Ms. Raney testified that she did not know how long
Claimant was in the stall before she was found by Ms. Darensborug.
19.Ms. Raney also testified regarding Claimant’s attendance issues. Per Ms. Raney,
Claimant had a lengthy history of attendance issues for which she had been
placed on corrective action. On the alleged date of injury, Claimant was on a
written warning for attendance issues, did not have any accumulated sick or
vacation leave to cover absences, and did not qualify for FMLA leave because
she had exhausted her FMLA leave for the current 12-month period. Per Ms.
Raney, Claimant had taken medical leave every year since her date of hire for
personal medical issues. Employer records contained in respondents’
Respondents’ Exhibit G documents the prior leave and accommodation requests
from Claimant for various non-work-related issues including anxiety, balance
issues resulting in frequent falls, and neuropathy in her legs. (See generally,
RHE G, pp. 130-134). These medical issues pre-dated the alleged work incident
by several years. Finally, Ms. Raney testified that while Claimant was not
approved for leave after her alleged June 27, 2025, slip and fall, her application
for short term disability (STD) was approved and that Claimant received STD
benefits in the gross amount of $15,297.92. These benefits covered the period
from July 4, 2025, through December 25, 2025. Employer paid 100% of the
premium for the short-term disability policy under which these benefits were paid.
6

The Independent Medical Examination of Dr. Burris
20.Respondents arranged for Claimant to attend an independent medical
examination (IME) with Dr. Burris. Dr. Burris completed the requested IME on
December 16, 2025. As part of his IME, Dr. Burris examined Claimant and
reviewed the medical records, the incident report, and the photographs taken by
Ms. Raney. During this IME, Claimant provided the following history as
summarized by Dr. Burris:
is a 59-year-old female who reports slipping while in a
bathroom stall at work on 6/27/2025. At the time, she was working
at the Charter Communications (Spectrum Cable) call center as an
inbound phone customer service representative. During a work
break at about 11:00 AM, she went to the restroom. While in one of
the restroom stalls, her right foot inexplicably slipped (she does not
recall seeing any water on the ground) and struck the adjacent wall,
and she stumbled forward hitting her head on the toilet paper roller
in the stall. To prevent herself from falling, she attempted to grab a
rail in the stall with her right hand, but her hand slipped behind the
rail. She did not fall to the ground and did not experience pain
initially but did experience anxiety and fear. She sat down on the
toilet seat and called for help and within 5 minutes, coworkers
heard her calls and came to her aid. Someone called 911 and
firefighters and EMS arrived at the scene, and she was taken by
ambulance to Memorial hospital in Colorado Springs. (RHE A, pp.
2-3).
21.Dr. Burris concluded that Claimant’s injuries were not work-related. Dr. Burris’
opinion was based on two factors. First, he noted that the advanced purple and
black bruising visible in the photographs taken by Ms. Raney were a minimum of
24 hours old and could not have developed in the time that elapsed between
Claimant’s alleged fall and the time the photographs were taken. (RHE A, p. 10).
7

Secondly, Dr. Burris felt that the nature of the wrist and foot fractures were not
consistent with the reported mechanism of injury. Placing causation aside, Dr.
Burris opined that Claimant had reached a point of maximal healing and that no
further treatment was reasonable, necessary, or related to the alleged June 27,
2025, slip and fall. (RHE A, pp. 11-12).
22.Regarding the bruising depicted in the photographs taken by Ms. Raney, Dr.
Burris explained that ecchymosis (bruising) is caused by a physiological process
where the small vasculature of damaged tissues around the area of injury are
disrupted, and release blood which then goes through “well-defined metabolic
stages of restoration.” (RHE A, p. 10). According to Dr. Burris, the skin covering
the area of injury appears bright red or pink due to fresh oxygenated blood
pooling under the skin immediately after the trauma. With the passage of time,
the color of the skin in the traumatized area changes as the blood, which leaked
into the area loses its oxygen and the body’s immune system quickly activates to
prevent further leakage and restore normal structure and function. Per Dr. Burris,
over the next few days following an injury, this “bruise” turns purple, black or blue
and as the immune system continues breaking down the hemoglobin in the
pooled blood, the black and blue color fades away and the bruise appears green
or yellow. Within about two weeks, the bruise fades away completely. Id.
23.The pictures admitted into evidence reveal a severely bruised and swollen right
foot. Indeed, the area encompassing the entire arch of the right foot appears
black and blue. There is similar deeply pigmented, i.e. black bruising over the
second, third and fourth toes of the right foot. This dark bruising extends to the
base of the toes and onto the skin covering the top (dorsum) of the right foot.
The great toe appears purple with areas of progressing darker bruising over the
top of the toe itself. Moreover, the entire foot appears swollen with an area of
concentrated (moderate to severe) edema over the right forefoot just proximal to
the base of the toes. (RHE D, pp. 76, 78). While not as dramatic and of inferior
quality, the picture of Claimant’s right forearm reveals an area of light purple to
brown bruising on the volar surface of the right forearm slightly proximal to the
8

right wrist. There is also an area of dark bruising on the inside aspect of the right
forearm in the area of the right elbow. Id. at 77.
The Review of Dr. Burris’ IME Report by Dr. Jack Rook
24.Claimant requested a review of Dr. Burris’ IME report. Dr. Rook completed the
requested review on February 27, 2026. Dr. Rook was asked to specifically
review and comment on Dr. Burris’ IME report. He did not review any other
medical records, nor did he see the pictures taken by Ms. Raney. Dr. Rook
disagreed with Dr. Burris’ opinion regarding the bruising and opined that because
bruising develops at different times depending on the location and severity of the
injury, Claimant could in fact develop bruising immediately following the incident,
especially because there is not much tissue overlying the boney structures of the
foot and wrist. (CHE 4, p. 452). He also opined that Claimant would likely have
had great difficulty with weight bearing on a foot with a Lisfranc fracture when
she reported to work on June 27, 2025. Id. at 453. He noted that if anyone could
confirm that she was seen having severe difficulty ambulating when she entered
the bathroom, he would likely change his opinion to conclude that the foot injury
occurred prior to the events in the bathroom stall on June 27, 2025. Id. Finally,
Dr. Rook concluded that the described mechanism of injury (MOI), i.e. a fall in a
bathroom stall wherein Claimant struck her foot on the bathroom wall and caught
her right forearm behind the grab bar (suspending her by her forearm/wrist) could
result in the injuries she was diagnosed with in the emergency room on June 27,
2025. Id. at 452-453.
The Deposition Testimony of Dr. Rook
25.Dr. Rook testified by deposition as a Level II accredited expert in Physical
Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) by deposition on March 30, 2026. His
testimony was consistent with the opinions expressed in his February 27, 2026,
9

report. Indeed, he testified that Claimant immediately developed pain and
swelling in her right wrist and right foot, as well as extensive bruising at the time
of her accident. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 7, ll. 8-14). He testified that Lisfranc
fractures are very painful and typically would lead to someone being completely
non-weight bearing on their foot. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 9, ll. 3-13). He testified
that, given Claimant’s body habitus and weight, he did not believe that she could
ambulate normally with a Lisfranc fracture and would likely require crutches to
walk. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 9, ll. 3- 15). In addition, Dr. Rook testified that it is
possible to have bruising within a very short amount of time with injuries involving
fractures that are just below the skin, such as the foot. He testified that the
severity and timing of onset of such bruising depends on the location of the
fracture. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 10, ll. 1-12; 17-20). He also testified that there
was nothing in Claimant’s records indicating that Claimant was non-
weightbearing prior to the injury. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 12, ll. 1-5). He also
testified consistently with his report that Claimant’s stated MOI could cause the
injuries she was diagnosed with, particularly catching her wrist in the
handicapped grab bar and striking the wall with her foot. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p.
12-13).
26.Dr. Rook acknowledged on cross-examination that he did not review any medical
records or photographs of Claimant’s bruising and did not listen to the audio
recording of Dr. Burris’ IME. Instead, he relied on Dr. Burris’s medical record
review, which he believed was a thorough recounting of the records in reaching
his conclusions. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 14, ll. 8-13; p. 19). Outside of the
medical records reviewed by Dr. Burris, Dr. Rook admitted he was not aware of
Claimant’s pre-existing right ankle fracture occurring in 2024. Id. at p. 14, ll. 15-
22. He re-iterated that Claimant’s right foot injury could result in immediate
purple-ish/black bruising but admitted that he did not know exactly where on the
foot that bruising was located. (Depo. Tr. Dr. Rook, p. 14, ll. 23-25, p. 15, ll. 1-6).
He surmised that Claimant may have had bruising through the toes and bottom
of the right foot. Id. at p. 15, ll. 6-9. Based upon the documentation outlined in
10

Dr. Burris’ IME report, Dr. Rook also expected to see bruising and swelling on
both sides of the right wrist. Id. at ll. 12-17.
The Hearing Testimony of Dr. Burris
27.Dr. Burris testified that Claimant told him during his evaluation that her co-
workers arrived within five minutes of the alleged fall. He elaborated on the
opinions expressed in his IME report with respect to both the bruising and the
MOI. Dr. Burris reiterated that when a fracture occurs, blood leaks out of the
vasculature around the broken bones resulting in pooling around the injured
structure causing bruising. As he documented in his report, Dr. Burris explained
that the red blood cells in the body carry oxygen on hemoglobin molecules and
when the blood first leaks out around the traumatized structure/tissue it has a
red/pink color. However, as time passes the leaked blood cells lose their oxygen
which causes the hemoglobin to change colors. Over the first few days following
an injury, bruises turn from red/pink to purple, blue, and black. Then within 5 to
10 days after injury, the bruise turns green and yellow and continues to fade until
it disappears after about two weeks. As noted, the photographs taken within
minutes of Claimant’s alleged incident reveal purple, blue and black bruising
encompassing most of the right foot/toes and light purple to brown bruising over
the volar surface of Claimant’s right forearm just proximal to the wrist. Dr. Burris
reiterated his opinion that the color associated with this bruising would take 24
hours to develop. Accordingly, Dr. Burris testified that when the known
physiologic process surrounding the evolution of bruising is accounted for, the
color of the bruising depicted in the photographs taken by Ms. Raney is
inconsistent with an injury occurring only minutes before. Simply put, the alleged
injuries were not fresh, and the bruising captured in the photographs was at least
24 hours old. Thus, while Dr. Burris agreed that the right foot bruising was
consistent with a Lisfranc fracture, he was adamant that it could not have
advanced to the stage depicted in the photographs in the short period, i.e. within
11

the 5-10 minutes, before the pictures were taken. The photographs also
documented advanced bruising near claimant’s elbow that Dr. Burris opined
could not be explained by any of the injuries allegedly related to a fall at work.
28.Dr. Burris testified that while he agreed with Dr. Rook’s opinion that it was
possible to experience immediate swelling around a fracture, he disagreed with
Dr. Rook’s conclusions concerning Claimant’s bruising. He testified that Dr.
Rook could not credibly opine with respect to Claimant’s bruising without seeing
the pictures taken by Ms. Raney. He also disputed Dr. Rook’s conclusion that
the red blood cells lose their oxygen within minutes of an injury testifying that the
loss of oxygen from the blood cells is more gradual and dependent on the
location of injury. According to Dr. Burris, the subcutaneous tissue surrounding
the anatomical areas of injury involved here is not highly metabolic. Thus, Dr.
Burris testified that the blood cells leaking into the area of injury in this case
would not lose their oxygen within minutes. Consequently, Dr. Burris restated his
opinion that the nature and color of the bruising captured in the pictures of
Claimant’s right foot and wrist could not be explained by a fall that occurred 5-10
minutes before the photographs were taken by Ms. Raney. Dr. Burris testified
that Dr. Rook’s opinions concerning Claimant’s asserted injuries were based on
flawed assumptions that were undermined by the photos. Specifically, he
testified that Dr. Rook accepted that Claimant’s foot hit the wall and that her full
weight had come down on the bar. However, the location of the bar in
photographs revealed that this assumption was not mechanically probable.
29.Dr. Burris also addressed Dr. Rook’s opinions regarding Claimant’s inability to
bear weight and ambulate with a Lisfranc fracture. Dr. Burris agreed that Lisfranc
fractures are painful and could make ambulating difficult. However, he noted that
Claimant had a demonstrated history of walking on an ankle fracture for an entire
month before seeking treatment and succumbing to corrective surgery. As
noted, Claimant testified to an alleged hip fracture after a fall in her bathroom for
which she also did not immediately seek treatment. Based on this history, Dr.
Burris felt that Claimant had proven she could ambulate with a broken bone
12

leading to an inference that she could also ambulate with a Lisfranc injury.
Finally, Dr. Burris opined that even if Claimant had slipped in the bathroom, her
foot could not have struck the wall with sufficient force to cause a Lisfranc
fracture given the confined area inside the stall. He also felt that the described
MOI that allegedly caused Claimant’s broken wrist was not mechanically
probable given Claimant’s height and the location of the grab bar in the stall.
Accordingly, it was his opinion that Claimant had injuries that could not be
explained by the described MOI in this case.
30.The ALJ finds the opinions and testimony of Dr. Burris more persuasive than the
contrary opinions of Dr. Rook. Based on the sum of the evidence presented, the
ALJ finds that Claimant has failed to prove that she sustained an injury arising
out of and in the course and scope of her employment on June 27, 2025.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
13

(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Compensability
D. A “compensable injury” is one that requires medical treatment or causes
disability. Romero v. Industrial Commission, 632 P.2d 1052 (Colo. App. 1981);
Aragon v. CHIMR, et al., W.C. No. 4-543-782 (ICAO, Sept. 24, 2004); H & H
Warehouse v. Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167, 1169 (Colo. App. 1990). No benefits flow to
the victim of an industrial accident unless the accident results in a compensable
“injury.” Romero, supra; § 8-41-301, C.R.S. To sustain his burden of proof
concerning compensability, Claimant must establish that the condition for which
she seeks benefits was proximately caused by an “injury” arising out of and in the
14

course of employment. Loofbourrow v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 321 P.3d
548 (Colo. App. 2011), aff’d Harman-Bergstedt, Inc. v. Loofbourrow, 320 P.3d
327 (Colo. 2014); Section 8-41-301(I)(b), C.R.S.
E. The phrases "arising out of” and "in the course of" are not synonymous and a
claimant must meet both requirements for the injury to be compensable. Younger
v. City and County of Denver, 810 P.2d 647, 649 (Colo. 1991); In re Question
Submitted by U.S. Court of Appeals, 759 P.2d 17, 20 (Colo. 1988). The latter
requirement refers to the time, place, and circumstances under which a work-
related injury occurs. Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 381 (Colo. 1991).
F. An injury occurs in the course and scope of employment when it takes place
within the time and place limits of the employment relationship and during an
activity connected with the employee's job-related functions. In re Question
Submitted by U.S. Court of Appeals, supra; Deterts v. Times Publ'g Co., 38 Colo.
App. 48, 51, 552 P.2d 1033, 1036 (1976). Conversely, the "arising out of" test is
one of causation. It requires that the injury have its origins in an employee's
work-related functions and be sufficiently related thereto so as to be considered
part of the employee's service to the employer. Horodyskyj v. Karanian, 32 P.3d
470, 475 (Colo. 2001). In this case, Claimant testified that she believed she
slipped and fell in the stall but could not explain what caused her to fall. She
believed her injuries resulted from striking her foot against the wall and catching
her arm in the space between the wall and grab bar. However, Dr. Burris credibly
testified that even if Claimant did slip in the bathroom stall her foot could not have
struck the wall with sufficient force to cause a Lisfranc fracture. Similarly, he
explained that reported mechanism of injury to the wrist was not mechanically
probable given the location of the grab bar relative to Claimant’s height. He
further testified that while the right-foot bruising evident in the pictures taken by
Ms. Raney was consistent with a Lisfranc fracture, that bruising was at least 24
hours old. Here, Claimant confirmed that the photos were taken within a few
minutes of the incident, i.e. her fall. It is also undisputed that there is significant
15

bruising noted on Claimant’s right foot and wrist in the pictures taken by Ms.
Raney. The question is not whether Claimant’s foot and wrist were bruised- they
most certainly are as established by the photographs. Rather, the question is the
probable age of that bruising, and therefore the age of the alleged injuries in this
case, based on the color of the bruises captured in Ms. Raney’s photographs.
G. As found, the ALJ credits the opinions/testimony of Dr. Burris that it is not
medically probable for the bruises shown in the photographs to have progressed
the state of being purple, black and blue within the few minutes that passed
between the Claimant’s slip and fall incident and the taking of the photographs
admitted into evidence. Based upon the evidence presented, the ALJ agrees with
Dr. Burris to find and conclude that the bruising captured in the photographs is
probably at least 24 hours old, meaning that the injuries that lead to that bruising
were also of similar age at the time the photographs were taken. The contrary
opinions of Dr. Rook regarding the age of Claimant’s bruising are unconvincing.
Indeed, Dr. Rook did not see the photographs demonstrating the nature and
extent of Claimant’s right foot and wrist bruising.
H. Based upon the totality of the evidence presented, the ALJ concludes that the
color of the bruising depicted in the photograph belies Claimant’s suggestion that
her right Lisfranc and wrist fractures are acute (fresh) and occurred when she
struck her right foot on the bathroom wall and caught her right wrist between the
wall and grab bar as she fell forward. The determination of whether there is a
sufficient "nexus" or causal relationship between a claimant's employment and the
injury is one of fact and one that the ALJ must determine based on the totality of
the circumstances. In Re Question Submitted by the United States Court of
Appeals, 759 P.2d 17 (Colo. 1988); Moorhead Machinery & Boiler Co. v. Del
Valle, 934 P.2d 861 (Colo. App. 1996). As presented, the evidence persuades
the ALJ that Claimant has a significant history of falls and fractures involving the
right lower extremity. Based upon the evidence presented, the ALJ is convinced
that Claimant probably sustained a Lisfranc and right wrist fracture at least 24
16

hours prior to the photos and while she may have slipped in the bathroom stall,
the ALJ is not convinced that this incident caused Claimant’s alleged injuries.
Because Claimant has failed to establish the requisite causal relationship
between her June 27, 2025, slip and fall in the bathroom stall and her right
Lisfranc and wrist fractures, her claim for benefits must be denied and dismissed.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant’s claim for compensation and benefits arising out of the June 27, 2025,
incident involving a slip and fall Employer’s bathroom is denied and dismissed.

Issue
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the reverse
➢
total shoulder arthroplasty recommended by Dr. Hatzidakis is reasonably
necessary to cure and relieve Claimant of the effects of his February 20, 2024
workplace injury.
Findings of Fact
1. On February 20, 2024, Claimant was unloading a pallet of boxes for his
employer, each box weighing 60 to 70 pounds. Three days after lifting the
boxes, he felt a gradual onset of pain in his left shoulder.
2. On March 19, 2024, Claimant saw Dr. Zuehlsdorff at On the Mend Occupational
Medicine. Claimant recounted his injury and told Dr. Zuehlsdorff that his pain is
different from what he experienced following a 2021 hockey injury that resulted in
a rotator cuff repair. Claimant reported that the prior injury and surgery resulted
in residual decreased range of motion with no pain. Dr. Zuehlsdorff prescribed
anti-inflammatory medications and physical therapy and provided Claimant with
temporary work restrictions that limited his lifting and carrying to five pounds with
no reaching overhead or away from the body with the left arm.
3. When Claimant returned to Dr. Zuehlsdorff on April 2, 2024, Claimant reported
that physical therapy and anti-inflammatory medications helped his pain, which
was down to a 1.5 out of 10. Claimant was to continue with the existing
treatment plan, but his restrictions were loosened to include lifting up to ten
pounds.

4. Following Claimant’s April 2, 2024 appointment, Claimant returned to work
performing light duty. Nevertheless, Claimant’s condition progressively
worsened such that he reported 2.5 out of 10 pain at his April 16, 2024
appointment with Dr. Zuehlsdorff. Dr. Zuehlsdorff restricted Claimant again to
five-pound lifting and carrying restrictions.
5. Claimant underwent an MRI of his left shoulder on April 30, 2024. The MRI
showed “Postsurgical changes of a prior supraspinatus and infraspinatus
tendons consistent with high-grade partial-thickness articular side re-tearing with
focal full-thickness component of tearing along the supraspinatus tendon. Long
head of biceps partial tearing. Acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joint
osteoarthritis. Superior labral degeneration/tearing.”
6. On May 10, 2024, Claimant transferred from Dr. Zuehlsdorff’s office to Dr.
Sharon Walker’s. Claimant reported that his left shoulder range of motion was
doing worse since he finished taking Mobic (NSAID). Dr. Walker kept Claimant’s
temporary work restrictions as they were. She also ordered a blood test for
possibility of an infection causing atrophy and tearing of the rotator cuff. The
blood tests did not show evidence of an infection. However, Dr. Walker later
recommended a shoulder aspiration to more definitively rule out the possibility of
a shoulder infection. Claimant’s pain as of May 10, 2024 was at a 3 out of 10
and increased to 3.5 out of 10 by the May 31, 2024 appointment with Dr. Walker.
However, Claimant reported a 1.5 out of 10 pain as of the June 28, 2024
appointment with Dr. Walker.
7. Claimant saw Dr. Faulkner on August 26, 2024, reporting localized pain over the
lateral aspect of his left shoulder at 3 or 4 out of 10 with significant limited range
of motion and weakness. Dr. Faulkner conducted a physical examination of
Claimant and ultimately recommended that Claimant undergo left shoulder
arthroscopic surgery with debridement, biceps tenodesis, and an in-space
balloon.

8. Dr. Walker reviewed Dr. Faulkner’s recommendation and referred Claimant to Dr.
Hatzidakis for a second opinion.
9. Respondents filed a General Admission of Liability (GAL) on September 18,
2024, admitting for a date of injury of February 20, 2024. Under the remarks
section, Respondents noted, “Accepted for left rotator cuff tear, Traumatic partial
tear of left biceps tendon Medical only claim with no lost time. . . .”
10. Claimant saw Dr. Hatzidakis on October 3, 2024. Dr. Hatzidakis reviewed
Claimant’s medical history. He felt that Claimant’s rotator cuff tear would
increase in size with time. He recommended rest and activity modification
accompanied by rotator cuff stretching and strengthening. He also discussed
with Claimant surgical options such as a reverse total shoulder replacement.
11. On November 19, 2024, Claimant underwent an IME with Dr. Qing-Min Chen.
Dr. Chen reviewed Claimant’s medical records, took Claimant’s history, and
conducted a physical examination of Claimant. Claimant reported his injury as
recounted above. He also reported that he had previously torn his left shoulder
in 2021 while playing hockey. Claimant reported that he had undergone surgery
for that rotator cuff tear and that he was 95% better after six months and able to
return to full-duty work with no problems until his February 2024 injury.
12. Dr. Chen opined that Claimant had a full-thickness rotator cuff tear of the
supraspinatus and infraspinatus with humeral head elevation and severe muscle
atrophy.
13. Dr. Chen ultimately opined that there was no specific diagnosis attributable to
Claimant’s workplace injury. He reasoned that Claimant’s onset of pain three
days after the accident was “not a true mechanism of injury,” and that there was
“nothing to suggest that an injury occurred at work that aggravated this particular

pre-existing condition especially given the fact that he did not feel any problems
until three days afterwards when he was reaching up overhead.” Rather, Dr.
Chen felt that Claimant’s condition was progressive and degenerative in nature.
14. Consequently, Dr. Chen opined that none of the surgeries recommended would
be related to Claimant’s work injury and that Claimant would have needed a
reverse total shoulder replacement regardless of the work injury.
15. Claimant returned to Dr. Walker on December 6, 2024. Dr. Walker reviewed Dr.
Chen’s IME report and issued a response. Dr. Walker expressed that she
strongly disagreed with Dr. Chen insofar as Dr. Chen opined that all of Claimant’s
left shoulder problems were preexisting and that Claimant did not sustain a work
injury. She explained that Claimant had been able to return to his regular job two
years prior to the injury without any restrictions. She noted that Claimant was
having no problems with his left shoulder until his date of injury and that
Claimant’s heavy overhead work was the only incident near that time that would
explain Claimant’s sudden onset of symptoms. In her opinion, if Claimant’s
symptoms were due solely to preexisting conditions, the decline would have
consisted of a much more gradual onset and deterioration of range of motion and
function.
16. Dr. Hatzidakis testified by deposition on March 17, 2026, as an expert in
orthopedic surgery and who has conducted several thousand reverse total
shoulder surgeries.
17. Dr. Hatzidakis testified regarding his October 3, 2024 examination of Claimant.
He testified that he reviewed Claimant’s April 30, 2024 left shoulder MRI and an
X-ray dated the same day as the examination. He also performed a physical
examination and took Claimant’s history.

18. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that Claimant reported his prior rotator cuff tear. Dr.
Hatzidakis’s understanding of that rotator cuff tear was that Claimant was injured
while playing hockey, tore his rotator cuff, underwent a rotator cuff repair surgery,
and recovered well.
19. On physical examination, Dr. Hatzidakis testified, Claimant had limited active
range of motion to about 90 degrees, could not lift his arm over his head, and
could externally rotate the arm to 45 degrees. Claimant exhibited weakness in
elevation, which Dr. Hatzidakis opined indicated the presence of rotator cuff
pathology.
20. Dr. Hatzidakis noted that the X-rays and MRI showed minimal arthritis of the
shoulder. One of the views, Dr. Hatzidakis noted, showed the ball of the
humerus somewhat up in the glenoid, indicating some element of rotator cuff
deficiency. He testified that the MRI showed fluid accumulation in the shoulder
evidencing a possible strain injury. He testified that the prior MRI showed the
anchors in the shoulder from Claimant’s prior rotator cuff repair surgery and that
the anchors appeared to be normal.
21. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that his diagnosis of Claimant after examination was that
of extensive rotator cuff tear with rotator cuff deficiency.
22. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that he recommended that Claimant either undergo
conservative treatment or a reverse total shoulder replacement surgery, as Dr.
Hatzidakis did not feel that rotator cuff surgery itself would be helpful for
Claimant.
23. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that he felt very confident in the chances of success of a
reverse total shoulder arthroplasty.

24. Dr. Hatzidakis disagreed with Dr. Chen’s assessment that Claimant’s shoulder
condition was caused by a pre-existing rotator cuff problem and degeneration
rather than the February 2024 injury. Specifically, Dr. Hatzidakis felt that Dr.
Chen’s analysis was simplistic, as it did not consider that Claimant was doing
very well prior to his February 2024 injury and that the MRI showed fluid buildup
in the glenohumeral joint, nor did Dr. Chen’s analysis consider the possibility of
an acute-on-chronic injury inciting the need for surgery.
25. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that his understanding of the mechanism of injury was
that Claimant lifted a fifty-pound box overhead and experienced an onset of
symptoms after the passage of several days.
26. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that one would likely have seen the cystic changes on an
X-ray had an X-ray been performed the day before the injury.
27. Dr. Hatzidakis testified that the mechanism of injury, as described, could be
sufficient to constitute an inciting event in light of Claimant’s prior history of
rotator cuff repair. He explained that a healed rotator cuff has scar tissue, and
that reinjury of that scar tissue would be more of a “stretch” and not necessarily a
“crack” or “pop.”
28. Regarding Dr. Faulkner’s recommendation for an in-space balloon in the
shoulder, Dr. Hatzidakis felt that it was a reasonable idea but that it was not likely
to restore the level of function and strength to Claimant’s shoulder as a reverse
total shoulder replacement would.
29. The Court finds Dr. Hatzidakis’s testimony credible and persuasive. Dr.
Hatzidakis is an experienced orthopedic surgeon and his testimony was logical
and internally consistent as well as consistent with Claimant’s medical history.

30. The Court notes that the dispute centers on the question of causation of
Claimant’s need for a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Dr. Chen
acknowledged that Claimant would require a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
regardless of the injury. Dr. Hatzidakis and Dr. Walker agree that Claimant
requires a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, but they attribute the need for the
procedure to Claimant’s February 20, 2024 injury. Therein lies the dispute.
31. The Court finds the opinions of Dr. Hatzidakis and Dr. Walker more persuasive
as to causation than those of Dr. Chen. Both Dr. Hatzidakis and Dr. Walker
considered Claimant’s full clinical presentation, including the fact that Claimant
had returned to unrestricted heavy work following his prior rotator cuff repair and
remained largely asymptomatic until the February 2024 lifting incident. Their
opinions account for the possibility that Claimant had preexisting degenerative
and postsurgical shoulder pathology that was aggravated or accelerated by the
industrial injury.
32. In contrast, Dr. Chen’s opinion focused on the delayed onset of symptoms and
the existence of preexisting degeneration while giving scant consideration to
Claimant’s ability to perform regular heavy-duty work without significant shoulder
complaints prior to the injury. The Court is persuaded by Dr. Walker’s explanation
that, had Claimant’s worsening condition been solely attributable to
degeneration, a more gradual decline in function and symptoms would have
been expected rather than the relatively sudden onset of pain and dysfunction
following strenuous overhead lifting. The Court also credits Dr. Hatzidakis’s
testimony that a previously repaired rotator cuff may reinjure through stretching
or aggravation of scar tissue without the dramatic sensation of a pop or
immediate acute pain, thereby explaining the delayed onset of symptoms
described by Claimant.
33. The Court finds that Claimant injured his left rotator cuff while lifting heavy
objects at work on February 20, 2024. Although Claimant had a prior rotator cuff
repair and some preexisting shoulder pathology, he was functioning well and was

largely asymptomatic before that date. The Court further finds that the onset of
Claimant's symptoms a few days after the lifting incident is consistent with the
type of injury Dr. Hatzidakis credibly described as occurring in a previously
injured and surgically repaired shoulder, namely a stretching-type reinjury of
healed scar tissue. As Dr. Hatzidakis explained, such tissue is not normal tissue,
so reinjury occurs as an in situ stretch rather than a discrete crack or pop and
may produce no dramatic sensation at the moment of injury, with pain instead
developing over the following days. The delayed onset of Claimant's symptoms
therefore does not undermine, but rather is consistent with, the causal
relationship between the February 20, 2024 lifting incident and Claimant's left
shoulder condition.
34. The Court finds that the reverse total shoulder arthroplasty recommended by Dr.
Hatzidakis is reasonably necessary to cure and relieve Claimant of the effects of
his February 20, 2024 work injury. Claimant pursued conservative treatment
without restoration of his function and, at Dr. Hatzidakis's October 3, 2024
examination, continued to exhibit significant limited range of motion, weakness,
and an inability to raise his arm overhead. Based on the credible testimony of Dr.
Hatzidakis, the Court finds that continued conservative treatment is unlikely to
restore Claimant's strength and function, that a rotator cuff repair alone would not
likely benefit Claimant given the extent of his rotator cuff tear and rotator cuff
deficiency, and that the reverse total shoulder arthroplasty offers Claimant the
best opportunity to regain strength and function and the ability to lift his arm
overhead. The Court further finds that the procedure is a definitive treatment with
a high likelihood of lasting success and that Claimant's symptoms, as presented
at the October 3, 2024 examination, justify the surgery. Accordingly, the Court
finds the recommended reverse total shoulder arthroplasty reasonable and
necessary.

35. Claimant has proved by a preponderance of the evidence that the reverse total
shoulder arthroplasty recommended by Dr. Hatzidakis is reasonably necessary to
cure and relieve Claimant of the effects of his February 20, 2024 injury.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceeding is the exclusive domain of the administrative law judge.
University Park Care Center v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637 (Colo.
App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a contrary
inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make credibility
determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at 641. When
determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other things, the
consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been
contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d

684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert testimony
is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Industrial Claim Appeals
Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is subject to
conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting part or none
of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Industrial Commission, 441 P.2d
21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Engineering, Inc. v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App.
2000).
Medical Benefits
D. The Colorado Workers’ Compensation Act (“the Act”) provides that an employer
must provide medical care “as may reasonably be needed . . . to cure and relieve
the employee from the effects of the injury.” Section 8-42-101(1)(a), C.R.S.
E. In a dispute over medical benefits that arises after the filing of a general
admission of liability, an employer generally can assert, based on subsequent
medical reports, that the claimant did not establish the threshold requirement of a
direct causal relationship between the on-the-job injury and the need for medical
treatment. Snyder v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off. of the State of Colo., 942 P.2d
1337 (Colo. App. 1997). However, the burden remains with the claimant to prove
by a preponderance of the evidence a causal relationship between the work
injury and the condition for which benefits are sought. Id.
F. The Court concludes, as found, that Claimant has proved by a preponderance of
the evidence that the reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, as recommended by Dr.
Hatzidakis, is reasonably necessary to cure and relieve Claimant of the effects of
Claimant’s February 20, 2024 work injury. Dr. Hatzidakis’s and Dr. Walker’s

reasoning for the causal relationship between Claimant’s work injury and his
need for a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is more logical and consistent with
Claimant’s medical history than the contrary opinions of Dr. Chen, as Dr. Walker
and Dr. Hatzidakis adequately considered Claimant’s pre-injury function and lack
of symptoms and presented a probable explanation for Claimant’s delayed onset
of symptoms following his injury. Therefore, as concluded, Claimant has proved
by a preponderance of the evidence that the reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
recommended by Dr. Hatzidakis is reasonably necessary to cure and relieve him
of the effects of his work injury.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant has proved by a preponderance of the evidence that
the reverse total shoulder arthroplasty recommended by Dr.
Hatzidakis is reasonably necessary to cure and relieve
Claimant of the effects of the February 20, 2024 work injury.
Respondents are liable for the reverse total shoulder
arthroplasty as recommended by Dr. Hatzidakis.
